docs.title: datarecord
docs.text:
datarecord is a Python package that stores a model's input data, and every scenario built on it, as one versioned dataset. It is for modellers who run a framework such as PyPSA over many variants of one dataset. With datarecord you keep every variant, see how each differs from its base, and read any of them back as one dataset.

A base record and two scenarios in one store, and one scenario read back A schema declares the dims entity, bus and snapshot, and the attributes p_nom over entity, p_max_pu over entity and snapshot, and marginal_cost over entity. A commit writes the base revision into one store of parquet directories, with p_nom 100 for wind1 and 50 for gas1. Two scenarios branch from base and hold only the rows they change: high wind sets p_nom for wind1 to 150, and carbon price sets marginal_cost for gas1 to 80. Reading high wind returns one record with p_nom 150 for wind1 from high wind and 50 for gas1 from base. The PyPSA tool, pandas or polars, and DuckDB SQL read that record. schema declares what a record may hold one store, parquet directories base p_nom carbon price marginal_cost only the rows it changes high wind p_nom only the rows it changes read high wind p_nom one record, deepest layer wins dim entity bus snapshot attribute over p_nom entity p_max_pu entity, snapshot marginal_cost entity entity value wind1 100 gas1 50 entity value gas1 80 entity value wind1 150 entity value wind1 150 gas1 50 commit branch branch read PyPSA tool pandas / polars DuckDB SQL

A schema shapes the base record, two scenarios hold only the rows they change, and reading high wind returns one whole record.

A modelling study often ends with dozens of variants of one dataset. One adds wind capacity, another sets a carbon price, a third swaps the demand series. Kept as full copies, the variants drift apart, and you cannot tell which rows differ without comparing every file. datarecord stores each variant as a layer that contains only the rows that differ from its parent, so a scenario costs the rows it changes. To see what a scenario changes, you read its layer.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
You build a scenario by editing a parent revision (one saved version in the store) and committing the edits. store.commit writes the edits as a new layer under that parent. When you read the scenario, datarecord combines its layers from the base down. Where two layers set the same row, the value from the layer nearer the scenario is the one you read. If many reads start from one revision, you can materialise it, so that later reads do not combine the layers below it again.

Each record has a schema, which lists the dims (the labels that values vary along) and the properties of each label. It also lists the attributes, with their dtypes and units. datarecord checks every edit against the schema and refuses it before it writes anything. For example, if the schema declares p_nom over entity, datarecord refuses a value of p_nom per snapshot. An attribute that the schema does not list raises KeyError. So every record you read from disk has the shape that its schema declares.

On disk, each layer is a directory of parquet files (a common columnar file format). You can open these files with any parquet library, such as pandas or polars, without datarecord installed. However, to read a scenario combined across its layers, you need datarecord. In Python, every read returns a DuckDB relation (a query that has not run yet). DuckDB reads the files only when you call .df(), .pl() or .to_arrow_table(). The calls are the same whether the store is on a local disk or on S3.

datarecord does not depend on any modelling framework. It needs only duckdb, pydantic and mathspec. A framework such as PyPSA reads a record through the RecordLike protocol, and a workflow engine writes one. So neither needs to know how the other works. The PyPSA tool, which translates between a record and a PyPSA network, installs as an extra.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
This example branches a scenario high off a committed revision base, raises the capacity of wind1 from 100 to 150 and reads both back:

from datarecord import WorkingRecord

w = WorkingRecord(base.record)
w.set("p_nom", 150.0, entity="wind1")
high = store.commit(w, meta={"scenario": "high"})

high.record.attributes["p_nom"].df()
#   entity attribute  breakpoint  value
# 0  wind1     p_nom         NaN  150.0
# 1   gas1     p_nom         NaN   50.0

store.layer(high.id).attributes["p_nom"].df()
#   entity attribute  breakpoint  value
# 0  wind1     p_nom         NaN  150.0

high reads as the whole record, with wind1 at 150 and gas1 unchanged. Its layer on disk contains one row. base still reads wind1 at 100.

The scenario tutorial builds this from an empty store in about ten minutes.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "datarecord @ git+https://github.com/energy-models/datarecord"          # core
pip install "datarecord[pypsa] @ git+https://github.com/energy-models/datarecord"   # with the PyPSA tool
pip install "datarecord[remote] @ git+https://github.com/energy-models/datarecord"  # with records on S3

The package on PyPI, 0.1.0a1, predates the design these pages describe, so install from GitHub until the next release. The install brings mathspec with it, at the commit that pyproject.toml pins.

Installation lists other package managers.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to datarecord are documented here. The format follows Keep a Changelog.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• select(record, **labels), exported beside settle, and Record.select return a Selection: a RecordLike holding any record at the labels named, as xarray's sel takes them. One label squeezes its dim out of the schema, its attributes' rows settled along it by the broadcast rule; a list, a slice or a partial date string keeps it. A keyword naming a multi-dim's coordinate narrows its tuples, and one naming a property narrows its subject. A label whose property names a dropped label goes, and so does a tuple naming one, until nothing more goes. Selection.select merges its labels and selects the base again, and Selection.lift puts the squeezed labels back on rows computed over the view. Attributes stay plans on the base's connection.
  • Properties. The schema has a properties section (PropertySpec) that declares, per dim or multi-dim, the values that describe one label. A record stores them as columns of dims/<dim>.parquet. A caller names a property as subject.name, as in set("bus.x", ...) and default_by keys such as {"entity.ctype": {...}}. Schema.resolve(name) returns the spec of a name, and Schema.column_type takes the property's subject. A property may share its name with an attribute, a dim or a property of another subject.
  • A property declares exactly one of dtype and one_of: <dim>. A property with one_of refers to that dim, and its values are live labels of that dim. set and add check them, and the writer checks every layer. remove(dim, labels) fails while such a property still holds a label.
  • A property that refers to a dim with one_of, on a subject in partial, a multi-dim among them, categorizes the subject. Categories select labels in flags(ctype="Generator") and in set("p_max_pu", 0.9, ctype="Generator"). default_by gives a default per category. Schema.categorizing lists the categorizing properties of a subject.
  • A dim of dtype str may declare one_of: [...], as in mathspec. Its column is an ENUM of those labels, and its axis is the list, in order.
  • WorkingRecord edits any dim: add(dim, labels, **properties), remove(dim, labels) and set(name, value, **coords). set writes attributes and properties, and a property keyword selects labels when set is called.
  • A multi-dim is a broadcast coordinate like any dim. A NULL multi-dim value means every tuple of the multi-dim, and partial may name a multi-dim.
  • Workspace holds the DuckDB database and Store holds one location. Each layer under layers/<id>/ carries its own manifest.json, a Manifest holding its id, its parent, the full schema it was written under, the files it wrote and a flat meta of strings, integers, finite floats and booleans. A read opens exactly the files the manifest lists and globs nothing. A Revision is its location and id: it compares, hashes and serialises as them, and reads its ancestry in a new process. rev.manifest and rev.meta answer from the workspace's revisions and schemas tables, which cache each manifest whole. ws.con is the cursor of the calling thread. The write and edit boundary rejects a relation from another connection or thread.
  • Writing is store.commit(source, parent=..., meta=...), with parent=None for a new root, and ws.write(source, uri, meta=...). store.claim(parent=, meta=) hands out a layer id by a create-only claim.json before any data is written, and claim.commit(source, meta=...) writes the data into layers/<id>/ and then the manifest, create-only. Until then the layer is pending and no read reaches it. A commit may add meta keys but not change a claimed one. A child whose schema is not compatible_with its parent's, or a parent from another store, is refused. store.commit(w) writes the edits of a WorkingRecord as a child of the revision it was built over, and refuses one built over anything else, naming ws.write(w, uri), which writes the flattened record. Each claim and manifest is written once, create-only.
  • A Claim serialises and pickles as its store's location and id, and reads its parent, meta and claim time back from its claim.json, so a job in another process commits it. store.claims() lists the pending layers, oldest first, with their meta, and store.revisions(meta={...}) returns the revisions whose meta holds every pair given.
  • store.cleanup(ids=[...]) and store.cleanup(older_than=timedelta(...)) delete pending layers, and refuse an id that is not pending. Nothing else deletes.
  • A store or standalone directory on s3://, through boto3 behind the datarecord[remote] extra and configured by the AWS environment. Claims and manifests are written create-only, and each writer checks its schema against its parent's manifest, which never changes, so two writers never race.
  • Tool.to_datarecord(model, con) takes the connection that its frames are planned on.
  • Removing an entity removes the group tuples that name it, and the values of a tuple go with it. An add of the name revives the entity alone. A layer that adds a tuple naming a removed label, or removes a label that a tuple names, fails at write.
  • A layer that changes an axis or a group restates it whole, in order. A label is removed where a restatement omits a label that the previous one held, and its order is the file's row order. The deepest file for an axis or group is the answer for a node. A WorkingRecord stages an edited axis or group whole, copied from the base at its first edit. A materialised node names the layer holding each axis's deepest file in resolved/dim_owners.parquet.
  • WorkingRecord.set checks that an attribute value names a label that its dim's axis, as staged, holds, for every dim, and a tuple that its group, as staged, holds. add checks that each label of a tuple is on its axis as staged, and that a value of a property with one_of is a label of that dim as staged. write_layer checks every attribute row against the final axes and groups of the layer, and every group tuple against the final axes. Each check is one DuckDB anti-join.
  • A schema is checked at load. A dim, group, group coordinate or attribute name that is not a plain identifier (mathspec's rule: ASCII letters, digits and _, not starting with a digit), starts with _, is a column that datarecord writes itself (value, layer_uuid and others, ignoring case), or differs from another name only in case fails with an error that names each offender. Based on #26 by @FBumann.
  • A manifest with an unknown key fails to load with pydantic's ValidationError.
  • The PyPSA tool declares buses and carriers as dims. A bus is a label of bus and a carrier a label of carrier. The properties of bus are carrier, type, x, y, unit and location, and those of carrier are color and nice_name. v_nom, v_mag_pu_*, co2_emissions, max_growth and max_relative_growth are attributes over their dim. marginal_price, v_mag_pu and v_ang are results over bus, and build sets them back. to_datarecord adds every carrier that a component names and carrier does not list, and stores "" as NULL. verify reports an entity attached to no bus.
  • The PyPSA tool declares the dims ctype and role with one_of, and entity.ctype, entity.carrier and connection.role as properties. partial is {"entity", "bus", "scenario", "connection"}.
  • PyPSA SubNetworks are labels of the dim sub_network, without a suffix. sub_network.carrier refers to carrier, and slack_bus is a property over sub_network. A solve that has SubNetworks restates the sub_network axis, and a solve without them restates it empty where the record has SubNetworks. SubNetwork.obj is not written, and build gives each SubNetwork a fresh one, so a built network passes PyPSA's topology code and optimises.
  • A static column that PyPSA's registry lacks is a property of its type's subject if it holds text, such as pypsa-eur's Bus.country as bus.country, or if as an attribute its name would hold two shapes, such as a custom Generator.v_nom. Any other, such as Bus.nom_max_onwind_2050, is an attribute over its type's dim. build sets either back on the types that carried it. to_datarecord refuses a custom property that types of one dim carry with different dtypes. Requirements.columns is gone, as no custom column clashes any more.
  • The PyPSA tool stores per-port results on connections like per-port inputs. p0, p1, p2 and a one-port type's p are one result p over the connection group, with a row per (entity, bus) that keeps the port's sign. q works the same way. Link.p and Process.p are p_internal, and a three-port Link's p2 is a declared result.
  • The PyPSA tool stores a Process's rate0, rate1, rate2 as one input rate over connection, static or per snapshot, and build puts each row back in its port's column. rate declares no default, so its ports default to -1 and 1.
  • The PyPSA tool round-trips multi-period networks. snapshot is a multi-dim over (period, timestep), PyPSA's own index, so a snapshot keeps its tuple whether or not a timestep repeats across periods, and a single-period network keeps a snapshot dim of timestamps. build restores snapshots, investment periods, time series and both weightings.
  • The PyPSA tool round-trips snapshot and period weightings: snapshot_weighting_objective, _stores and _generators over snapshot, period_weighting_objective and _years over period, and scenario_weight.
  • The PyPSA tool round-trips a network's shapes. A shape is the property shape_{type} of the label it outlines, its geometry as WKT: a Bus shape is bus.shape_onshore, and a component that is no PyPSA type, such as pypsa-eur's country, is a dim of its own whose labels are the shapes' idx. Such a dim is no dim of the record's own, and a network is built from no selection squeezing it. A custom text column named like a dim refers to it, so pypsa-eur's bus.country is {one_of: country}. The CRS is crs in the schema's meta, and build restores n.shapes in that CRS. to_datarecord refuses a shape without a component, idx or type, two sharing (component, idx, type), one naming no member of its PyPSA type, a custom column named shape_... or like a key dim (scenario, entity, ...) and a custom value naming no label of the dim it refers to. build names each shape "{component} {idx} {type}".
  • PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, con, results_only=True, base=record) writes a solve as a thin layer. The layer restates the SubNetworks of base and sets NULL on the results of base that it does not write again. A NULL series value on export leaves the component at its static value.
  • PyPSA.build takes any RecordLike, so PyPSA.build(PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, con)) builds the network its committed record does.
  • Record.register(name) creates DuckDB views of a record's dims, properties and attributes in the schemas name.dims, name.properties and name.attributes. Over a WorkingRecord they are live and show every edit. Workspace.unregister(name) drops them, and Workspace.registered() lists them.
  • WorkingRecord.close() drops the record's staging tables, as does garbage collection, and with WorkingRecord(base) as w: closes it on exit. A closed record raises ValueError on every read and edit. A registration of the record keeps the tables until Workspace.unregister(name). The workspace keeps its tables out of main: a revision's fold in _fold."<id>", a WorkingRecord's staging tables in _staged."<id>", and a call's intermediate tables in _scratch, so register refuses these three names. A workspace reopened on a file can unregister the registrations it lists.
  • Record.close() releases the record's folds, and with record: closes it on exit. The workspace drops a revision's fold once no open record or registration holds it. A record collected unclosed keeps its folds for the workspace's life, so a chained read stays valid. A closed record raises ValueError on every read, and Revision.record builds a new one once its cached record is closed. Workspace.registered() lists the schemas each registration held, which a reopened workspace holds for it again.
  • PyPSACollection, a tool wrapping PyPSA, writes and builds a pypsa.NetworkCollection, each member through PyPSA, as a full export or as results over base. The collection's dim is the name of its one index level. Over period it is a myopic solve, written as the one network holding every member's period, whose static values must agree among the members holding the entity active, and build gives one multi-period network per period, record.select(period=[p]). An asset a later member lacks retires there, its lifetime ending at the first period lacking it, and one held again after a gap is refused. Over any other name, a dim of the record's own, that dim is added to the schema and to partial, an attribute whose values differ across the members varies over it, and one whose values agree is written once, as declared; build gives one network per label, record.select(dim=label). A dim the PyPSA schema declares, scenario included, is refused: a stochastic network is written by PyPSA. Members hold one set of snapshots, components and custom columns per type, their axes are one union in one order, checked with their properties, which must agree, before any attribute, and every check runs when to_datarecord is called. build takes the record's dim of its own, else period, and verify reports what any member, narrowed on its own, lacks, and each dim of its own of a record declaring more than one in Requirements.unsupported_dims, a new field for dims a tool has no place for; Requirements merge with |. A record has at most one dim of its own: a collection over another is refused over a base that has one. PyPSA builds no record with a dim of its own, verify reporting it in unsupported_dims, and refuses to write results over one.
  • A collection's results over a base holding labels of its dim the collection lacks write every result at each member's label and leave the dim's axis and the SubNetworks to base. Over a base holding the dim, each member restates its series at its own label alone. A network built from the selection at one label of the dim, record.select(weather_year=2013), writes its results over that selection as that member.
  • PyPSA.build and PyPSA.verify take a selection, record.select(...), as any RecordLike. One label of period, scenario or a dim of the record's own squeezes the dim: a single-period network indexed by its timesteps holding the entities active in that period, a global constraint for another period dropped, a deterministic network, or the member of a collection at that label. A list keeps the dim, renormalising the kept scenarios' weights, and a list of periods holds the entities active in at least one of them. On top of the selection, a period left without snapshots goes, and an entity attached to a dropped bus. A selection squeezing any other dim, such as snapshot, timestep or bus, or holding no snapshot, is refused. A network's results are written over the selection it was built from, base=view, and lifted back to the labels it squeezes.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Breaking: the schema models (Schema, Dimension, AttributeSpec, PropertySpec) are frozen; derive a changed one with model_copy(update=...). Schema.digest is the sha256 of its manifest JSON.
  • Breaking: RecordLike declares con, the connection its relations are planned on; a hand-written RecordLike adds it.
  • WorkingRecord over a RecordLike that is no Record raises a TypeError naming the fix, WorkingRecord(ws.write(source, uri)).

  • Breaking: the PyPSA dialect declares every component attribute over scenario, except those PyPSA keeps the same in every scenario (*_nom_extendable, *_nom_opt, committable, lifetime, ...), so a static p_nom that differs per scenario round-trips (#28). A keyed set("p_nom", {...}) is then open in entity and scenario; pass the labels as entity=[...] or as a series indexed by entity.

  • A workspace validates each distinct schema once. Revisions sharing a schema hand out one Schema object, so reading a long lineage no longer re-runs the schema's checks per layer. A Schema obtained from a revision is shared: copy it before changing it.

  • A materialised node no longer copies its axes into resolved/dims/. resolved/dim_owners.parquet names, per dim, the layer whose dims/<dim>.parquet is the deepest at or below the node, and a read opens that file. Its has_dead column says which dims have dead labels in resolved/dead/, so a read opens those by name and lists no directory. Store.dim_owners_uri(id) is where it lives. A node materialised before holds no such file and fails the read: delete its resolved/ and materialise it again.
  • datarecord requires DuckDB 2.0. A relation it returns is a DuckDB 2.0 relation: it re-runs on every fetch and has no fetchone().

  • duckdb is capped at 2.0.0, the newest release the suite passed on.

  • The PyPSA tool melts a time series one entity at a time, so a parquet row group holds few entity names and encodes them by dictionary. The p_max_pu file of an 80,000-generator hourly network shrinks from 4.7 GB to 2.3 GB.

  • Every parquet file datarecord writes is zstd-compressed parquet v2, with a row group's dictionary capped at 4 KB, so a series' snapshots are delta-encoded and its values byte-stream-split. That p_max_pu file comes to 406 MB. Attribute files are written without keeping row order, so writing a long series no longer spills tens of GB; dims files keep theirs, which is the axis order.

  • The pypsa extra requires PyPSA 1.4.

  • PyPSA.to_datarecord takes base on a full export too, and drops the ValueError for base without results_only. Over base a static value is left out only where it repeats base's value, else the default, so a value set back to PyPSA's default over a parent holding another is written and no longer lets the parent's show through. A series, a weighting among them, repeating base's at every snapshot is left out too, one differing anywhere written whole, and an input at a port or a custom column is compared with base's, so the layer holds what changed rather than every series.

  • Groups are multi-dims. A dim declared under dimensions with over, and neither dtype nor one_of, is a multi-dim: its labels are tuples of other dims' labels, carried as one struct column named for it. Its table is dims/<multi-dim>.parquet, keyed by that column with its properties beside it; groups/ and resolved/groups/ are gone, so every record with a group is written again. record.dims["connection"] is the struct column alone and record.properties["connection"] adds role. add and remove take a multi-dim's tuples as a frame holding its struct column, so add("connection", record.dims["connection"]) round-trips, or one with a column per coordinate instead, or as a list of mappings from coordinate to label. connection.bus names a coordinate wherever subject.name stands, and set refuses it. No property refers to one. New on Schema: multi_dims, over, multi_dims_of, check_multi_dim_columns and coordinate_over; dims lists every dim but the multi-dims. The PyPSA tool declares connection under dimensions.

  • A dim with one_of has its axis derived from the list: record.dims["ctype"] is the list, and no dims/<dim>.parquet is written or read for it, nor is it named in resolved/dim_owners.parquet. The writer refuses a LayerData handing one over, a read refuses a layer holding one, and a RecordLike's axis of it is dropped where it is the list, same labels in the same order, and refused otherwise, naming a NULL, a repeated, missing or extra label, or else the order. add and remove on it are refused, and a property declared on it is refused at load. A record carrying such a file is written again. New on Schema: one_of_dims; Schema.require_listed is require_one_of. The PyPSA tool no longer writes the ctype and role axes.
  • A multi-dim in partial is categorized by a property that refers to a dim with one_of, as a dim is: connection.role categorizes connection, so a default_by keyed connection.role loads, Schema.categorizing("connection") lists role, and flags(role="output"), default_for(name, role="output") and the set keyword role="output" select by it. A role keyword picks the tuples of an attribute over connection, narrowed by a coordinate keyword, and of a property of it: set("connection.note", v, role="output") patches the output connections, as set("entity.note", v, ctype="Generator") does the generators, and ctype="Link" on it the connections of links.
  • The design pages are grouped by topic: the data model, layers, using a record, storage, frameworks and the package. Each old design page URL redirects to its new page. The usage pages are organised by task, and the API reference uses the design section names.
  • An attribute over a multi-dim carries it as one struct column named for it, with a field per coordinate, such as connection STRUCT(entity, bus). Its table is keyed by that column, and dims/connection.parquet is connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role. The PyPSA tool declares no bus attribute. A port's bus is the connection tuple.
  • The dims that a multi-dim draws on broadcast. A per-bus value with bus = NULL holds for every bus, and bus must be in partial to patch one bus at a time. WorkingRecord.set still takes bus=. Naming a multi-dim next to a dim that one of its coordinates is named for, as in dims={"connection", "bus"}, is an error.
  • entity is an ordinary dim. It broadcasts, and it must be in partial to be patched or categorized per label. entity_type is entity.ctype.
  • An attribute reaches every label that its dims address, whatever the categories of the labels. A NULL on a categorized dim reaches every label. flags(**categories) holds every attribute with a row that reaches a matching label. The PyPSA tool keeps the per-type vocabulary. build leaves out a value that its type does not take and reports it in Requirements.ignored, and to_datarecord records custom entity columns per type in the schema's meta.
  • Every layer holds its attributes in one attributes/ directory, and a result inherits through layers like any attribute. The PyPSA tool declares its outputs as attributes, and build copies them.
  • record.dims, properties and attributes return DuckDBPyRelations. Frames and LazyFrames are now Relations and LazyRelations. set, add and the writer take a relation or a pandas, polars or arrow frame, which DuckDB reads with its own scanner. They refuse timestamps with a time zone and cast a column only to a wider type of its kind. A dtype is mathspec's: float, int, bool, str or datetime.
  • The owner map's key is the partial dims and groups plus attribute. A dim or group outside partial is owned whole, so a layer that patches one connection's value restates every connection's. The PyPSA tool declares partial so that it keeps per-connection ownership. Schema.input_key is Schema.owner_map_key, Schema.input_columns is Schema.owner_map_columns, and Requirements.unsupported_keys reports "owner_map_key".
  • A Record is constructed from revision_id, sources and workspace, and reads under its last source's schema. A caller reads it through its mappings: rev.record.sources, dims[dim], properties[dim] and attributes[name]. attributes[name] raises KeyError for an undeclared attribute.
  • PyPSA.build raises TypeError for a RecordLike that is not a Record. Schema.long_columns_for and Schema.coordinates_of raise KeyError for an attribute that the schema does not declare.
  • LayerData declares no frozen, and its axes(), groups() and attributes() return set[str]. A whole Record reaches the writer through the adapter for a RecordLike.
  • The modules live in the subpackages datarecord.schema, datarecord.resolve and datarecord.store. datarecord.record is datarecord.protocols, datarecord.files is datarecord.store.files, and datarecord.layered.categories is datarecord.schema.categories. The dtype helpers moved from datarecord.duck to datarecord.schema.dtypes. Every public name imports from datarecord.
  • A WorkingRecord folds its staged layer onto the folded axes, groups and removed labels of its base, which the workspace keeps as tables. Folding the staged edits opens no file of the base.
  • A label or group tuple that one layer removes and a later layer adds again takes its place where it is added again, in a working record, a written record and a materialised node.
  • A key held twice in a dims/ or groups/ file, and a column that is neither the key nor a declared property of its subject, fail at read. write_layer refuses a restatement that orders the labels of its parent differently.
  • A reference to a removed label in a group tuple or a property is checked in every subject that a layer restates, whole. A reference that an ancestor left dangling fails the next layer that restates its subject.
  • A layer's id is its manifest's. A standalone directory is one layer with no parent, and ws.at refuses a manifest naming one, a layer of a tree being read alone through store.layer(id).
  • A value over a dim or group outside partial that names a removed label is dropped at read, including the per-bus values of a removed bus label. A materialised node keeps the removed labels in resolved/dead/.
  • attributes[name] returns the owned rows as written. A NULL coordinate stays NULL, rows of two layers may cover one coordinate, and the row order is unspecified. A consumer settles each coordinate by the broadcast rule, the row naming every dim the others there name winning. The owner map holds each layer's keys as written, plus one row naming both wherever a deeper layer's row crosses a parent's, so it grows with the rows layers write rather than with the labels a broadcast reaches.
  • A deeper layer owns only the coordinates its rows reach. A shallower row keeps every coordinate that no more specific row covers.
  • A label removed and added again takes every broadcast covering it, written before or after the removal, and no row that named it below the removal.
  • flags() counts a broadcast that more specific rows shadow at every label, and reports in varies and broadcast only the dims an attribute uses.
  • WorkingRecord.set writes a row that leaves a dim outside partial NULL out along the labels a parent row names there. The fold refuses a layer written otherwise that leaves such a crossing, naming the layer, the attribute, the dim and the key.
  • The writer refuses a dims/ file of a dim that the schema does not declare, as it refuses an undeclared attribute. A descendant declaring the dim would read its labels.
  • The writer accepts two rows that each name a dim the other leaves NULL where a row naming both is there, so ws.write(w, uri) writes a record of several layers. A set staging two rows that cross with no row naming both is refused.
  • The fold reads each layer under the schema in its own manifest. Where a deeper layer's schema is wider, the map folded so far, materialised or not, is extended to it, so a materialised node keeps counting after a descendant adds a dim to partial, and a workspace holds one fold table per node, owner_map_<id>. A layer that restates a key along a dim outside partial and omits a label its parent held there deletes that value, and a later widening of partial no longer brings it back.
  • The fold of a layer onto the map below it is one query whose joins its schema fixes, whatever named sets its rows hold (fold_layer, replacing fold_attributes). A frozen layer leaving a dim outside partial unfilled is refused when a workspace first folds it, not on every read.
  • Every Record lists every dim, property subject and attribute its schema declares, a typed empty relation where no layer holds a row, rather than raising KeyError.
  • A relation of a WorkingRecord is planned without reading a staged row, only the frozen layers' rows, so one built before an edit reads it. Every staging table exists from the start, an axis holding a copy of the base's, and rollback() empties them rather than dropping them. Each edit runs in one transaction, which also refreshes the staged owner-map rows the fold, flags() and the write read.
  • A set whose row crosses a staged row, with no staged row naming both, also stages the row naming both with its value: the later edit wins where the two meet, rather than the read failing.
  • The edits of a WorkingRecord restate an axis only where it differs from the base's, and write no attribute without rows.
  • A fold starts from the deepest proper ancestor whose fold is materialised or already held by the workspace, so a record opened on a child after a commit folds only the child's layer.
  • A Record builds the coords of its frozen layers once per thread rather than on every relation it reads, about halving a warm read of a deep record. A write checks a new layer's axes against its parent's fold.
  • The cold fold of a deep record's owner map takes about a third of the time: each layer's owner rows, the parent rows they leave and the pairs the check reads are each built once, the crossing pairs are taken from the check's, unions bind once per arm, the parts of the plan a schema fixes are built once per schema, and a layer's flags test only the attributes it holds. Revision.materialise writes the fold its workspace already holds rather than folding again.
  • A write builds each attribute and axis carrying a multi-dim once. It checks for a tuple with some fields NULL on the file it wrote, not on the source.
  • An edit inside a transaction the caller holds open on the same cursor is refused with a TransactionException that says so, since an edit runs in its own transaction.
  • Attr.resolve and Schema.resolve take labels and flags, and settle each source by the broadcast rule over labels before a rename or a computation. settle(rel, labels, flags), exported from datarecord, does the same for one relation, dropping rows that name a label outside labels.
  • A failed write, local or remote, leaves its files in the pending layer rather than staging them locally and renaming the directory into place.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• Breaking: PinnedRecord is gone. A write reads a WorkingRecord through its per-attribute plans directly.
  • Group, the schema's groups section, Schema.groups, Schema.group_columns, Schema.group_type, Schema.groups_of, Schema.group_key, Schema.check_group_columns, Schema.field_over, RecordLike.groups, LayerData.groups() and LayerData.group(), WorkingRecord.add_group and WorkingRecord.remove_group.
  • set takes no expression. Compute the new values from attributes[name] and set the frame.
  • Dimension.within is gone. Every axis is keyed by its label alone, with labels unique across the dim. A nested dim is a property with one_of on the parent dim, such as snapshot.period with one_of: period. add takes no parent keys, and Schema.axis_key is gone.
  • Traits are gone: Trait, Schema.traits, Schema.attributes_for and Schema.properties_for.
  • Schema.results, Record.outputs, Kind, set(..., kind=...) and Tool.results are gone.
  • narwhals is not a dependency. Frames and LazyFrames are replaced as listed under Changed.
  • Resolver and Revision.resolver are gone, with with_source, inputs and the enumerators axes(), groups() and attributes() of the resolver.
  • write_record, Revision.create, the source-less Revision.child(), NewChild, Directory, commit, connect, layer_dir, DATARECORD_BASE_URI, the process default connection and on_connection are gone. Record.at takes a workspace.
  • Schema.membership_keys, Schema.group_coordinates, Group.coordinates, WorkingRecord.set's indexed_by, entity_types and the entity_type dim with its member files are gone.
  • store.root, rev.child, Schema.id, the store's one manifest.json with its compare-and-swap, and the revisions/ tree are gone, as is the local staging directory of a write. A store written before has no layer manifests, so it is unreadable and is written again.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• PyPSA.build refuses a record whose rows of an attribute name several labels of a dim PyPSA's registry declares it without, such as a generator's marginal_cost over period in a multi-period record, rather than keeping one label's value, and PyPSA.verify reports the attribute in Requirements.unsupported_values. The view at one label, record.select(period=[2030]), builds, as PyPSACollection builds each period. Requirements.describe lists the field as unsupported values.
  • PyPSA.build settles an attribute's rows over every dim but snapshot that the record holds one label of, not only over entity, scenario and connection. In record.select(period=[2030]), a generator with a row at 2030 and one leaving period NULL holds the 2030 value once, rather than both.
  • Reading a property's default keeps the rows in their order. A relation filtered by several IN (SELECT …) subqueries no longer comes back reordered.
  • The PyPSA tool keeps a network's own line and transformer types. A LineType or TransformerType that PyPSA's standard library does not name is a label of the dim line_type or transformer_type, every column of it a property, and build adds it to the library. A PyPSA-Earth network, whose lines use its own ZM_330kV_bison_2bundle, no longer builds back with lines that reference a missing type. As in PyPSA's netCDF export, a library row the network has changed is not written.
  • A results layer writes a series at the network's snapshots alone, restating base's values at the others, and over a multi-period base a result over no snapshot, such as p_nom_opt, for the entities active in the network's periods alone, so base's results stand at every period, snapshot and entity the network does not hold. Writing one period's solve after another's no longer zeroes the earlier period's dispatch and capacities, and the write no longer builds base first. The network may carry any of base's investment periods, or none where it is written over the selection at one period it was built from; one carrying fewer than all is written with results_only=True, and one holding a snapshot, bus or entity base lacks is refused at the call.
  • The PyPSA tool declares a custom column of dtype object by its non-null values, so a column of bools, ints or floats holding a NaN, numpy scalars among them, is written as bool, int or float rather than failing as str, and one of mixed types is written as text.
  • A results layer restates as NULL only base's results at the scenarios, buses, entities and connections the network holds, so a re-solve of a selection keeps every other label's results. A result over no scenario, such as p_nom_opt, is one value across every scenario, so a re-solve of fewer scenarios than the record holds is refused rather than written for every scenario beside the others' joint solve. A re-solve of fewer buses or entities than base leaves base's SubNetworks, since it numbers its own over the selection alone. The results of a deterministic network over a base holding scenarios are refused rather than written over every scenario.
  • PyPSA.build of a stochastic record indexes n.shapes by (scenario, name), as PyPSA indexes every other component.
  • A results layer writing a result equal in every scenario once, with a NULL scenario, no longer restates base's rows of it at each scenario as NULL, which hid the new value at every scenario.
  • PyPSA.to_datarecord refuses a stochastic network whose scenarios hold different values of a property, such as a custom text column, rather than writing the first scenario's.
  • The writer's check that no coordinate of a file is held twice groups 64-bit hashes in passes of at most 100 million rows, so a file of hundreds of millions of rows is checked in bounded memory and spill.
  • A pointwise set leaving one of two dims outside partial NULL keeps the rest of the series.
  • A broadcast reaches every label the record holds, including one added below a materialised revision or staged in a WorkingRecord, so materialising changes no answer.
  • set refuses a frame column that the schema does not declare for the attribute, and names the column and the columns it takes.
  • A later set replaces the rows of an earlier one that it covers. A row is covered where, at each coordinate, it names the same label or leaves NULL, including labels that a property keyword or a group's fields select. set("p_nom", 0.9, entity=["a"]) and then set("p_nom", 0.95) reads 0.95 at a. The other order keeps both rows, and a reads 0.9.
  • Within one layer the more specific row wins, so a layer that holds a default and its exception, such as set("p_nom", 0.95) and then set("p_nom", 0.9, entity=["a"]), reads one value at each coordinate. A row that names a label of a dim is more specific than a row that leaves that dim NULL. Two rows that cover one coordinate, where each names a dim that the other leaves NULL, fail at write and at read, naming the attribute and the coordinate.
  • A layer with two rows of one attribute that name the same labels at one breakpoint fails at write and at read, naming the attribute and the coordinate.
  • The writer casts every column to its declared dtype, as set does. An attribute's value is stored as its dtype, and an integer column under a float attribute is DOUBLE. A column of a type that does not fit its dtype, such as a string for a datetime dim or a float property, fails with the attribute, property or dim and its dtype named. A column that holds only NULLs passes as the NULL of its declared type, in set and add as well. The PyPSA tool's static rows keep an integer snapshot.
  • A label of a type that does not fit its dim's dtype fails with the dim and its dtype named. This covers a series index, mapping keys, a keyword of set, a multi-dim's coordinate keyword, the labels of add and remove, and a value of a property that refers to a dim. snapshot="2030-01-01" on a datetime dim is refused.
  • add checks that a property value is a label of its dim, and its error says to use one of the labels where the dim has one_of.
  • Removing an entity drops the values of every group row that names it, in any field. A contract over (from, to) loses its values when either party is removed, and flags(ctype) counts such a row for the type of each party.
  • materialise() writes owner_map/inputs.parquet last and each file through a temporary name, so a node reads as materialised only when its cache is complete.
  • A map materialised under a parent's schema reads under a child's wider one.
  • An attribute whose dims gained a dim reads its earlier rows, NULL along it, where that dim is in partial too. flags() reports such rows as broadcast along the gained dim, whether it is in partial or not, and whether or not the schema declared it before.
  • Reading an attribute over a partial dim scales linearly with the length of that dim. Folding the owner map no longer compares every row with every label of the dim's axis, so the first read of a record with long series is linear.
  • A record whose layers are all written scans its owner map once for the layers that own each attribute.
  • A pickled Revision unpickles through Workspace.process() and reads its ancestry, and pickles after .record was read.
  • A standalone record's manifest.json carries an id that ws.write mints, and the workspace keys its folds by that id. A record deleted and written again at one URI, or one relative path read from another working directory, reads its own folds. ws.at resolves a local path as ws.store does and refuses a manifest without an id.
  • ws.write to an existing empty directory raises FileExistsError up front and says that a standalone record is written to a URI that does not exist yet.
  • PyPSA.to_datarecord melts a time series whose component name holds a " or is snapshot or period, and accepts components whose names differ only by case, such as Gen and gen. PyPSA.build keeps the time series of a component named snapshot, or period in a multi-period network. No name is pasted into the UNPIVOT or PIVOT as an SQL identifier.
  • PyPSA.build turns a per-connection input back into PyPSA's port columns. efficiency on a Link's bus2 connection is efficiency2, static or per snapshot.
  • The PyPSA tool skips Line.v_nom and ShuntImpedance.v_nom, which PyPSA derives from the bus, and writes no Bus.p, q, control, generator or sub_network, so a solved network exports.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page shows how to install datarecord for use and for development. datarecord needs Python 3.12 or later.

docs.title: Install for use
docs.text:
pixiuvcondapip 
pixi add --pypi "datarecord @ git+https://github.com/energy-models/datarecord"

uv add "datarecord @ git+https://github.com/energy-models/datarecord"

conda create -n datarecord "python>=3.12" pip
conda activate datarecord
pip install "datarecord @ git+https://github.com/energy-models/datarecord"

pip install "datarecord @ git+https://github.com/energy-models/datarecord"

Two extras add optional parts. Write datarecord[pypsa] in place of datarecord for the PyPSA tool, and datarecord[remote] for records on S3.

Each form installs from GitHub, because the release on PyPI, 0.1.0a1, predates the design these pages describe. The install brings mathspec with it, at the commit that pyproject.toml pins, so there is nothing to install beside it.

docs.title: Install for development
docs.text:
The repository manages its environment with pixi, which installs mathspec at the pinned commit for you:

git clone https://github.com/energy-models/datarecord
cd datarecord

pixi run test    # the test suite
pixi run lint    # ruff, prettier, taplo, typos, zizmor, reuse, mypy

The contributing guide lists the workflow and conventions.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
These pages argue for the design of datarecord: what it chose, what it rejected and what each choice costs. The rules themselves are in the reference.

  • One record: why one interface reads a directory and a tree of layers, and what datarecord leaves to others.
  • The data model: why a dim is flat, a multi-dim is one struct column, a category is a dim and a result is an attribute.
  • Layers: why a layer is written once, restates an axis whole and overrides one value per label only along partial.
  • Storage: why parquet and DuckDB, why writing a manifest creates a revision, and why writers never share a file.
  • Open questions: what the design leaves unsettled, and the questions it has settled.

docs.title: The data model
docs.text: datarecord stores each construct as flat as it can, so that datarecord and a reader apply one rule to every instance of it.

docs.title: Why a dim is flat
docs.text:
A dim is a set of unique labels, stored as one key column, and every dim is declared in the schema (the data model). datarecord fixes no list of axes, so a record with region, technology or vintage needs a schema entry and no code change.

The rejected alternative is a nested dim, keyed by its parent's label and its own. A multi-period snapshot would be (period, snapshot), and every series over snapshot would contain its period. Each check that placed a label by one column would need a branch for two. mathspec, which supplies datarecord's dtypes, gives every dimension one flat list of labels, so a tool would flatten the key anyway.

datarecord states the nesting in one of two flat forms instead. A property maps each label to a label of another dim: bus.country names each bus's country, and you read it as you read bus.carrier. A multi-dim names both in each label: PyPSA's multi-period snapshot is a multi-dim over (period, timestep), one struct column (below). With one key column either way, datarecord applies one rule to the axis, the fold key and the broadcast rule. No dim has a parent, so no series can leave a parent's label NULL.

A source whose labels repeat across parents takes the multi-dim form. PyPSA reuses its timesteps in every period, so the PyPSA tool makes each snapshot the tuple of its period and timestep. "The same timestep in every period" is then the coordinate keyword timestep=[t], which selects that tuple in every period.

docs.title: Why a multi-dim is one struct column
docs.text:
A multi-dim is a dim whose labels are tuples of other dims' labels, such as connection over (entity, bus). A multi-dim is one struct column named for it, in its axis file and in every attribute row over it.

The rejected alternative flattens the tuple into a column per field, so an attribute over connection has the columns entity and bus. The column bus then means two things: the bus of a connection, and the dim bus. A NULL there cannot mean every bus, because a connection's bus has no axis of its own to expand against. Declaring connection would stop a per-bus marginal_price from having one value for every bus.

With one struct column, the two stay apart. A NULL connection means every connection, a NULL bus means every bus, and the column's name states which multi-dim a row belongs to. A struct is a whole tuple or NULL, so a row cannot set only part of a tuple.

The other alternatives lose more. Without multi-dims, with valid pairs stated by a condition, the record loses the whole-or-NULL broadcast and the axis file that contains connection.role. A surrogate dim with one label per tuple makes you write a value against a port label and look up its entity and bus. Then the port label, not the tuple, is the value's key.

datarecord applies every rule for a dim to a multi-dim. It is declared under dimensions, has its file under dims/, takes add and remove, and may sit in partial. Each of those rules is stated once for both.

The cost is a struct at the boundary. A filter on one field is connection.entity = 'wind', which DuckDB pushes into the parquet scan as it does a plain column. A numpy-backed pandas frame has no struct dtype, so a pandas reader unnests on the DuckDB side first.

docs.title: Why a category is a dim with one_of
docs.text:
A category is a label's value of a categorising property, such as entity.ctype, which refers to the dim ctype declared with one_of: [Generator, Link, Load]. That dim's axis is the schema's list, and no layer writes or changes it (the schema).

datarecord checks a category against the schema's list wherever a default_by, flags or a selection names it. That check needs the vocabulary in the schema. If a layer could shrink the axis, a category the schema accepted could match no label in the record. The check could then run only against the folded record.

The rejected alternatives each declare the same closed set a second way. An Enum dtype beside a reference to a dim would make a closed set categorise or not by how you declared it. A one_of list that only bounds an axis a layer writes would make every PyPSA export restate the schema in a file.

A property categorises its subject only where the subject is in partial, the set of dims along which a layer overrides one value per label. A default per category is a default per label, so the owner map must assign the subject's keys label by label.

The cost is that a new category is a schema change. A custom PyPSA component type needs a new schema, not a data edit. Open questions lists whether such a dim may grow in a layer.

docs.title: Why properties and attributes differ
docs.text:
A property is one value per label of its subject, stored as a column of the subject's axis file. An attribute is the values at points over the dims it lists, stored as long rows, one file per attribute (the data model). You declare which a name is.

The rejected alternative places a value by its shape: a value over one dim goes on that dim's axis, and anything wider in a file. That groups p_nom with carrier, which both vary over entity alone. Yet p_nom is data a model optimises against and a scenario changes, while carrier describes the generator. Placing by shape also makes a compatible change move a file. Widening p_nom over scenario would move it off the axis, away from the rows earlier layers wrote.

When the schema section sets the file, the file never moves. Widening p_nom over scenario adds a column to attributes/p_nom.parquet, and earlier rows are NULL there, which means every scenario.

A property's name belongs to its subject, so bus.x, a map position, sits beside the attribute x, a line's reactance. The record-wide name rule exists so that one attribute is one file with one dtype, and a property's file is already its subject's.

The cost is a declaration that can be wrong. datarecord does not derive whether a bus's x is metadata or data, and moving a name between sections is an incompatible schema change.

docs.title: Why results are attributes
docs.text:
A solve's results are attributes like any other, with the same spec, file layout and fold. A child layer inherits its parent's results as it inherits its inputs.

The rejected alternative keeps results apart, in a second mapping, a separate directory or behind a flag on the spec. A result already has an input's spec and file shape. A split would add a branch to every reader in return for one rule about inheritance. Which attributes a solve fills is the framework's vocabulary, which the PyPSA tool reads from PyPSA's registry (tools).

datarecord runs every check on results that it runs on inputs, so a reader that joins a result to dims["entity"] never finds an orphan.

The cost is staleness. A child that edits an input keeps results computed from its parent's inputs, which describe a record that no longer exists. datarecord keeps both and leaves their coherence to you (open questions).

docs.title: What you can now judge
docs.text: You can now judge whether a construct of your framework is a dim, a multi-dim, a property or an attribute, and what each choice costs. Declare a schema shows each declaration.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text: A layer's data is written once, and the rules for overriding values, restating axes and removing labels each follow from that choice.

docs.title: Why a layer is written once
docs.text:
A layer is the data one revision adds on top of its parent, and revisions form a tree (layers). Once store.commit writes a layer, nothing changes its data. A WorkingRecord stages edits until a commit writes them as a new child.

The rejected alternative is a layer edited in place. Its descendants would then read a base that can shift under them, so branching from it would be unsafe. Every cache derived from it would also need invalidating on each edit.

With an immutable base, both problems go. Any revision can be a parent, so a scenario branches from any revision without a copy. A materialised revision has its owner map and resolved axes written under resolved/. That cache derives only from immutable layers, so it never goes stale, and a read returns the same rows with or without it.

The cost is depth. Every change is a new layer, and a read folds the layers from the root or from the nearest materialised ancestor. In a fresh workspace that fold grows with the depth of the tree until you materialise (branch and materialise).

docs.title: Why partial sits on the axis
docs.text:
partial is the set of dims along which a layer overrides one value per label. Along any other dim, a layer restates the whole extent of each key it touches. With snapshot outside partial, changing one hour of a generator's p_max_pu restates that generator's whole series.

The reason lies in how a framework reads a series. A framework that stores a constant apart from a series, as PyPSA does, cannot receive half a series. If a layer could patch one snapshot, a read would mix the layer's values at the snapshots it wrote with its parent's at the rest. That holds for every attribute over snapshot, so the rule belongs to the dim and not to each attribute.

partial and an attribute's dims set different things. dims states which dims an attribute varies over, so p_nom_opt, a capacity an optimiser fixes before the scenario is known, is declared over entity alone. partial states how finely a layer may patch. A flag on the dim alone would make every attribute vary per scenario, the first-stage decision included. Keeping the two apart lets the writer refuse a p_nom_opt row that sets a scenario.

The rejected alternatives are partial per attribute, and every dim in partial. Per attribute, the fold's key would vary by attribute, where the fold needs one fixed key. Each dim in partial widens that key, and every read of every attribute scans the wider key. A dim left out adds work once per edit, bounded by the length of its axis. The PyPSA tool puts entity, bus, scenario and connection in partial, and leaves snapshot and carrier out.

docs.title: Why a layer restates an axis whole
docs.text:
A layer that changes an axis writes its file whole: every label, with its properties, in order. A revision's axis is the deepest file for that dim on its path from the root.

The rejected alternative patches an axis label by label, with a tombstone row for each removed label. No single file then states which labels an axis has, or in which order. The order matters, because the PyPSA tool numbers a component's ports by the order of its connections. Every cache and staged fold would derive that order from the history, and a patched axis would need an owner map of its own.

With one file per axis, a cache or a staged fold always lists the same labels, in the same order, as a full fold. The writer refuses a restatement that reorders its parent's labels, so an edit renumbers no port.

The cost is storage that grows with the axis and not with the edit. On a record of 60,000 entities and 150,000 connections, a one-entity property edit wrote 0.30 MB where a label patch wrote 0.8 kB. An axis is small beside the series over it, so the cost stays small beside a solve's results.

docs.title: Why the owner map contains keys as written
docs.text:
The owner map is the fold's result: per attribute, each key a layer wrote and the layer the map assigns it to (resolution). datarecord keeps each key as the layer wrote it, NULL included. Where rows of two layers cross, the fold adds one overlap row that sets the labels of both. The map assigns that row to the deeper layer.

The rejected alternative expands each NULL to the labels of its dim when the fold runs. The map then grows with those labels, so one broadcast over 60,000 entities and two scenarios takes 120,000 rows. A materialised map also contains the expansion, so it has no row for a label a child adds later:

An owner map that expands a broadcast against one that keeps it as written The parent layer writes p_nom with entity NULL and value 50. The child layer restates the entity axis as gas, wind and solar, adding solar. An owner map that expands the parent's broadcast contains one row per label that the broadcast applied to when it was folded, gas and wind, both assigned to the parent, and has no row for solar, which came after that fold. An owner map that keeps the key as written contains one row, entity NULL, assigned to the parent, and NULL means gas, wind and solar. parent layer p_nom child layer restates entity owner map, expanded rejected owner map, as written kept entity value NULL 50 entity gas wind solar entity layer gas parent wind parent entity layer NULL parent added no row: solar came after the fold NULL covers gas, wind and solar fold one row per label fold key as written parent layer child layer owner map no row

Kept as written, the parent's NULL means every label the axis has at the revision you read, solar included. A label added below a materialised revision, or staged in a WorkingRecord, gets the broadcast value as it would without the cache.

A second alternative keeps a depth on each row and works out at every read which layer's row applies. Every read would then repeat work the fold does once, and a reader would have to handle layers.

On unusual trees, this design reads more slowly than expansion would. Where many layers override one attribute along ever different sets of dims, the crossing pairs multiply. In a benchmark of 32 layers that mostly cross each other, the first read took 1.5 times as long as with expansion. A workflow rarely builds such a tree.

docs.title: Why removing a label is a restatement
docs.text:
A layer removes a label by restating its axis without it. Removing a label also removes its values on every attribute and every multi-dim tuple that sets it (layers).

The rejected alternatives add a second mechanism: a tombstone row per removed label, or a list of removals in the manifest. The fold would have to apply it as well as the restatement. With removal as a restatement, datarecord reads every axis by one rule: the deepest file for its dim. The labels a layer removes are its parent's axis minus its own file.

The writer refuses a layer whose values, tuples or properties refer to a removed label. remove refuses a label that a property still refers to. Every row a read returns sets only labels the record has, so a reader that joins a value to its axis finds no orphan.

Along a dim in partial, a label added again after its removal gets back none of the values written for it below the removal. Under PyPSA's partial, a new bus that takes an old bus's name inherits neither the old bus's carrier nor its series. A broadcast value still applies to it, because a NULL means every label the axis has. Sibling branches keep a label that one branch removes.

docs.title: What you can now judge
docs.text: You can now judge which dims to put in partial, what an axis edit costs and when to materialise a deep tree. Edit a record shows the edits that write a layer.

docs.title: One record
docs.text: datarecord reads a directory and a tree of layers through one interface, so code that reads a record never depends on how it is stored.

docs.title: One interface over a directory and a tree
docs.text:
RecordLike is the interface a reader codes against (the record), and Record is the one class that implements it. A Record folds the layers of a revision, where each layer is the data one revision adds on top of its parent. A standalone directory folds as a tree of one layer. A WorkingRecord folds its pending edits as one more layer over its base, so the edits read back before anything is written.

The rejected alternative is a record class per form: one class for a directory, one for a revision and one for pending edits. Each would answer the same members by its own code, and every rule about rows would be written, tested and kept in step three times. With one fold, datarecord applies one set of rules to all three forms. A reader of a hundred-layer tree calls the same members as a reader of one directory. A tool builds a model without handling layers.

Even a plain directory is read through the fold, as a tree of one layer. That fold scans each attribute's rows once to build the owner map. A directory needs the scan in any case. flags reports which dims each attribute's rows set or leave NULL. No parquet footer states that for a file that mixes a series and a constant.

The protocol is structural, so a framework's own object may satisfy it too. A PyPSA network presented as a record depends on nothing in datarecord. The code that reads it cannot tell it from a Record (present a framework object as a record).

docs.title: Frameworks and workflows
docs.text:
A record sits between two kinds of software that need not know each other. A workflow produces a record and branches its scenarios. A framework such as PyPSA reads the record and builds a model. Neither reads the other's code, and core datarecord depends on neither.

A tool translates between a record and one framework. It is a module under datarecord.tools that you import explicitly. Importing datarecord pulls in no framework, and importing one tool pulls in no other (tools).

The rejected alternative is a schema that contains a framework's vocabulary, such as which attributes a component type takes and which attributes a solve fills. The writer could then enforce those lists. datarecord leaves both to the tool, because the framework's own registry already lists them. A copy in the schema would make datarecord enforce a vocabulary it never defines.

The cost is a looser record. set("p_max_pu", 0.9) writes one row that applies to every entity, loads included. The PyPSA tool leaves out and reports a value that a component type does not take. With the vocabulary in the schema, datarecord would refuse the write instead.

docs.title: One engine
docs.text:
A record exposes DuckDB relations, and DuckDB is the one engine from the fold to the reader. A relation is a query plan, so listing every attribute reads no data, and you decide when to fetch with .df(), .pl() or .to_arrow_table().

The rejected alternative is an abstraction over engines: a dataframe wrapper such as narwhals around each relation, or an engine interface inside the fold. Every record is DuckDB underneath, so a wrapper adds a conversion to each read and write, and gives a caller nothing it uses. The fold is relational algebra of real complexity. An engine interface with one implementation would be work done for a second engine that does not exist.

The cost is DuckDB as a hard dependency. A reader written in polars or pandas expressions uses SQL or relation calls instead, or fetches a frame first. No RecordLike can be backed by another engine, and a tool plans a framework object's relations on the DuckDB connection the caller passes it.

docs.title: Rows as written
docs.text:
A record exposes an attribute's rows as its layers wrote them, with each NULL coordinate left NULL. A NULL coordinate means every label of its dim, which is the broadcast rule. You, or a tool, apply the rule with settle when you need one value per point (read a record).

The rejected alternative is a read that applies the rule first. It would expand a constant p_max_pu to one row per snapshot, and DuckDB would run the expansion for every reader, needed or not. With rows as written, a value stored once is returned once. A framework that stores a constant apart from a series then tells the two apart without comparing values.

The cost is a step that the reader must run. A reader that ignores the rule takes a NULL coordinate for a missing one. Where two rows cover one point, datarecord guarantees that one sets every dim the other sets. So settle always keeps one row at each point (resolution).

docs.title: What is out of scope
docs.text:
datarecord covers the RecordLike protocol and WorkingRecord, the data model and its schema, layers and the fold, the write path, and the parquet format. An implementation on an engine other than DuckDB is out of scope, for the reasons above. So is a layer stored as anything but parquet, since a layer of a store and a standalone directory share one layout (the format).

What a framework does with a record is out of scope too. PyPSA's documentation covers how PyPSA builds or solves a network. The PyPSA tool's reference states only what the tool reads from a record and writes back.

docs.title: What you can now judge
docs.text: You can now judge whether your framework can read a record through RecordLike alone, and whether DuckDB as a hard dependency suits your code.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text: This page lists what the design of datarecord leaves open, and below it the questions it has settled.

docs.title: Should partial ever be per attribute?
docs.text: partial sits on the dim because it applies to every attribute over that dim (layers). A counter-example would be an attribute whose series a reader can take in pieces while others cannot, and none is known. Allowing it would make the fold's key vary per attribute, where the owner map has one fixed key.

docs.title: Should a later input edit invalidate results?
docs.text: A result is an attribute and is inherited, so a child that edits an input keeps results computed from its parent's inputs (the data model). Dropping them on the next input edit was rejected, because it discards work the caller may want. datarecord does not guess which results to keep, so it keeps both. You decide whether a record's results still fit its inputs. If this causes trouble in practice, the next step is a warning, which costs little to add.

docs.title: How can datarecord detect intermediate results that no longer fit their inputs?
docs.text: A results layer of the PyPSA tool replaces the SubNetworks of its base. A child that edits the topology keeps its parent's until the next solve (tools). Marking them stale needs a list of the inputs that each came from.

docs.title: Can a property's value name a label as the dim's own keyword?
docs.text: A record may label a dim by position and keep what each label means as a property, such as a snapshot's timestamp as snapshot.timestep. select matches snapshot= against the positions (selecting). Taking a timestamp there needs a rule for when select matches a keyword against a property rather than the label. PyPSA's multi-period snapshots need no such rule, because they are a multi-dim whose timestep is a coordinate keyword.

docs.title: Does a multi-dim left with one coordinate read as that dim?
docs.text: Squeezing a coordinate's dim projects a multi-dim's tuples on the others (selecting). A multi-dim left with one coordinate stays a struct of one field, rather than reading as the dim it draws on.

docs.title: Can a WorkingRecord edit through a selection?
docs.text: A WorkingRecord over a Selection would stage at the base's coordinates through lift (selecting). Today an edit goes to the base.

docs.title: Can a selection follow a WorkingRecord's edits?
docs.text: select resolves the axes it narrows when you call it, so a label a WorkingRecord adds later is outside them (selecting). Following the edits, and registering a selection as views, needs the narrowing as a plan rather than as labels.

docs.title: Should a WorkingRecord stage against a snapshot of its base?
docs.text: A WorkingRecord may sit over another WorkingRecord, and its reads include that base's later edits. Staging against a snapshot taken at construction is simpler and arguably more correct. A sequence of edits should not pick up another writer's changes mid-way. The cost is a record that can go stale.

docs.title: What else should a Record answer about its labels without handing over a frame?
docs.text: flags is the model for this: cheap derived metadata a reader plans with before opening a file, per attribute (the record). entity -> ctype is a column of the resolved axis, one frame across all categories (the format). "Which categories have live labels" and "how many labels a category has" are still frames to collect. The open part is how much one method should answer. flags answers every attribute in one call, and one method per question would add more to RecordLike than collecting the frames costs a reader. Any answer has to come from the fold, where a record's labels are settled.

docs.title: May a property referring to a dim without one_of categorise a partial dim?
docs.text: entity.carrier refers to carrier, and a default_by keyed on it would make a vocabulary of data: a category that a layer adds and removes. Today a category is a label of a dim with one_of (the schema).

docs.title: May a dim with one_of grow in a layer?
docs.text: Its axis is the schema's list, so a custom PyPSA component type is a schema change and not a data edit (the schema). That is the cost of checking a category at load. The alternative is an axis that a layer writes and the list bounds. A tool or a layer could then set which labels exist, and the dim could have properties. It costs a file that restates the schema and a category that may match no live label (DEP 24).

docs.title: May a multi-dim be over another multi-dim?
docs.text: Each coordinate of a multi-dim draws on a dim that is not a multi-dim, and datarecord refuses one that does (the schema). Nothing needs a tuple of tuples yet, and the refusal stands until something does.

docs.title: Does a functional mapping over two coordinates justify a dim?
docs.text: A zone per plant and period is a multi-dim plant_period with the property zone (the data model). The multi-dim exists only for zone, and you add its tuples before you can set the property.

docs.title: How does the published package depend on mathspec?
docs.text: Core reads its dtypes from mathspec.program. The environment pins mathspec at a commit of a pull request branch, which lasts only while the commit exists on GitHub. Before a release the pin moves to the merged commit. pyproject.toml declares that pin as a direct git dependency, which PyPI refuses in an upload, so a PyPI release waits until mathspec is published.

docs.title: How does a property that refers to a dim map onto mathspec?
docs.text: mathspec spells it as a relation, carrier_of: { key: generator, values: carrier }, declared beside the dims. datarecord declares one_of: carrier on a property of generator. Unifying the two is left for later.

docs.title: Must a default name a live label?
docs.text: bus.carrier defaults to AC in PyPSA's schema. datarecord never stores a default, so it does not check that AC is a label of carrier (the schema). A selection applies the default when it drops labels. select drops a bus whose default carrier it drops, and keeps one whose default is on no axis (selecting).

docs.title: Does bus earn its place in the fold key?
docs.text: PyPSA's partial includes bus so that a layer can patch one bus's v_nom, and every read scans every partial dim in the fold key (layers). Measuring it on a record the size of PyPSA-Eur would settle it.

docs.title: May partial name a coordinate of a multi-dim?
docs.text: partial may name a multi-dim whole. A layer overrides an attribute one value per label along each dim in both its dims and partial (layers). So period in partial does not apply to a series over snapshot, the multi-dim over (period, timestep). A per-period, myopic re-solve then restates the whole series, every other period's values included (tools). With a coordinate in partial, p would be keyed by (attribute, connection, period), and the re-solve would restate its own period's series alone. The cost is a wider fold key on every read of every attribute over snapshot.

docs.title: Do selector keywords need a qualified form?
docs.text: set refuses a bare selector keyword that is the name of a property of two dims that one attribute is indexed over (editing). The only way to say which is meant is to set per dim.

docs.title: Should Schema declare a dim with its mapping property in one call?
docs.text: A snapshot mapped to its period is a dim plus a property that refers to the period. A helper could make the two declarations one (the schema).

docs.title: May a WorkingRecord delete one value along a dim outside partial?
docs.text: A layer that restates a key along such a dim and leaves out a label its parent had there deletes that value (layers). A WorkingRecord stages the label's whole extent, so today only a hand-written layer can.

docs.title: May a layer remove a dim from partial?
docs.text: Schema versioning refuses it (the schema). To allow it, the layer would restate as resolved each key of its partial where a parent's map row sets a label of the dim. The fold would then project the dim out of the parent's map, dropping every row that set it. It would refuse a layer that leaves one uncovered (resolution). compatible_with would accept the smaller partial, and a helper would build such a layer from a revision.

docs.title: What does PyPSA#1474 land as?
docs.text: Upstream making buses and carriers indices may turn an unlisted carrier into an error, or stop "" meaning none. The PyPSA tool adds the first and stores the second as NULL today (tools).

docs.title: Can the checks at set and at write take the fold's fixed plan?
docs.text: The fold carries the set of dims a row sets as data, so its joins do not depend on the rows (resolution). set and the writer refuse two crossing rows by looping over the pairs of such sets, fetching once per pair (editing).

docs.title: Can set stage a scoped or crossing broadcast without spreading it?
docs.text: set stages a broadcast scoped to a scenario, or one that crosses another row, as one row per entity and snapshot it applies to (editing). A large edit then stages rows in proportion to the labels it applies to, not to the rows it sets.

docs.title: When does a deep ancestry materialise its map?
docs.text: A cold fold in a fresh workspace grows linearly with depth, about 0.1 s per layer (resolution). Materialising every N layers, or at a branch point, would bound it, and no policy is chosen.

docs.title: May an edit join a caller's open transaction?
docs.text: An edit runs in its own transaction, and DuckDB nests none. datarecord therefore refuses an edit while the caller has a transaction open on the same cursor (editing). Joining the caller's would lose the edit's own rollback on refusal.

docs.title: What does a schema change on a WorkingRecord do to its registered views?
docs.text: A WorkingRecord has no method that changes its schema, which changes only at commit. Such a method would refuse a change that alters a column or the fold of a registered view, or replace the views it affects. A client would then see them change (the format). Widening an attribute's dims, adding a property and adding a dim to partial are such changes. Adding an attribute or a dim would add its view (DEP 34).

docs.title: How does a SQL client settle rows?
docs.text: Registered views are raw, so a client applies the broadcast rule itself (the format). settle ported to the frontend, and a page on the raw format for SQL clients, are still to write (DEP 34).

docs.title: Who drops an abandoned registration?
docs.text: A server that crashes or forgets leaves its views and the folds they read. The registered table lists every registration with its created time, but datarecord does not yet unregister one by any rule (DEP 34). Unregistering frees the staging tables that the registration uses, so the rule also sets how long they stay (the store). A workspace reopened on a file keeps an earlier run's _staged and _fold schemas, which no record uses. Those that no registration's held column lists could be swept, but datarecord does not sweep them yet (DEP 35).

docs.title: Will DuckDB's create_view take a qualified name?
