docs.text: register calls DuckDB's private _render and _create_view, because DuckDBPyRelation.create_view takes one identifier and no nested path (storage). That caps DuckDB at the newest release the tests passed on until a public method takes a qualified name, which is to be requested upstream.

docs.title: When will DuckDB stop a read seeing part of a committed transaction?
docs.text: DuckDB 2.0 can show a reader on another cursor part of a committed transaction of about 300,000 rows or more. A reader sees such a part in 0.1 to 1% of reads. No edit can rule it out until DuckDB does, so a reader sees each edit whole only where the edit is smaller (the format). It is to be reported upstream (DEP 34).

docs.title: Who pays the cold fold of a registered revision?
docs.text: register, or the first read of a view, runs the cold fold of a deep revision, once per lineage in a workspace (resolution). It grows linearly with depth until the revision's map is materialised.

docs.title: Can a record be filtered before build?
docs.text: select(record, period=2030) returns a selection of the record at those labels, which any reader reads as a RecordLike (selecting). One label squeezes its dim, and what refers to a dropped label goes with it.

docs.title: What does a pointwise set cover when it leaves one of two dims outside partial NULL?
docs.text: Every label of the dim it leaves NULL, at the label it names. The rest of the series keeps the parent's values, whether staged, committed or over a materialised parent (resolution).

docs.title: Does a broadcast survive materialisation?
docs.text: It does. The owner map contains keys as written and the fold reads no axis. A NULL therefore means every label the axis has at the revision you read. That includes a label added below a materialised revision or staged in a WorkingRecord (layers). A map materialised before partial widened is extended to the wider key, as a map folded live is (resolution).

docs.title: Does flags need a record-level counterpart?
docs.text: It is one. flags() returns flags per record, every attribute included, and flags(**categories) per category, restricted to the rows that apply to its labels (the record). An attribute over an axis alone, or over a multi-dim outside partial, appears only in the first.

docs.title: What does a NULL multi-dim struct cover?
docs.text: Every tuple, as a NULL on a dim means every label (the data model). A constant efficiency applies to generators' connections too, and one for links alone is set("efficiency", 0.7, ctype="Link").

docs.title: What does build do with a value its type does not take?
docs.text: It leaves the value out and reports it in Requirements.ignored, as it reports an unknown type, and does not raise (tools).

docs.title: May a multi-dim in partial have categories?
docs.text: It may, by the rule a dim follows. connection.role: {one_of: role} categorises connection in partial, so a default_by keyed connection.role, flags(role=...) and the keyword role= work as they do for entity.ctype (the data model).

docs.title: What should a connection value staged without its bus mean?
docs.text: Nothing: set refuses the call (editing). A multi-dim value is a whole tuple or NULL, so {entity: dc, bus: NULL} is no value, and datarecord refuses it wherever a row comes in. The alternative, "every connection of this entity", would broadcast over part of a tuple, where a multi-dim's column broadcasts only whole.

docs.title: Can a record's relations be named views?
docs.text: They can, in the workspace's own database, one schema per registration with a nested schema per kind (storage). Over a WorkingRecord the views are created once and follow every edit, since a relation's plan never reads a staged row.

docs.title: When does a server drop the folds it opened?
docs.text: When the last open record that reads a fold is closed, unless a registration still reads it. A record collected unclosed leaves its folds to the workspace for the workspace's life, so a server closes each record it opens (the store).

docs.title: When are a WorkingRecord's staging tables dropped?
docs.text: When it is closed or collected, unless a registration of it still reads them, and then on that registration's unregister. Its tables sit in a schema of their own, which the workspace drops whole (the store).

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: A record is a set of plain parquet files read through DuckDB. A store creates each file once and never overwrites it, so the files record the order of each write.

docs.title: Why parquet and DuckDB
docs.text:
A record on disk is a directory of parquet files and one manifest.json (the format). A layer's data files contain no schema and no layer ids. So you can open attributes/p_nom.parquet as an ordinary table with any parquet library, such as pandas or polars, without datarecord installed. The same layout works on a local disk and on S3.

The rejected alternative is a DuckDB database file as the store. A DuckDB file takes one writer at a time, so parallel jobs would queue on its lock. DuckDB also cannot write such a file to an S3 bucket. A store keeps the record at its location instead. The object that opens stores (a workspace) has a DuckDB database. It contains only what can be rebuilt or lost: cached folds and the staging tables of WorkingRecords.

DuckDB is the engine because it reads parquet locally and remotely, plans lazily, and pushes a filter into the scan, a struct field's included. One file per attribute suits that, since a read of three attributes opens three files.

The cost is that a parquet file is never changed in place, so every edit writes new files. That matches layers written once. To query a record in SQL, a client runs DuckDB, directly or through registered views.

docs.title: Why a manifest is written last
docs.text:
A layer becomes a revision when its manifest is written, and not before. A write to a store runs in three steps: a create-only claim of a fresh id, the data files, then a create-only manifest.json (the store).

The reason is S3, which has no rename. A local write could stage its files and rename them into place, but a remote write that fails can leave part of a layer behind. Every read opens a layer through its manifest and reads only the files the manifest lists, so the leftovers of a failed attempt are unreachable. A remote write is then atomic for every read.

The claim exists for jobs that run for days. It makes a pending layer visible to a listing and to cleanup, which must not delete a job still running. The claim stays after the commit, so a second claim of one id fails at any time and an id identifies one revision for good. datarecord never deletes a pending layer on its own, because no timeout is both safe and useful for a job of unknown length.

The rejected alternatives each break on S3 or on a long job. Claiming an id by creating its directory is atomic only on a local file system. Dropping the claim after the commit would let a reused id fail only at its manifest, days later. A heartbeat would need a file a job rewrites for days, for a timeout no long job can meet.

Each manifest contains the full schema rather than a delta from its parent, so reading one file gives a revision's schema without walking its ancestry. A schema is small beside a layer, so the repetition costs little.

The cost is a clean-up you ask for. A failed write leaves files under its id until you call store.cleanup (store a record).

docs.title: Why relations are registered views
docs.text:
Record.register(name) creates a DuckDB view per dim, property subject and attribute, under a schema of that name in the workspace's database (the format). Any client of that database then reads the record in SQL, a client with no Python included.

Over a WorkingRecord, each view is created once and never replaced. A relation's plan does not depend on the staged rows, so a view created once returns every later edit. A client's query stays valid through any edit, with no message between the server and the client. The rejected alternative replaces a view whenever an edit adds something new. That ties the record to its registrations, and a client's query can fail between two edits.

The views are raw, as the relations are. A settled view would expand every broadcast and give up the lazy model, so a client applies the broadcast rule itself. Nested schemas keep the names of dims, properties and attributes apart, where one flat schema would need prefixed names such as attr_p_nom.

The cost is a private DuckDB call. DuckDB's public method for a view takes one identifier and no nested path, so register uses its private API. datarecord therefore caps DuckDB at the newest release its tests passed on.

docs.title: Why writers never share a file
docs.text:
Each writer claims a fresh id, writes into its own layer directory and commits by its own manifest. Every file a write coordinates through is created once, so two writers never write one file.

The rejected alternative is one schema per store, in a shared manifest that each widening write updates. Every widening write would update that one file. Each write would race on it, a writer could lose the race after writing its layer, and one branch's new attribute would widen its siblings.

With a manifest per layer, a commit checks its schema against its parent's manifest, which no later write changes. No write has a shared file to race on or retry, so two writers that widen one parent at once both commit.

The cost is that a widening applies only to the revisions whose ancestry declares it. Two sibling branches may declare one name differently, which matters when you read them side by side. materialise, which caches a revision's fold under resolved/, writes the one kind of file that is not create-only. Two writers that materialise one revision write the same content. A standalone directory has no claim, so it takes one writer, and ws.write refuses a URI that already exists.

docs.title: What you can now judge
docs.text: You can now judge where to put a store, whether to keep a DuckDB file between runs, and how many jobs may write at once.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
These pages are for a contributor who changes datarecord. A modeller who uses it needs none of them.

  • Contributing: the workflow, the conventions and how to release.
  • The package: where the code lives, and the order in which its modules import each other.
  • Design enhancement proposals: how a change to the design is argued before the code makes it, and every proposal so far.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contribution rules and conventions for datarecord. We welcome all contributors. A good place to start is the issues tagged "help wanted" and "good first issue".

By opening a pull request you represent that your contribution is your own original work and that you agree to license it under the project's MIT license.

docs.title: Reporting issues
docs.text:
Open a GitHub issue to report a bug or request a feature:

  • Report a bug and include a full traceback where there is one.
  • Request a feature.
  • Report a documentation problem.
  • Anything else.

docs.title: Development workflow
docs.text:
• Manage the environment with pixi and run every command inside it: pixi run <command> (e.g. pixi run pytest).
  • Run the test suite with pixi run test, and lint, format and type-check with pixi run lint before every commit. It runs the full lefthook hook set (ruff, prettier, taplo, typos, zizmor, reuse and mypy).
  • Lockfiles must stay consistent with package metadata: after any change to pixi.toml, run pixi lock.
  • The per-python environments (py311 … py314) mirror CI.

docs.title: Project conventions
docs.text:
• Branch off main for every change and open pull requests via the GitHub CLI (gh). A one-line commit message is fine for a small change. A larger one has a summary line of at most 50 characters, a blank line, then a body describing what changed and why. Before opening a pull request, check you have updated CHANGELOG.md, added or updated documentation, and added tests for new functionality. Give the pull request a clear summary of the change.
  • Write tests for new features and bug fixes under tests/ as test_*.py, reusing the shared fixtures in tests/fixtures.py and tests/conftest.py where useful. Run the tests after making changes and make sure they pass.
  • The reference and about pages are the authoritative design. Cite them from a docstring's numpydoc Notes section rather than restating the argument. A comment that re-argues the design is a defect. When behaviour changes, update the page, not just the code. (Notes, not References: numpydoc discourages web links under References and expects entries there to augment a docstring rather than be required to understand it. These pages are required to understand it.)
  • Documentation is mkdocs: pixi run -e docs docs serves it locally, and pixi run -e docs docs-build is the strict build CI runs, which fails on a broken cross-reference. Every pull request publishes a rendered preview to https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/pr-<N>/, linked from a comment on the pull request itself. The preview is removed when the pull request closes, and a weekly job removes any that remain. Both live in .github/workflows/docs.yml.
  • No tool import may leak into core datarecord (the package): everything framework-specific lives under datarecord/tools/ behind an optional extra.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text: A reference section that describes what the fold or a read does to rows has a figure. The docs-writing skill sets how to draw, embed and check it.

docs.title: Design enhancement proposals
docs.text:
A change to the design starts as a design enhancement proposal (DEP): a page in docs/development/proposals/ that argues for the change before the code makes it. Copy the template to dep-NNNN-slug.md under the next free number. The docs-writing skill sets the rest: the header and its statuses, the word limit, and what moves to which page when the DEP lands.

A landed DEP's argument and decisions do not change, and a change to the design is a new DEP. Its prose may be edited to the prose rules, so long as no decision, number or rejected idea changes.

Nothing outside docs/development/proposals/ links to a DEP, except the open questions page. pixi run lint fails on such a link.

docs.title: Architecture in one paragraph
docs.text: datarecord stores dimensioned attribute data with a declared schema. A record has entities (labels of the entity dim, unique record-wide) and multi-dims over them, such as connection over (entity, bus). It also has attribute values over both, and the axes those values vary along. The RecordLike protocol defines a record by the relations it exposes, whatever the storage, and a parquet directory is its form on disk. The concrete Record folds the layers along a revision's ancestry, and where two layers set the same row, a read returns the deeper layer's row. Workspace.at(uri) reads a single directory as a record, so a reader gets the same relations however many layers there are. Queries are DuckDB relations that run only when you fetch them, and the dtypes come from mathspec. Beyond duckdb, pydantic and mathspec, core depends on nothing. Keep new features consistent with this schema-declared, DuckDB-backed, lazily-evaluated design.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
The version lives in [project].version in pyproject.toml, and there is no VCS-derived versioning. CHANGELOG.md tracks user-facing changes under an [Unreleased] heading between releases.

To cut vX.Y.Z:

  1. Confirm pixi run test and pixi run -e docs docs-build pass , ideally on a release pull request.
  2. Rename the [Unreleased] heading in CHANGELOG.md to vX.Y.Z with the release date, set version in pyproject.toml, and set Version to vX.Y.Z in every DEP header reading Unreleased.
  3. Merge the release pull request, then tag the merge commit vX.Y.Z and create the GitHub release from that tag.
  4. Open a follow-up adding a fresh [Unreleased] heading to CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: AI-assisted contributions
docs.text: If you use AI tools when contributing, please read AGENTS.md for how AI-generated content must be marked and what we expect you to write by hand.

docs.title: The package
docs.text:
datarecord is a core of subpackages that import each other in one direction, and a tools subpackage that nothing in the core imports.

datarecord/
├── __init__.py        # every public name, which a user imports from here
├── duck.py            # relation helpers, transactions and shared tables
├── protocols.py       # RecordLike, LayerData, Relations, LazyRelations, EMPTY, Flags
├── schema/
│   ├── __init__.py    # re-exports Schema, Dimension, AttributeSpec, PropertySpec
│   ├── dtypes.py      # DUCK_TYPES, enum_type, enum_labels, takes
│   ├── specs.py       # Dimension, AttributeSpec, PropertySpec
│   ├── schema.py      # Schema, flag_type, LAYER_COLUMN, LONG_TAIL, DERIVED, packed, unpacked
│   └── categories.py  # selecting a categorised dim's labels, and their defaults
├── settle.py          # settle, the broadcast rule over long rows
├── select.py          # select, Selection
├── resolve/
│   ├── __init__.py    # re-exports Record
│   ├── sources.py     # LayerSource, ParquetLayer, DirectorySource
│   ├── coords.py      # Coords, mortal: folded axes and dead labels
│   ├── owner_keys.py  # owner_keys: one layer's keys as it wrote them
│   ├── fold.py        # Fold: a revision's folded axes, owner map and reads
│   ├── owner_map.py   # fold_layer, uncovered: the owner map folded one layer at a time
│   └── record.py      # Record
├── mutable.py         # WorkingRecord, StagedSource
├── store/
│   ├── __init__.py    # re-exports Workspace, Store, Claim, Revision, Manifest
│   ├── files.py       # Files, LocalFiles, RemoteFiles
│   ├── manifest.py    # Manifest, LayerFiles, ClaimFile
│   ├── cache.py       # materialise, materialised, sources_to_read
│   ├── write.py       # write_layer, layer_data
│   └── store.py       # Workspace, Store, Claim, Revision, ancestry
└── tools/
    ├── __init__.py    # imports no tool module
    ├── base.py        # Tool, Schema, Attr, Requirements, UnsupportedRecordError
    └── pypsa.py       # PyPSA, PyPSACollection

docs.title: The import order
docs.text:
Runtime imports follow the order duck → schema → protocols → settle → select → resolve → mutable → store → tools. A module imports at runtime only from modules earlier in that order or in its own subpackage. An import under TYPE_CHECKING may point the other way, as when resolve/record.py names Workspace in an annotation.

A subpackage's __init__.py re-exports its public names, and datarecord/__init__.py imports them from there, so a user imports from datarecord alone. Code inside the package imports a name from the module that defines it, so no internal import runs through an __init__.py.

Some modules are one module because their classes need each other at runtime:

  • store/store.py contains Workspace, Store, Claim and Revision. Claim and Revision are pydantic models with a field of type Store, and Store constructs both.
  • mutable.py contains WorkingRecord and StagedSource, because StagedSource reads private members of WorkingRecord.
  • protocols.py contains the protocols apart from Record, because resolve/fold.py imports Flags, and a module that defined both would import the fold back.

store/ sets where a connection and a location come from, so duck.py contains no state. The modules in resolve/ take a Workspace and read workspace.con on each call, so each call runs on the calling thread's cursor.

docs.title: Core and tools
docs.text:
Code that refers to a modelling framework lives under datarecord/tools/, and no other code may refer to one. So the core depends only on duckdb, pydantic and mathspec.

A tool is one module per framework, datarecord/tools/<name>.py, and a caller imports it explicitly:

from datarecord.tools.pypsa import PyPSA

Neither datarecord/__init__.py nor datarecord/tools/__init__.py imports a tool module. Importing the core pulls in no framework, and importing one tool pulls in no other. A tool's framework is an optional extra, such as datarecord[pypsa].

See also

Tools describes what a tool reads from a record and writes back, and contributing the workflow for a change.

docs.title: Design enhancement proposals
docs.text:
A design enhancement proposal (DEP) is a page that argues for one change to the design of datarecord before the code makes it. A key of the schema, the format on disk, the RecordLike protocol, the fold and the API each change through a DEP. Its reader is a contributor who was not in the discussion.

The contributing guide sets the process: how to number and write a DEP, its statuses, and what moves where when it lands. To start one, copy the template.

Once a DEP has landed, it stays as the record of the argument. Where the pages it landed in and the DEP differ, follow those pages. A number is never reused, even when its PR closes, so the table has gaps.

docs.title: DEP 1: dims, mappings, groups and traits
DEP 1: dims, mappings, groups and traits
docs.text:
DEP 1 Title dims, mappings, groups and traits Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented (2026-08-16) Created 2026-08-15 Version v0.1.0a1 Superseded-By DEP 16 (its traits part), DEP 20 (its entity tombstones, and an order the fold generates)

The design landed in the data model, the schema, the record format and the fold. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages. DEP 2 absorbs the on mapping into groups as into.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: AttributeSpec.dims becomes the one way to address an attribute. The component name becomes a dim, entity. Attributes are declared flat, types subscribe through traits, groups replace connections, mappings classify one dim by another, and Dimension.keys goes.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
An attribute that belongs to no component type has nowhere to live. A snapshot weighting varies by snapshot alone, and Schema.attributes is keyed by component type. The PyPSA tool stores it as an undeclared objective column on dims/snapshots.parquet and recognises it by name.

Such a column has no dtype, default, unit or description, appears in no flags and does not fold across layers. Scenario weightings have the same problem. Yet name is an axis like snapshot, and only looks structural because the schema nests attributes under it.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
Four mechanisms declare where labels come from. within stays a fifth, distinct from a mapping.

Mechanism Declares Lives in dim an axis of labels dims/<dim>.parquet, with any attribute addressed by it alone mapping each label of the dim it is on has one of its own its own axis file, plus a column on the classified dim's file group which tuples over several dims exist its own table, which subsumes connections trait which entities an attribute applies to a subscription on the component type
  • entity is a declared dim. dims/entity.parquet has the columns entity | component_type | deleted, so a label is unique by construction, entity -> component_type is a column read, and a deletion has one home.
  • order_key is a column of the owner map and never of a layer's file, and persists only where a node's maps are materialised. The fold computes it per layer as max(parent) + row_number() OVER (ORDER BY _row), before the union. Nothing sorts eagerly: a reader applies ORDER BY order_key. A table that gains rows across layers has it, and an ordinary dim does not.
  • dims/components/<Type>.parquet contains only the values that vary over nothing, partitioned by type because each type has its own attribute vocabulary.
  • Schema.attributes is flat: one spec per attribute, one file, one dtype. AttributeSpec.bus is deleted.
  • An attribute whose dims contain exactly one addressing coordinate is a column on that thing's table. Any other attribute is long rows in inputs/<attr>.parquet. varying means "has dims beyond its address". role becomes AttributeSpec(dtype="VARCHAR", dims={"connection"}), a column of the group's table.
  • A trait is a named set of attributes. Schema.attributes_for(ctype) returns the union of a type's traits and its own attributes. Two traits that declare one attribute with different specs fail validation.
  • A group's over maps coordinate name to dim. An attribute over a group has the group's coordinate names as columns and never the group's name, so two groups may share a coordinate set. A group in dims expands to its coordinates, and an attribute not addressed by a coordinate writes NULL there.
  • bus is no longer structural. The long schema's fixed prefix is entity | attribute | breakpoint | value. entity is the one dim whose name the format fixes, because the component types partition it.
  • A NULL group coordinate broadcasts over the group's rows, not the product of its dims.
  • The protocol's connections becomes groups, keyed by group name. dims includes entity and every mapping. shape() joins flags(ctype), keyed by attribute and record-wide, with dims, broadcast, breakpoints and types.
  • A mapping is a Dimension with on, and is a dim. It has its own axis file, is not in partial, never scopes existence, and is not denormalised down a chain. Dims and mappings share one namespace, so a name declared twice fails validation. A many-to-many classification is a group. The record does not project an attribute across levels of a mapping.
  • Dimension.keys is deleted and nothing replaces it. An entity or a group row exists or does not, and neither varies along another dim.

So {"entity"} is a column of dims/components/<Type>.parquet, {"scenario"} a column of dims/scenario.parquet, and {"entity", "snapshot"} long rows.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Nesting attributes under a type lets two types declare one attribute with different dtypes over one file and one value column. Nothing rejects that, and the read is silently wrong. Flat declaration makes the case unrepresentable.

datarecord keeps traits because the shared sets are measured from PyPSA's registry, and lpspec dispatches an equation on a trait. Someone has to write traits and keep them up to date.

over maps names to dims because a corridor between two entities needs two columns, from and to, from one dim. The fold's key stays one tuple, the union of plain dims and coordinate names.

within does not subsume bus, because groups do it. The recorded blocker was that bus inverts the NULL rule. Expansion already depends on whether a dim is in dims ∩ partial, so bus is not an exception.

The fold assigns order_key before the union, because row_number() over what UNION ALL emits has no defined order. datarecord keeps it for a group because a framework numbers positional ports by it, and a reshuffle would move a connection's attributes to another port.

A mapping has its own axis file so that it has an order and a place for data such as co2_budget. A denormalised chain would let a layer that restates dims/state.parquet leave every bus's country stale. A generator's country follows from its bus, so a mapping cannot scope existence.

within scopes a dim's labels per parent, so the axis key is (period, timestep). on classifies another dim with one flat set of labels. Neither can express the other's case.

keys cannot survive groups, because KeyKind lists a "connection" table that groups delete. A replacement was drafted and removed, because its meaning is unsettled. Dropping a mechanism whose meaning is unresolved is better than carrying it into a redesign under a new name.

Flattening brings out three vocabulary questions that the storage already had:

  • One concept has one name. PyPSA's p_nom, s_nom and e_nom become capacity, so investable can contain the capacity itself. The record's vocabulary is not PyPSA's.
  • The tool renames attributes through its schema on the way in and out.
  • Bus.x and Line.x already collide in one inputs/x.parquet, and now fail at declaration. A tool prefixes, renames or refuses in verify.
  • Link.efficiency2 collapses to a stem over the connection group, and bus0 and bus1 become rows of the group.

Every step is incompatible: version bumps once, a record is rewritten, and scenario-scoped membership becomes unrepresentable.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
attributes = {
    "p_max_pu": AttributeSpec(
        dtype="DOUBLE", dims={"entity", "snapshot", "scenario"}, default=1.0
    ),
    "efficiency": AttributeSpec(
        dtype="DOUBLE", dims={"connection", "snapshot"}, default=1.0
    ),
    "objective_weighting": AttributeSpec(
        dtype="DOUBLE", dims={"snapshot"}, default=1.0
    ),
}
groups = {
    "connection": Group(over={"entity": "entity", "bus": "bus"}),
    "corridor": Group(over={"from": "entity", "to": "entity"}),
}

objective_weighting lands on dims/snapshot.parquet, declared and typed.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Flat attributes and traits. Only the manifest changes.
  2. Singular parquet names, dims/<dim>.parquet, which fixes dims/buss.parquet.
  3. Mappings, which the fold treats as dims.
  4. entity as a dim, with no order column. The long schema's columns become schema-derived.
  5. Groups, with the fold's key schema-derived, and keys deleted in the same step with KeyKind, _keyed, component_dims, connection_dims and the tests of scenario-scoped existence. This is the one functional regression, and should not land before the existence question is answered.
  6. The protocol: connections becomes groups, and shape() joins flags.
  7. WorkingRecord can address attributes with no entity and groups of two coordinates.

Two breaks do not announce themselves. At step 4, add routes by varying, which turns true for dims={"entity"}. And _overlay would put entity in broadcast, so it would apply a staged row with a NULL entity to every entity and overwrite each value. The fix derives the key's address coordinates instead of spelling them, and a group coordinate belongs in the key.

The PyPSA tool's trait table and its p_nom -> capacity renames must exist before step 1 ships against a real network.

On implementation, shape() was not built, so flags(ctype) stands alone. set has no bus= parameter: every coordinate but entity goes through **dims, so a group of two coordinates can be addressed.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• A separate payload declaration on Group or Dimension: two ways to say one thing.
  • Trait roles: one more indirection for what the tool's schema already records.
  • Qualified names or per-type namespaces: both put the component type back into an attribute's address.
  • Widening flags to record-level attributes: flags is per type by construction.
  • A field declaring per-dim existence: drafted, then removed, because its meaning is unsettled.
  • Last-wins for conflicting traits: a conflict fails validation instead.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Whether flags(ctype) survives, or becomes shape() filtered by types.
  • Outputs are out of scope.
  • Whether existence may depend on a dim, as a generator built in high and absent in low. If entity varies over scenario and connection does not, one connection row cannot be both kept and dropped. The fold drops it, pinned by an xfail. A validator could forbid a group whose existence dims are coarser than those of entity, which is a decision and not a default.

Three questions follow from the last, and a "no" to the first deletes the whole area:

  1. Is per-dim existence needed, or does an active-style attribute cover it? PyPSA has both.
  2. If needed, may tables disagree, or is uniformity enforced?
  3. If they may disagree, what does the coarser table's row mean, and can the fold compute it?

docs.title: DEP 2: groups, one construct for classification and sparsity
DEP 2: groups, one construct for classification and sparsity
docs.text:
DEP 2 Title groups, one construct for classification and sparsity Author Jonas Hörsch Status Superseded (2026-10-26, implemented 2026-09-01) Created 2026-08-27 Version v0.1.0a1 Superseded-By DEP 23 (its groups, which become multi-dims)

The design landed in the data model and the record format. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: A group with an optional into replaces both the group and the on mapping of DEP 1. Every group is one file, groups/<name>.parquet. into declares that each tuple of over has one label of a declared dim. The group is then checkable, and a reader can aggregate along it with by=.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
The schema has two ways to declare "which tuples over dims exist". You state it directly with a Group, or with Dimension(on=...) for the case where each label appears once. The two are stored, addressed, aggregated and validated by different code, for the difference of one uniqueness constraint.

A modeller pays for this when writing maths. Summing along a mapping is GROUP BY country, while to sum along a group you must say which coordinate survives. GAMS, Calliope and PyPSA all use one construct for both, so the split is datarecord's and not the domain's.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
• groups absorbs Dimension.on. Dimension.on, Dimension.mapping and Schema.mappings_on are deleted.
  • over declares the coordinates, as a list where coordinate names equal dim names, or as a dict where they do not. The list is sugar for the dict.
  • into is the name of a declared dim. Each tuple of over has exactly one label of into, checked on write. into may sit over several coordinates, such as over: [bus, scenario].
  • Without into, a group is a set of sparse tuples, is not a dim and never appears as a column.
  • A group may share its name with a dim. The rule against the two colliding is dropped.
  • In an attribute's dims, X is the dim X if one is declared, and otherwise the group X expanded to its coordinates. into is not consulted.
  • Every group's rows are groups/<name>.parquet, keyed by its coordinates. The dims/<group>/<Type>.parquet split and the mapping column on the classified dim's axis file are gone, and Schema.group_columns no longer leads with entity_type.
  • A reader collapses coordinates in its maths language with over=<group>[coords], whose brackets list what goes. The bracket is required on every over= over a group of several coordinates. by=<group> keeps the group's into dim and collapses all of over, and exists only where into is declared.
  • A NULL group coordinate still means the group's rows, and a group in dims still expands to its coordinates. The record does not project across levels. within and traits are unchanged.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
into is the declaration that was missing. Without it, a group can only happen to be single-valued, and a duplicate row is an error the schema has no name for. GAMS and Calliope both leave functional lookups undeclared, so every sum silently counts a duplicated label twice. datarecord's schema is meant to make the shape of data checkable, so datarecord should close that gap.

into must be a declared dim because a functional group needs the axis file. It gives the labels an order and a place for a per-country CO2 budget. The argument for the axis file in DEP 1 stands unchanged.

Sharing a name is the natural spelling for a group with into. dims: [country] resolves to the dim and by=country to the group, so a rule against sharing would force a name like country_map. datarecord resolves dims first when it addresses an attribute, so the case without into is not ambiguous either. The cost is that a shadowed group without into loses its only spelling in dims without an error.

group stays the word, because country groups buses too. GROUP BY, PyPSA's group_constraints and Calliope's group overload it, so prose about aggregation says which is meant.

One file per group gives the no-denormalisation property of DEP 1 for free: a layer that restates a group restates one file. The <Type> split put a Link's and a Line's connection rows in two files with identical keys. It had no type to split on for corridor or contract.

A relation between two entities, such as a contract between a seller and a buyer, gets a file, an aggregation spelling and an optional into. over: [entity], into: parent declares a hierarchy of components, which Dimension.on could not express.

by= and over= are two keywords because they mean opposite things. A bare over=country read as "keep country" would give one keyword two senses. The bracket is required because a functional group needs it wherever a coordinate must survive that by= would collapse: over=country[bus] on over: [bus, scenario] keeps a per-scenario country total. Inference from the enclosing scope also fails under nesting. In sum(sum(x, over=connection), over=siting), the inner sum would collapse bus, which the outer sum needs, and return the right shape with the wrong number.

The change needs a rename across the tree and a format migration with no reader of both layouts. Reading a bus's country becomes a join instead of a column read. WorkingRecord's kind= and the CONNECTION constant in mutable.py stop naming one group specially.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
groups:
  country:
    over: [bus]
    into: country
  connection:
    over: [entity, bus]
  corridor:
    over: { from: bus, to: bus }
attributes:
  efficiency:
    dims: [connection, timestep] # entity | bus | timestep
  co2_budget:
    dims: [country] # the dim

sum(x, over=connection[entity]) keeps bus, and sum(x, by=country) keeps country.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
• into is sugar resolved at parse: Group(over=["bus"], into="country") returns ["bus", "country"] from coordinates. The file layout, the fold's key and dims expansion read coordinates and never branch on into.
  • The model keeps into for the uniqueness constraint, whose key is coordinates minus into, for by=, and to write the manifest back as authored.
  • A validator beside the over check refuses an into that is no declared dim. Otherwise dims: [country] would expand silently to bus | country. The collision check goes.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• A group whose into is a label set of its own: it loses the axis file.
  • Keeping the rule against a group sharing a dim's name: a lint naming the shadowed group is the better answer.
  • Restricting into to one coordinate: needed only if a functional group were a column on an axis file, which is not kept.
  • Overloading over= for "keep": one keyword would have two senses.
  • Inferring the bracket from the enclosing scope: wrong under nesting.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Whether a shadowed group warrants a lint at load.
  • Whether a group's rows are checked against the labels of its coordinate dims, as GAMS does for a relation.
  • Whether every aggregation a reader needs factors into a declared dependency plus a reader's operation. This is untested against a second reader.

docs.title: DEP 3: trait switches, a trait a component opts into
DEP 3: trait switches, a trait a component opts into
docs.text: DEP 3 Title trait switches, a trait a component opts into Author Jonas Hörsch Status Superseded (2026-10-20) Created 2026-08-27 Superseded-By DEP 16

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: A trait gains an optional switch: a boolean attribute over entity that turns the trait on per component. A value of a switched trait on a component whose switch is false is refused on write. It shares a direction with DEP 2 without depending on it. With a switch, you declare what a record states about a component, instead of encoding it in a type name.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
A trait is scoped by entity type alone. A distinction finer than a type, or one in a record with no types, has nowhere to go. In PyPSA a generator may be unit-committed, and only then do start_up_cost, min_up_time and ramp_limit_start_up apply to it. The schema can only declare them on every generator. A record then has them on 3000 generators to describe the fifty that are committable. The same shape recurs for cyclic_state_of_charge, e_cyclic, link losses and extendable capacity.

Most traits are scoped correctly by type: every generator is dispatchable. A trait scoped by data, such as country, is rightly banned, because attributes_for must answer from the schema alone. A switch is a declared attribute with a dtype and a default, and both vocabularies it selects between are known before any row is read.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
• A trait narrows two ways, both optional. on lists the entity types that have it, and without on every type has it. switch is an attribute that turns it on per component, and without switch every component of those types has it.
  • switch is a declared attribute whose dims are exactly {"entity"}, and its dtype is bool.
  • The switch joins the trait's attributes at parse. The author does not list it.
  • The switch is an ordinary attribute, stored where an attribute over entity alone is stored. Its default applies where it is unset, and false is the one to declare.
  • The trait does not narrow its own switch. Every type the trait is on has the switch attribute.
  • on applies first and switch second, and neither changes what the other means.
  • attributes_for(ctype) includes a switched trait's attributes, because it answers which attributes a type may have.
  • A value set on a component whose switch is false is refused on write.
  • record.entities_with("committable") returns the components whose switch is true.
on switch Applies to no no every component of every type yes no every component of the listed types no yes the components whose switch is true yes yes those of the listed types, switch true

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
The third row of the table is the new case. A record that declares no types can still say that some components are committable, which the type scope could never express. A switch is a validation and query mechanism, not a change to the vocabulary. It turns "3000 generators with a mostly NULL min_up_time" into "fifty may, and the fifty-first is a mistake".

Listing the switch in attributes as well as in switch would be two ways to say one thing, so datarecord completes the trait at parse. A trait that gated its own switch could never be turned on. A switch belongs only where components of one type differ: on dispatchable it would be a column of true with no information.

The design has three costs. A trait now cuts by type and by component, and a reader holds both, though they compose in one direction. The writer reads the switch column to validate a value, a join against dims/entity.parquet on a path that already reads it. And a record may still have committable as a plain attribute and ignore the trait, so two spellings exist.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
traits:
  committable:
    attributes: [start_up_cost, shut_down_cost, min_up_time, ramp_limit_start_up]
    on: { entity_type: [Generator, Link] }
    switch: committable
attributes:
  committable:
    dtype: bool
    dims: [entity]
    default: false

The committable trait applies to no Store whatever its switch is, and to a generator only where its committable is true.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
• At parse, Trait(attributes={...}, switch="committable") folds the switch into attributes. The model keeps switch, as DEP 2 keeps into.
  • attributes_for reads switch to exclude it from its own trait's narrowing. The write-time check reads it to find the gating column.
  • The existing trait validator checks switch as it checks a bundled attribute, plus that its dims are {"entity"}.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• Scoping a trait on data such as country: attributes_for must answer from the schema alone.
  • A switch over entity and scenario: coherent, but what a coarser row means is unsettled, as for existence along a dim in DEP 1. Worth revisiting only with a case.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• An Enum switch with a switch_value field, such as capacity_mode of fixed, extendable or committable. Deferred because no tool needs it, and a bool switch is its case with the label fixed at true.
  • Whether attributes_for needs a per-entity counterpart. This is the same shape as the open question about a record-level flags.

docs.title: DEP 4: staging as a layer, one fold, two sources
DEP 4: staging as a layer, one fold, two sources
docs.text:
DEP 4 Title staging as a layer, one fold, two sources Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented (2026-09-01) Created 2026-09-01 Version v0.1.0a1 Superseded-By DEP 20 (its per-label axis fold, and partial as how many labels an axis layer carries)

The design landed in the fold and WorkingRecord. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: The fold reads each layer through a LayerSource, so parquet layers, a plain directory and a WorkingRecord's staged edits fold the same way. The staged edits become the last source. The fold is materialised up to the last frozen source and stays a relation after it. pending goes, and result attributes are declared in the schema.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
The editing page says a set of pending edits is a layer, an unwritten one. The code does not deliver that. mutable.py reimplements the algebra of layered/resolve.py three times over, and each copy drifted from its twin:

  • The overlay: fold_inputs drops each parent row whose key the layer also has, then adds the layer's rows. _overlay, _entity_union and _group_union do the same against staged rows. That makes five sites for one rule.
  • The flags: the fold computes varies and broadcast in its ownership GROUP BY, and _flags_arm computes them again over the staging tables.
  • The collapse: _latest_per collapses staged rows by _seq, and the fold collapses layers by depth.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
• A LayerSource hands over one layer's own rows as the layer would be written. It has layer_id, frozen, and one member per file: axes(), axis(dim), entity_type(name), group(name), attribute(name, kind) and all_attributes(kind). A member returns None where the layer wrote nothing. Kind is Literal["inputs", "outputs"].
  • entity is an axis, read through axis("entity"). all_attributes exists only for inputs/ and outputs/, because their files share one key, and returns the union unprojected. attribute(name) reads one file with its own columns, since a padded column is ambiguous under the broadcast rule.
  • axes() lists a directory once, replacing a probe per declared dim.
  • Everything the fold does to rows stays in the fold: padding, broadcast expansion, the ownership aggregate and order_key. _seq collapsing and tombstones stay behind the source.
  • ParquetLayer, DirectorySource and StagedSource implement the protocol. NodeCache folds a list of sources, root first. A WorkingRecord is sources + [StagedSource(self)].
  • The fold is materialised up to the last frozen source, and everything after it stays a relation. Nothing needs invalidating. NodeCache.dims becomes a plain property that caches the frozen prefix's axes.
  • A staged axis edit merges per column, so two set calls on one axis do not blank each other.
  • As rows are staged, _complete_owned_whole carries the parent's rows that complete each key an edit named along the dims not in partial. A staged row that leaves such a dim NULL is excluded. staged_only() then contains what gets written.
  • WorkingRecord.pending is removed.
  • Schema declares result attributes beside inputs. outputs still lists what a layer contains, as attributes does. long_columns_for loses its fallback, and value_hint retires with _value_dtype and _scalar_dtype. A result row may still carry a component that the record never declared.
  • A base that is neither layered nor a directory is out of scope, and _base_revision refuses it.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
A written layer's extent along every dim outside partial is already complete. The fold drops each parent row whose key the layer also has, and loses nothing. Without that completion, the fold would drop the base's whole series for one staged point. Completing as rows are staged removes the difference, so the algebra needs no second copy. The completion runs per insert, because it is scoped by the keys an edit named.

Removing pending is cheaper than marking carried rows in every staging table. After completion, a one-value set on a thousand-snapshot attribute would report a thousand pending rows. To see what the record contains, you read it.

Stating the cache rule over frozen, not as a mode, means a second staged layer needs no new code. Truncating at a materialised ancestor becomes building fewer sources.

The design has these costs:

  • A protocol in layered/ that mutable.py and directory.py implement structurally. mutable.py keeps importing from layered/ only inside function bodies, to avoid a cycle.
  • A tool must declare a result before attaching it, though PyPSA's SubNetwork exists only after a solve. The tool declares its result vocabulary up front or amends the schema at solve time, and Schema.compatible_with decides whether old layers survive.
  • set reads the base the first time it touches an attribute with a dim outside partial.
  • A read with pending edits re-folds the staged step every time.
  • NodeCache's invariant becomes "nothing up to the last frozen source can go stale".

The change deletes about 250 lines from mutable.py, and the _collapsed_* helpers move into StagedSource. It has no format change of its own.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
Three changes landed first, each in its own PR:

  1. components becomes entity_type across the API and on disk.
  2. Axis discovery by glob in resolve_dims and fold_axis.
  3. order_key becomes a struct (depth, row). A layer's numbering no longer depends on its parent's values, which removes a subquery that would re-run on every read with a live tail. A key restated deeper keeps its first (depth, row). DuckDB orders structs by field, so ORDER BY order_key works unchanged, and a child of a materialised parent takes max(order_key.depth) + 1. This one is a format change.

Steps 0 to 4 added the identity spike and extended the both fixture to read one record four ways. They moved the completion out of commit, declared results and added LayerSource. Steps 5 to 7 landed in two commits. The build added two things:

  • ResolvedLayer, a third source for a materialised ancestor, whose axes and owner map come from resolved/ and whose own rows still come from its layer.
  • _axis_layer merges per column on an axis in partial too, because the fold keeps a label's whole row from the last layer that wrote it.

Step 8, sharing the flags aggregate with DirectoryRecord, was dropped. With _flags_arm gone, the two aggregates share three bool_or lines, and a helper's parameters would outweigh them.

Two things stay unfixed by choice. attributes_of re-executes under a live tail, bounded by the map. commit still needs a revision, so a WorkingRecord over a DirectorySource is readable but cannot commit.

Over both bases, the tests check that an unstaged WorkingRecord reads like its base and a staged one like its commit. A second set after a read is visible. One more test asserts that the grouping grain of the fold's flags is invisible after attributes_of unions them.

Measured over a 20-layer unmaterialised ancestry of the ac_dc network, best of five:

Operation Time deep read, nothing staged 2.4 ms deep read, one staged edit 61 ms set, first touch of an attribute 166 ms set, again on the same attribute 16 ms set, again, all dims in partial 10 ms directory flags, scanned ~0 ms directory flags, through the fold 12 ms

Of the three performance claims, two hold. A read after a set takes one more fold step, but against a cached base, so 61 ms against 2.4 ms. In a repeat set, the completion takes about 5 ms. A WorkingRecord over a directory folds flags where a bare one scans and memoises them. A repeat set first measured 188 ms, because its validation rebuilt name-to-type from member frames. Reading the owner map instead brought it from 157 ms to 10 ms. Building StagedSource's collapses on 50k staged rows over 500 entities and 20 periods takes about 1.4 ms to plan and 4.3 ms to run. tests/test_scaling.py covers none of this.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• Marking carried rows apart from edited ones to keep pending: a second row class in every staging table.
  • A combined read across axes or groups: each folds on its own key.
  • A raw-rows member on the source: _seq is staging state, and the fold must not see it.
  • A shared overlay(older, newer, on) helper: no second caller remains.
  • Synthesising a source from a framework's object: it rebuilds the layer format, and all_attributes would materialise the whole record per read.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Memoising StagedSource's collapses on the highest _seq staged, which is local to the source.
  • Whether materialise could run over a staging area, freezing the tail into the prefix.
  • Whether the commit path collapses further. DEP 5 made flattened() equal to self in every field but entity_type. staged_only() stays open, because an adapter deletes about as much as it adds without a second caller.
  • Whether a DirectoryRecord gains a map. DEP 5 resolves this the other way: it deletes DirectoryRecord, and a directory reads through the fold more cheaply.

docs.title: DEP 5: one Record, over a NodeCache
docs.text:
DEP 5 Title one Record, over a NodeCache Author Jonas Hörsch Status Superseded (2026-10-21, implemented 2026-09-01) Requires DEP 4 Created 2026-09-01 Version v0.1.0a1 Superseded-By DEP 19 (its Record over a NodeCache)

The design landed in the fold and the RecordLike protocol. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: DirectoryRecord is deleted, because a plain directory is a DirectorySource and folds like any layer. LayeredRecord becomes the one class, Record, a narwhals view over a NodeCache. The protocol becomes RecordLike, and WorkingRecord subclasses Record.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
DEP 4 made a staging area a source of one fold. A plain directory is a source too. The read-path page lists four ways the directory and layered implementations differ, but on one directory all four give the same answer:

Compared Result dims, entity_types, groups, attributes, outputs identical flags, every declared type identical member order, every declared type identical resolved rows per attribute identical flags, first call 6.6 ms scanned, 2.9 ms folded

Over one source the fold is a scan. It computes flags in its ownership GROUP BY, where DirectoryRecord scans twice, and order_key over one source is file order. partial is inert over one layer. The table described an implementation that predated the fold reading anything but a tree.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
• NodeCache does not grow. It stays the DuckDB view over a list of sources.
  • Record is one frozen dataclass that has a NodeCache and adapts its relations to narwhals frames. Record.over(*sources, con=...) builds one, and Record.at(uri) reads a plain directory as its one layer.
  • Record is the class and RecordLike the protocol. The 17 annotation and isinstance sites in reader positions take RecordLike.
  • WorkingRecord subclasses Record. Its NodeCache is its base's with a StagedSource appended. It inherits every read member unchanged except outputs, because results do not overlay. set, add, remove and commit stay on WorkingRecord alone. Its NodeCache is fixed at construction: an edit changes the tables the last source reads, never which sources there are.
  • Record caches its key sets only where NodeCache.stable is true, so a staged new attribute stays visible.
  • Record.at reads a standalone directory's own manifest.json, and NodeCache has it as declared. A WorkingRecord over such a base reads under that schema.
  • directory.py and its flags aggregate are deleted, and LayeredRecord is renamed. There is no format change.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
tools/ builds against narwhals frames, so keeping NodeCache and Record apart keeps that interface. A framework object still satisfies the protocol structurally, so the protocol stays and takes the longer name, RecordLike, for "anything shaped like a record".

Two arguments for keeping DirectoryRecord fail. A one-source fold leaves no owner map on the connection, because a DirectorySource's id derives from its URI and nothing is created: five tables before, five after. And a directory copied out of any tree, with no revisions row, folds identically, because the fold needs a layer layout and not a node.

The change withdraws a design property: a directory is now read with resolution. If reading it as a one-layer record is wrong, it is wrong here. DirectoryRecord.flags memoised per type, so the fold is faster on the first call and the cache on the tenth.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
• The cached key sets, not frozen=True, were the real obstacle. NodeCache.stable and Record._stable_cache fix it without an override in WorkingRecord.
  • over takes con explicitly, because a LayerSource has none.
  • A LayerSource.own_schema member was tried and dropped: a fold has at most one directory, always at the root.
  • The both fixture compares one directory read as a directory with the same rows read as a revision's layer. A foreign directory with no tree must read through the fold. test_tools.py must pass unchanged. A test lists the members WorkingRecord defines beyond Record, with outputs the one allowed read member.
  • WorkingRecord already has its base's NodeCache, resolved once in __init__. NewChild() asks the revisions table whether there is a node to branch from.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Whether Revision still needs record, one construction away from node_cache.
  • Whether WorkingRecord's base cache becomes a slice of its own, minus the last source.

docs.title: DEP 6: a member file contains values, and nothing else
DEP 6: a member file contains values, and nothing else
docs.text:
DEP 6 Title a member file contains values, and nothing else Author Jonas Hörsch Status Superseded (2026-10-13, implemented 2026-09-04) Created 2026-09-02 Version v0.1.0a1 Superseded-By DEP 12

The design landed in the record format and the schema. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages. DEP 12 makes the entity-type axis an Enum property of entity. A record with categories and one without then share one entity-axis layout with no member files.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: A member file, dims/entity_type/<Type>.parquet, has a type's attribute values and nothing else. Where the schema declares no entity-type axis, a non-varying attribute over entity is a column of dims/entity.parquet, and no member files exist. In every record, deleted leaves the member file and stays on the entity axis alone.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
A schema may omit the entity-type axis, which makes the type labels data. Values over entity alone still land in one member file per label, so a label the schema never declared becomes a filename:

dims/entity.parquet             entity, entity_type, deleted
dims/entity_type/thing.parquet  entity, p_nom
dims/entity_type/other.parquet  entity, p_nom

The entity_type column there matches no declaration. A special case in _validate_frame admits it and a fallback in _axis_columns types it as String. Every member file also has deleted, so remove writes a tombstone twice, to the axis and to the member table.

Dropping the column alone does not fix this. entity_types(), entity_type_frame and attributes_of all read the label off the resolved entity axis, so a column of NULLs would make entity_types() return {None}. Deriving the label from filenames needs a listing per layer per fold, which the entity axis exists to avoid.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
• Where the schema declares no entity-type axis, which is entity_type_dim is None, a non-varying attribute over entity is a column of dims/entity.parquet. dims/entity_type/ does not exist, and attributes_on("entity") returns those attributes.
  • In that case the entity axis a source supplies is (entity, deleted, *attrs), with no entity_type column. The materialised resolved/dims/entity.parquet has none either.
  • entity_types() returns the empty set. entity_type(ctype) raises. attributes_of(ctype) scopes to the whole axis.
  • A producer with no types supplies one dims["entity"] frame with the member columns merged in, and no entity_types mapping.
  • A member file has entity and its type's columns, and no deleted. remove writes one row, on the axis.
  • A schema that declares the axis keeps the per-type layout unchanged.
  • _validate_frame's special case and the String fallbacks in _axis_columns go.
  • ResolvedLayer's axis and axes become layer-local first, as DEP 8 argues. This DEP depends on that split.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Both changes follow from one claim: a member file has values, and the entity axis has everything about a component's existence. Every column of the format then matches a declaration, and entity_type appears only where it has a dtype. A record with no kinds has one axis file, not one file per label an add used. Record.entity_types stops reporting filenames as a vocabulary.

_FileLayer, ParquetLayer and DirectorySource need no change, because they read whatever columns a file has. A file-backed source reads both configurations the same way. The PyPSA tool always has types, so it is unaffected in practice.

The design adds a second layout for one construct, keyed on one schema property. It replaces the entity_type special case and does not add to it. attributes_on("entity") changes meaning, so every caller needs an audit. Every record without a type axis is re-exported. A materialised cache written under the old layout needs a rebuild.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
• tests/test_untyped.py asserts that record.entity_types is empty and reads values off dims["entity"].
  • A written untyped layer has no dims/entity_type/ directory.
  • An entity_type column on the entity axis of an untyped record is refused.
  • A materialised node of an untyped record reads the same as an unmaterialised one. This test lands before either change.
  • The resolved entity axis and the materialised file have no entity_type column. Checking only entity_types() == set() would pass with a column of NULLs.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Whether a declared entity-type axis typed String, with no Enum, is the same case. The build keys on entity_type_dim is None, so such a schema keeps the per-type layout.
  • Whether attributes_for narrows at all without types.
  • Whether a materialised cache has a schema version or is invalidated when the schema changes. This is still unsettled.

docs.title: DEP 7: staging without _seq
docs.text:
DEP 7 Title staging without _seq Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented (2026-09-02) Created 2026-09-02 Version v0.1.0a1

The design landed in WorkingRecord. Where it and this DEP differ, follow that page.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: Each edit replaces the staged rows it names, by deleting their keys and inserting the new rows. _seq then leaves all four kinds of staging table, with the four folds that read it. A staging table contains the rows the layer will write, and reading one is a table scan.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
The staging rule requires every table to be shaped like the file it becomes. No table meets it, because each has a _seq that no file has, and three of the four need a fold to mean anything:

Kind What _seq does Folded by axis orders two partial rows for one label _collapsed_axis entity axis orders two whole rows for one name _collapsed_entities inputs/outputs orders two rows for one coordinate _collapsed_inputs groups orders two rows for one group_key _collapsed_group any long table _CARRIED_SEQ marks a row as a fill, not an edit none

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
• An edit deletes the keys it names and inserts the new rows, from the arrow relation _values_relation builds, by replacement scan.
  • The key per kind is the one the fold partitions on. It is the label for an axis, entity for the entity axis, the coordinates for a long file and group_key for a group.
  • On the entity axis, remove replaces the row with a tombstone. A remove then an add under another type is one row.
  • _seq, _CARRIED_SEQ, _latest_per and the four _collapsed_* folds go. The tombstone anti-join (a query that keeps the rows with no match in another table) in _collapsed_inputs stays. It stays because a tombstone also applies to other attributes' rows, which is a fact across tables.
  • _complete_owned_whole's anti-join and the long-row replace key both read _long_key.
  • Staging is no longer append-only.
DELETE FROM <table> WHERE <key> IN (SELECT <key> FROM _rows);
INSERT INTO <table> BY NAME SELECT * FROM _rows;

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
The delete removes what _latest_per would have discarded, so the answer does not change. _CARRIED_SEQ never fires. _complete_owned_whole's anti-join already drops any coordinate the table contains, so a fill and an edit cannot meet on one coordinate. A later set on a filled coordinate now deletes the fill first. Deriving both keys from _long_key retires the risk that the two key sets only agree.

An axis row's columns are independently editable, and a membership row's are not. Without a fold, staging handles both kinds of row with the same code. Only the data shows which columns you can edit one at a time.

The design has three benefits. Reads become table scans, where _axis_layer ran an aggregate, an outer join and a coalesce on every commit and staged read. A staged table goes to write_record with no fold between. StagedSource members return tables.

The design has three costs. First, an edit now deletes staged rows and inserts their replacements, so code that expects staged rows only to accumulate is wrong. Second, each edit runs two SQL statements instead of one. A workflow runs far fewer edits than reads, so the second statement adds little time. Third, a fill can overwrite an edit unless one step prevents it: _complete_owned_whole drops from the fill every coordinate that the staging table already contains.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
• An axis set patches its one column in place, with UPDATE ... FROM and an INSERT for a label no row has yet. This keeps a sibling attribute without completing the row. The proposed step that staged the complete row from the base, _complete_axis, was drafted and dropped for it.
  • _axis_layer stays, reduced to a scan for an axis in partial and a union with the untouched base labels for an axis outside partial.
  • No staging table declares _seq.
  • Two set calls on different attributes of one label commute.
  • test_a_partial_axis_stays_a_patch pins that a layer's axis in partial has only the touched labels.
  • test_a_freed_name_may_be_reclaimed_by_another_type passes by construction.
  • After a second set at another coordinate of an attribute over a dim outside partial, the first edit's fills survive and the second edit replaces the fill on its own coordinate.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• INSERT … ON CONFLICT (<key>) DO UPDATE SET: it needs a primary key, so DDL after _shape(...).create(name), and a column list built per call. Neither is fatal, and it is one statement. Re-evaluate once this shape settles, on whether _shape can have a key and stay the single source of a table's shape.
  • INSERT … VALUES: it turns rows into Python objects.

docs.title: DEP 8: one interface over two objects: a source returns its own rows, and a fold returns the resolved rows
DEP 8: one interface over two objects: a source returns its own rows, and a fold returns the resolved rows
docs.text:
DEP 8 Title one interface over two objects: a source returns its own rows, and a fold returns the resolved rows Author Jonas Hörsch Status Superseded (2026-10-21, implemented 2026-09-04) Created 2026-09-02 Version v0.1.0a1 Superseded-By DEP 19 (its fold that is LayerData)

The design landed in the fold, the RecordLike protocol, layers and the package. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: axis(dim) means "the rows of the object I hold" wherever it is written. A LayerSource returns the rows of its own layer, and a fold returns the rows of everything folded into it. ResolvedLayer is deleted and NodeCache becomes Resolver. A materialised node becomes a Fold that the fold finds among its sources. write_record takes LayerData, the interface a source and a Resolver share.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
ResolvedLayer is a persisted NodeCache: Revision.materialise() writes the fold of a node to resolved/, and ResolvedLayer reads it back. It is typed as a LayerSource and sits in the fold's own input list. So a fold result appears as a fold input. The seed paths of resolve_dims and _fold_map read its folded axes and owner map, while source_for reads its own layer's rows through the same object.

DEP 6 needs axis to be layer-local on every source, and its sketch adds resolved_axis beside map_uri to get there. That hides the dual role instead of removing it.

WorkingRecord already keeps the two views as two objects: the Record over base and staged rows, and the StagedSource. But staged_only() returns a _Written, a third spelling of the staged layer's rows, because write_record's input is spelled as neither interface.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
• NodeCache is renamed Resolver, and stable becomes frozen, true when every source is frozen. Dims is renamed Coords.
  • Fold, in datarecord/layered/fold.py, has schema, the folded axes, groups and owner map, and the reads attributes(), owners(attribute) and flags(entity_type=None). flags covers the whole record when entity_type is None. Fold.read(revision_id, con) reads resolved/ and folds nothing.
  • LayerSource.materialised(con, schema) returns the node's Fold or None. _base_and_above(sources, con) scans all but the last source, deepest first, and the first hit is the base. The last source is never the base: a node resolves from its own layer, never its own cache, so materialise never reads its half-written cache back.
  • The base seeds each fold as depth 0, below every layer. So per key the fold still keeps the row of a layer above, and that layer's tombstones still remove a base key.
  • ResolvedLayer is deleted. sources contains only plain LayerSources, source_for returns an own-rows source and never the base, and axis is layer-local on every source.
  • LayerData, in record.py, is schema, frozen, and the pairs axes/axis, entity_types/entity_type, groups/group and attributes/attribute. Its enumerators return Iterable[str], because Resolver.attributes is ordered and a source's is a set. LayerSource and Resolver both satisfy it structurally.
  • layer_id, uri and all_attributes stay source-only. with_source, source_for, owners, flags, fold and revision_id stay on Resolver.
  • A source gains entity_types, groups and attributes as plain directory listings. Every source gets the schema its caller already has, and Resolver.schema is a required field. declared and the fallback to read_schema(con) go.
  • Resolver renames entity_type_frame to entity_type and routes attribute(name, kind) to private _relation and _outputs, which return an empty relation and not None. group_frame stays as the presentational read Record uses.
  • write_record takes LayerData | RecordLike. A RecordLike producer goes through _RecordLikeAsLayerData in write.py. commit passes sources[-1] for NewChild and the Resolver for Directory. _Written, staged_only() and the _staged_* frame builders are deleted, except _staged_groups.
  • write.py works on DuckDB relations throughout.
  • An enumerator returns the empty set exactly when entity_type_dim is None. A declared String axis still lists its member files.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
What axis returns depends on the object you call it on, not on a resolved_ prefix or a mode flag. A file-backed source then needs no branch for the configuration it reads. The name Resolver describes the job, where NodeCache described an implementation detail, and Coords has groups and the broadcast algebra as well as axes.

frozen and materialised mean different things. frozen means that a source's rows cannot change under a reader, and gates the in-memory cache per connection. materialised is a filesystem fact set only by .materialise(), and gates the base that shortens the fold. Every materialised node is frozen, and almost no frozen node is materialised.

flags sits on Fold because scoping to a type needs both the owner map and the entity axis. LayerData contains only the members that mean the same for a layer and a fold. A method that only one of them has shows that the two are different types.

The writer needs exactly LayerData: the schema, plus per kind the keys an object has and the rows of each. The read never needs the enumerators, because the fold learns keys from the schema and the owner map. The writer must list what a layer contains, where the schema declares more. The Directory commit writes the resolved record, which is a fold, through the same interface.

The change reshapes the source list, and sources_to_read, resolve_coords and source_for move together. It also moves write_record's contract.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
It landed as three commits on refactor/staging-as-a-layer: cd2ce92, 006c159 and 7f244a9.

  1. The read-path split: materialised, the base from the deepest materialised source, ResolvedLayer deleted, and the Resolver rename. Fold lives in its own module to break an import cycle with sources.py.
  2. The Fold object. Folding a live Fold needs Coords' broadcast algebra, so Fold.compute is a resolve.py concern and Resolver.fold wraps dims and _map("inputs"). No cache moved. The live Fold has entity_types={}, because it is never a base.
  3. LayerData and the write path.

test_resolved_reads_same_as_unresolved landed first, green before and after. It folds one node through its base and one from the root, and compares the owner map, the entity axis and every attribute. def axis in sources.py is only on _FileLayer, and sources.py changes only by deletion. On a materialised untyped node, entity_types() is the empty set on both the base Fold and the head's ParquetLayer.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• resolved_axis and resolved_axes beside map_uri: a third folded-answer name that hides the dual role.
  • A stored base field on Resolver: the base is discovered from the sources.
  • flags on a map-only OwnerMap: it would need the entities relation handed in from outside.
  • all_attributes on LayerData, with a folded Resolver.all_attributes: no caller reads it on a fold. A layer's share of the owner map needs the resolved axes to expand a NULL, so the split falls between raw rows and expand-and-aggregate.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Whether Record's public narwhals interface joins the shared vocabulary, or only the internal rows interface does.
  • Whether a later Store refactor makes a Resolver.owner_map(kind) and a folded all_attributes worth having.

docs.title: DEP 9: a `Workspace` holds the connection, a `Store` holds a location
DEP 9: a Workspace holds the connection, a Store holds a location
docs.text:
DEP 9 Title a Workspace holds the connection, a Store holds a location Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented (2026-10-10) Created 2026-10-09 Version Unreleased

The design landed in Workspace and Store, layers, WorkingRecord, tools and the package. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: duck's module globals split into two objects. A Workspace has the DuckDB connection and file access, local or remote, which is all a standalone directory needs. A Store has one location, with its manifest, revision tree and layers, and works through a workspace that several stores share. A revision crosses a process boundary as its store's location.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Checked against 49b7268:

  • default_connection() is a process singleton on :memory:, and the revisions table lives only there. A revision deserialised in a new process has an empty ancestry.
  • Only the code that reads the schema calls base_uri_of(con). Layers and caches use DEFAULT_BASE_URI, so connect(base_uri=X) writes its manifest under X and its layers elsewhere. With an empty default, datarecord writes layers/<id>/ into the working directory.
  • PyPSA.results(n) builds relations on DuckDB's default connection, so the next union fails.
  • Revisions cannot be listed.
  • A remote manifest is unreadable and unwritable, and a failed remote write leaves part of a layer.
  • Of eight threads on one DuckDB 1.5.5 connection, seven fail.
  • materialise() writes the inputs owner map first, so a reader can fold from half a cache.

One object holding location and connection would fix these, but a standalone directory would then carry a location it never uses.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
class Workspace:
    con: DuckDBPyConnection

    def __init__(self, database: str = ":memory:") -> None: ...
    @classmethod
    def process(cls) -> Workspace: ...
    def store(self, uri: str) -> Store: ...
    def at(self, uri: str) -> Record: ...
    def write(self, source: LayerData | RecordLike, uri: str) -> Record: ...
    def close(self) -> None: ...


class Store:
    uri: str
    workspace: Workspace

    def root(self, source: LayerData | RecordLike) -> Revision: ...
    def revision(self, id: UUID) -> Revision: ...
    def revisions(self) -> list[Revision]: ...
    def layer(self, id: UUID) -> Record: ...
    def layer_dir(self, id: UUID) -> str: ...
    def resolved_dir(self, id: UUID) -> str: ...


class Revision:
    def child(self, source: LayerData | RecordLike) -> Revision: ...
  • Only ws.store, ws.at, ws.write and a tool's con name the workspace. Everything else takes it from its source.
  • ws.store(uri) returns one store per normalised location, filled with dict.setdefault. ws.store("") raises ValueError, and a local path becomes absolute. A store has no connection and no close.
  • ws.at(uri) requires the directory's own manifest.json. A tree layer reads through store.layer(id).
  • A Record keeps exposing con, the calling thread's cursor, so that a tool can run DuckDB SQL.
  • There is no empty revision. store.root and rev.child write the layer, then widen the manifest, then write revisions/<id>.json, create-only. The layer counts as written once its revision file exists, and a failed or incompatible layer leaves the manifest untouched.
  • ws.write writes the manifest last. Before any COPY, a remote ws.write refuses a URI under which Files.list finds anything, because COPY would overwrite an existing record's files before the Absent manifest write fails.
  • materialise() writes owner_map/inputs.parquet last, and each local file goes to a temporary name and is renamed.
  • WorkingRecord(record) takes no con and has no commit. w.edits is its staged LayerData. rev.child raises when a staged source's base is another revision. A WorkingRecord that still has its edits after a write reads as before.
  • The tree is <location>/revisions/<id>.json, {"id", "parent"}, with a UUID drawn in Python.
