The error maps String, Float64, Int64, Boolean and Datetime to str, float, int, bool and datetime, and Enum to one_of. For Date it names datetime, and for into it names one_of: <dim>.

docs.title: The read API
docs.text:
The mappings stay, and their values are relations. Each of dims, properties, groups and attributes maps a name to a duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation on the record's connection. Frames becomes Relations, LazyFrames becomes LazyRelations, and Record moves into record.py.

RecordLike is no longer engine-neutral. A tool's record builds its relations on the caller's connection, and the PyPSA network source scans its pandas frames with con.from_df.

docs.title: The write API
docs.text:
set, add and add_group take a DuckDB relation, or a pandas, polars or arrow frame. DuckDB reads a frame through the frame's own scanner, uncollected, and no scanner package becomes a dependency. A relation on another connection is still refused, and a scalar stays a scalar.

A column is checked against its dtype's DuckDB type. A lossless widening, such as INTEGER to BIGINT, is cast, and anything else is refused with the declared dtype named. datarecord refuses a frame with time-zone timestamps and does not convert it to naive time. check_group_columns takes a relation and runs in SQL, with the partial-NULL check as one LIMIT 1 query.

docs.title: Snapshot timesteps
docs.text: A property takes no datetime dtype, so PyPSA's snapshot.timestep becomes {one_of: timestep} on a new datetime dim named after PyPSA's index level. Its labels are the timesteps a multi-period network uses. snapshot.period becomes {one_of: period}.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
The resolver already returns relations, so handing them over bare removes a wrap per read and a conversion per write. A record feeds a mathspec model, so the manifest uses mathspec's five dtypes, as the model does.

into on a property, into on a group and an Enum property were three spellings of one idea. one_of: <dim> is one, and it is the relation column that a mathspec model reads. A category is then a label that a dim lists, so ctype gets an axis file and an order like any dim.

Seven entries in a fixed map replace a private narwhals import, and change only when mathspec does.

What it costs: a caller who reads record.attributes[...] with narwhals or polars expressions rewrites them as SQL or relation calls. A non-DuckDB backend for RecordLike is no longer possible. A record that declares Date, a width, Enum or into is re-exported, as breaking changes are free. A functional group loses its single-valuedness guarantee. PyPSA records gain timestep, ctype and role dims.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Before:

PropertySpec(dtype=nw.Enum(["Generator", "Line"]))
PropertySpec(into="carrier")
record.attributes["p_nom"].filter(nw.col("value") > 0).collect().to_pandas()

After:

Dimension(one_of=["Generator", "Line"])  # the ctype dim
PropertySpec(one_of="ctype")
PropertySpec(one_of="carrier")
record.attributes["p_nom"].filter("value > 0").df()
w.set("p_nom", polars_frame)  # or pandas, arrow, a relation

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. pixi.toml: mathspec pinned at 8982c55, and narwhals removed from it and pyproject.toml.
  2. schema.py and duck.py: mathspec dtypes and one_of, the type map, into and old names refused at load, and DuckDB struct types.
  3. record.py: Relations and LazyRelations, and Record moved in from layered/record.py.
  4. mutable.py: as_relation for every frame, DuckDB type checks, and add refusing a label outside one_of.
  5. Tools: to_relation goes, and the PyPSA tool has ctype, role and timestep dims.
  6. Tests, pages and CHANGELOG.md, with the group single-valuedness tests deleted.

Checks: no narwhals in src/, pyproject.toml or pixi.toml. A manifest with "Float64" or into is refused with its replacement named. Every record.*[...] value is a DuckDBPyRelation. A PyPSA network round-trips.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• narwhals kept in tools only: two value types for one record, and the conversion stays.
  • DuckDB type names in the manifest: an engine's vocabulary, where mathspec's is the framework's.
  • A declared struct dtype: it would restate the group's key.
  • datetime kept on properties: mathspec's ParameterDtype refuses it, so the model could not read it.
  • A local Enum dtype on properties: mathspec puts the labels on a dimension, and a property list would be a second vocabulary.
  • into kept beside one_of: two spellings of one declaration.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text: • Recovering single-valuedness for a functional group, where a group property may be NULL. The recommendation is nothing until a reader needs it. A later required flag on a property would cover it.

docs.title: DEP 19: one Record and a package layout
DEP 19: one Record and a package layout
docs.text:
DEP 19 Title one Record and a package layout Author Jonas Hoersch Status Implemented (2026-10-21) Requires DEP 18 Created 2026-10-21 Version Unreleased Replaces DEP 5 (Record over a NodeCache), DEP 8 (a fold that is LayerData) Superseded-By DEP 20 (its re-added key introduced where it is re-added)

The design landed in the package, the record, the fold, layers and editing. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: Record absorbs Resolver, so one class folds a record's layers and implements RecordLike. A record with staged edits folds only its staged layer per read. The package splits into three subpackages, schema/, resolve/ and store/, under one dependency rule, which breaks the import cycle between store.py and layered/revision.py. The internal names that still contain "inputs" are renamed after the owner map.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
DEP 8 split Resolver from Record so that the writer could read a Resolver as LayerData. Since WorkingRecord.commit was removed in a17bf6e, the writer no longer does. Each member of Record still forwards to one member of Resolver, and code that needs the record carries both objects. Revision caches a Resolver but builds a new Record, with an empty cache of key sets, on every access to rev.record.

To write a working record whole, _pinned sets a PinnedResolver on a copy of the Record through object.__setattr__. Resolver.axes(), Resolver.groups(), group_frame and LayerData.frozen have no caller.

With edits staged, every read of the axes, groups or dead labels folds again from the deepest materialised revision, opening every layer file above it. The owner map already folds only the staged step.

store.py imports layered/revision.py lazily in three methods, because revision.py imports store.py. schema.py (1,554 lines) and layered/resolve.py (1,499 lines) each contain several separable parts.

docs.title: One Record
docs.text:
Record is a frozen dataclass in resolve/record.py with the four fields of Resolver: revision_id, sources, workspace and schema. sources lists the layers root first, truncated at the deepest materialised one.

You read a Record through the RecordLike members, and its other public members are its four fields, con and frozen. The Resolver methods that read the same rows a second way are deleted: axis, group, group_frame, attribute, axes(), groups(), attributes(), with_source and inputs. The private _fold has the owner map and _coords the folded axes, groups and dead labels. _relation resolves one attribute, and raises KeyError where the owner map assigns it to no layer. That happens only to a key set read before rollback() and used after it. Record has its cache of key sets, which now checks self.frozen.

On a record with staged edits, _coords folds only the layers after the frozen prefix onto that prefix's coord tables. resolve_coords takes those shared DuckDB tables as its seed, as _fold_map does, so the fold opens no file. The key set of groups comes from one such fold, not one per group.

A label or tuple that one layer removes and a later layer adds again is introduced where it is added again. The seeded tables keep a tombstoned key at most as a dead label, which has no place in axis order. fold_axis therefore counts only the rows of a key that are deeper than its deepest tombstone. The seeded fold, the fold over every layer and a fold over a materialised revision then agree.

WorkingRecord reads through dims, properties, groups and attributes of itself and of its base where it called the deleted methods. The base axis rows that it unions into a layer that owns the dim whole come from properties. properties adds each declared property that no layer stored as a typed NULL column, so a written axis layer reads back as before.

PinnedRecord subclasses Record and replaces PinnedResolver. It folds the unfrozen tail once, into a table that release() drops. It creates the table at the first access to _fold, so a write that fails before write_layer enters its try leaves no table behind. layer_data builds one from any unfrozen Record, and write_layer releases it after the write. WorkingRecord calls Record.__init__ with its base's fields and [*base.sources, StagedSource(...)], and sets _base to the base.

Revision caches its Record, and materialise clears that cache. Revision.resolver is deleted, and Workspace.at and Store.layer construct a Record. A Record looks up workspace.con on each call, so several threads can read one Record. A PinnedRecord has its relations on the cursor of the thread that built it.

DEP 5 made Record the interface over a NodeCache, and it is now the fold itself. Against DEP 8, the writer reads no fold as LayerData, and Record does not implement LayerData.

docs.title: LayerData
docs.text: LayerData stays separate from RecordLike. It loses frozen, which the writer never reads, and its enumerators return set[str] instead of Iterable[str], a type that existed only so that a Resolver could return an ordered list. A LayerSource has its own frozen, because the fold reads it.

docs.title: The package layout
docs.text:
datarecord/
├── __init__.py        # every public name
├── duck.py            # relation helpers
├── protocols.py       # RecordLike, LayerData, Relations, LazyRelations, EMPTY, Flags
├── schema/            # dtypes.py, specs.py, schema.py, categories.py
├── resolve/           # fold.py, sources.py, coords.py, owner_map.py, record.py (Record, PinnedRecord)
├── mutable.py         # WorkingRecord, StagedSource
├── store/             # store.py (Workspace, Store, Revision), files.py, cache.py, manifest.py, write.py
└── tools/             # unchanged

Runtime imports follow the order duck, schema, protocols, resolve, mutable, store, tools. A module imports at runtime only from modules earlier in that order, and nothing outside tools/ imports tools/. An import under TYPE_CHECKING may point the other way. A subpackage's __init__.py re-exports its user-facing names, and datarecord/__init__.py imports them from there. A user imports only from datarecord, and code inside the package imports a name from the module that defines it.

Workspace, Store and Revision share store/store.py because they need each other at runtime. The modules in resolve/ take a Workspace, not a connection, to get the calling thread's cursor. mutable.py stays one module, because StagedSource reads eight private members of WorkingRecord.

docs.title: Renames
docs.text:
Before Under this DEP Schema.input_key Schema.owner_map_key the tool requirement "input_key" "owner_map_key" Schema.input_columns Schema.owner_map_columns Resolver.inputs deleted, in favour of the fold's owner_map resolve.fold_inputs owner_map.fold_attributes tests/fixtures.write_input write_attribute resolve.write_schema moved to tests/fixtures.py, its one caller

Schema.owner_map_key is partial_dims plus attribute, and Schema.owner_map_columns is that key plus _layer and the flag columns. "Inputs" is left over from the inputs/ directory that DEP 17 replaced. The pages keep "fold key" for partial_dims alone.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Every caller of Resolver already has the Record or the Revision beside it. Each caller needs both the fold and the members that read from it, so a second class only adds forwarding.

The protocols get their own module because Record now lives in resolve/. A module with both Flags and Record would import resolve/fold.py, which imports Flags back from it.

A Revision is a pydantic model with a Store field and calls Workspace.process() when it loads, while Store constructs Revisions. In two modules, one of them would need a lazy import.

What it costs: every internal import path changes, with the monkeypatches and the API pages' ::: paths. About 50 test lines move to rev.record. Another 24 read the private _fold and _coords, because no public member exposes the owner map or the folded coords.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# before
from datarecord.layered.resolve import Resolver
from datarecord.layered.revision import Revision

rev.resolver.sources
Record(Resolver(layer_id, sources, ws, schema))

# after
from datarecord.resolve.record import Record
from datarecord.store.store import Revision

rev.record.sources
Record(layer_id, sources, ws, schema)

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. One commit merges Resolver into Record, moves WorkingRecord onto the mappings, seeds the staged coord fold and trims LayerData.
  2. One commit moves the modules, breaks the import cycle and applies the renames.
  3. CHANGELOG.md, and the pages that name Resolver, the inputs key or fold_inputs.
  4. DEP 5 and DEP 8 take Superseded-By this DEP, for the parts named under Replaces.

Checks: no module imports layered, and no runtime import breaks the dependency rule. Resolver and input_key appear nowhere outside the DEPs. Folding the staged layer onto the frozen prefix's coord tables gives the same axes, groups and dead labels as folding over every layer, axis order and tombstones included.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• Folding LayerData into RecordLike would remove the adapter. A staged axis has a deleted column that RecordLike.dims cannot have, so the writer would split each axis and join it back.
  • Moving Record next to Resolver without merging keeps the forwarding, the copy in _pinned and the duplicate members of Revision.
  • A separate Layout object for the path helpers on Store: the lower layers need the Workspace anyway, so it turns every store argument into two, to save five one-line methods.
  • One _coords shared by each mapping's key set and values halves the folds per read. Each fold still opens every layer's files, unless it starts from a seed in DuckDB.
  • A format/ subpackage would not contain write_layer and _FileLayer, the code that writes and reads the format. An edit/ subpackage would contain only mutable.py.
  • Revision importing Store only under TYPE_CHECKING fails, because pydantic needs the store field's type at runtime.

docs.title: DEP 20: a layer restates an axis whole
DEP 20: a layer restates an axis whole
docs.text:
DEP 20 Title a layer restates an axis whole Author Jonas Hoersch Status Implemented (2026-10-22) Requires DEP 19 Created 2026-10-21 Version Unreleased Replaces DEP 1 (entity tombstones, and an order the fold generates), DEP 4 (the per-label axis fold, and partial as how many labels an axis layer carries), DEP 10 (group tombstones, by which the fold drops owner-map rows), DEP 11 (removal by tombstone, and dead labels as winning tombstones), DEP 17 (a SubNetwork as an entity, and its tombstones), DEP 19 (a re-added key introduced where it is re-added)

The design landed in layers, the fold, the format and tools. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: A layer that changes an axis or a group writes its file whole and in order, and the deepest such file is the resolved one. A restatement that omits a label removes it, so no file has a deleted column. Attributes stay per-key overrides under partial. A PyPSA SubNetwork becomes a label of its own dim.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
_fold_axis folds an axis per label from every layer that touched it. A label takes its deepest row, is dropped where that row is a tombstone, and sits where its first row after its deepest tombstone sits. No single file lists a revision's axis or its order.

The PyPSA tool numbers a component's ports by connection order, so the order matters. DEP 19 reshaped the order rule to make a cache agree with a full fold. Every new seed or cache needs that check again.

The per-label fold also hides a file out of order or with a label twice. On an axis, partial also sets how much of it a layer writes, a second meaning beside attribute ownership.

docs.title: An axis is its deepest file
docs.text:
A layer that adds or removes a label, or changes a property, writes dims/<dim>.parquet whole: every label at that revision, with its properties, in order. groups/<group>.parquet follows the same rule. A revision's resolved axis or group is the deepest such file on its path, in row order. attributes/<attr>.parquet still contains only the keys a layer sets.

A materialised revision's resolved/dims/ and resolved/groups/ contain copies of the deepest layer file at or below it, so a read still stops there. resolved/dead/ and owner_map.parquet stay folds.

docs.title: Removal
docs.text:
A label is removed at a layer whose restatement omits it while the previous restatement lists it. The previous restatement is the deepest file below that layer, a materialised base's resolved axis, or the frozen prefix's table. A first restatement removes nothing.

For a partial dim or group, the owner-map fold drops the parent rows that contain a removed label. A mortal coordinate is one outside the owner-map key, or one that a group's field ranges over or a property takes its labels from. Its dead labels are the labels some layer removed that the final axis lacks: the base's dead set, the base's resolved axis and every restatement above the base, minus the final axis. The reference check takes a layer's removed labels from its parent's axis minus its restatement.

In every case probed on a prototype, the rule gives the earlier answers. A keyed label's values from below its removal stay gone after it is added again, and an unkeyed coordinate's come back, as DEP 11 accepted. A label removed and added again in one staging area keeps its parent's values, and a broadcast applies to a label added after a restatement.

WorkingRecord.remove restates the axis without the label, and each group over its dim without the tuples that contain it. set refuses a label missing from any dim's staged axis, or a tuple missing from a staged group. add_group refuses a tuple whose label is missing from a field's staged axis. Each message names the dim or group, the field where there is one, and up to three labels. Where remove follows a set in one staging area, the fold drops the staged rows that contain the removed label.

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
An axis's order is its deepest file's row order. A label added again after its removal sits where the later restatement puts it, which subsumes the rule of DEP 19.

WorkingRecord stages an axis or group as a whole table, copied from the base at the first edit, with a position column. add appends a new label, or returns a base label to its base position. StagedSource hands the table over in position order, so a read composes nothing. write_layer refuses a restatement whose order on its parent's labels differs from the parent's, naming the first label out of place.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
datarecord refuses a dims/ or groups/ file with a deleted column, at read and in write_layer, so an old layer fails instead of losing labels:

dims/bus.parquet carries a `deleted` column; a layer removes a label by
restating its axis without it (.../design/layers/#deletion). Re-export the
record, or flatten it with `ws.write` under the previous release.

The fold and write_layer refuse a key that occurs twice in one such file. datarecord refuses at read a column that is neither the key nor a declared property, as write_layer already does. deleted stays a reserved name.

write_layer applies the checks of set and add_group to every layer, hand-written or not. Each check is one DuckDB anti-join (a query that keeps the rows with no match in another table). It runs against the layer's final axis or group: its own file, else its parent's resolved one.

docs.title: The reference check
docs.text: The reference check reads each subject a layer restates, or whose rows contain a removed label, whole and in its final state. Where an ancestor left a reference dangling, the next write that touches its subject fails, and that write can repair the row. The promise that such a reference "fails no later write" goes.

docs.title: SubNetworks are a dim
docs.text:
A solve's SubNetworks written into the entity axis would remove every other entity. A SubNetwork becomes a label of the dim sub_network, which a results layer restates alone:

Before Under this DEP the entity label 0 SubNetwork, ctype="SubNetwork" the sub_network label 0 SubNetwork listed by ctype not listed, so datarecord refuses flags(ctype="SubNetwork") entity.carrier, slack_bus over entity sub_network.carrier, slack_bus over sub_network a Line's sub_network value 0 SubNetwork 0, still over entity

sub_network.carrier takes its labels from carrier. sub_network stays outside partial, because a results layer writes every SubNetwork's values. A full export writes the axis beside bus and carrier. A solve without SubNetworks over a base with the axis restates it empty, with the declared column types. Over a base without the axis, a results layer writes none.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
No seed, cache or staged fold can then disagree with a full fold. Groups follow the rule because port order is connection order.

Each number here is one DuckDB run at PyPSA-Eur scale, 60,000 entities and 150,000 connections, unless stated. A sub_network axis is 12 rows and 0.4 kB, or 18 kB where each of 4,000 buses is its own SubNetwork. The change needs no migration of its own, because every record the tool wrote has deleted columns and is re-exported anyway.

On a chain of 20 edit layers over 40,000 entities and 80,000 connections, a prototype without the order and duplicate checks wrote the chain in 4.3 s against 5.7 s, and read p_nom cold at its leaf in 1.07 s against 2.17 s. The entity fold drops from 80 to 95 ms, whatever the override count, to a 50 ms read of the deepest file.

What it costs: storage grows with the axis, not the edit. A one-entity property edit writes 0.30 MB, where an override wrote 0.8 kB. Adding a connection writes 0.43 MB, removing an entity restates both for 0.73 MB, and a connection.role edit restates every tuple. The chain takes 5.57 MB, not 10 kB. The cost multiplies in trees with many small leaves and on a remote store. Each restatement adds a diff to every fold, 6 ms for the entities and 18 ms for the connections. Building the dead set reads every restatement above the base, 23 ms over 20 of the entities. A duplicate check costs 5 to 11 ms per file. A WorkingRecord's first edit of an axis copies it, an estimated 15 ms for the entities and 41 ms for the connections.

A tree with deleted columns is flattened with ws.write under the previous release, losing its history. A full PyPSA export is refused as a child where its parent's entity order interleaves types, and is written as a root instead. datarecord applies the same refusals to a foreign directory, so not every parquet directory reads as a layer. A hand-written restatement that omits a property column blanks it for every label. A hand-written override without a deleted column reads silently as a restatement that removes every label it omits, and datarecord has no format version by which to detect it. src loses an estimated 100 to 130 lines and gains 135 to 235.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. The fold, the writer and WorkingRecord as above, then the PyPSA tool's sub_network dim.
  2. Test fixtures restate from the parent, and at least 18 tests change.
  3. CHANGELOG.md and the pages. DEP 1, 4, 10, 11, 17 and 19 take Superseded-By this DEP for the parts under Replaces.

Checks: a label removed and re-added reads in one order, materialised or not, staged or committed, with connection in partial and out. No file that write_layer writes under dims/ or groups/ has a deleted column.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• The 7-line fold fix of DEP 19 fixes the order without a format change, but keeps tombstones, partial's second meaning and a derived order.
  • A format version in manifest.json would catch an old override, at the cost of a second version beside schema.version.
  • Restating the entity axis per results layer writes 0.30 MB per solve in 20 ms, plus 10 ms for its order check, small beside one marginal_price result over 4,000 buses and 8,760 snapshots, at most 301 MB. It rewrites an axis the solve never changed, and fails on an ancestor's dangling reference.
  • Checking only the rows a restatement changes keeps the old promise. It costs one more anti-join per subject, and the dangling row stays.
  • Sorting an out-of-order restatement brings the per-label fold back at write time.
  • Dropping undeclared columns loses a foreign column silently at the first edit of its axis.
  • Pruning the owner map per restatement drops a broadcast's rows for later labels, and against the final axis alone it brings back removed values.
  • Without the dead cache, series reads run 4.4 times slower: 78 ms against 18 ms on 43.8M p_max_pu rows.
  • A pointer in resolved/ instead of a copy saves 0.73 MB per materialised revision, but a read would open an ancestor's file.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• The order check allows a new label before one of its parent's. In a group, a new tuple there renumbers an entity's later ports. WorkingRecord appends, so only a layer written another way can do this.
  • DEP 14's open issue, extending a tree without restating its base, gets no easier.

docs.title: DEP 21: the owner map contains keys as written
DEP 21: the owner map contains keys as written
docs.text:
DEP 21 Title the owner map contains keys as written Author Jonas Hoersch Status Implemented (2026-10-25) Requires DEP 20 Created 2026-10-21 Version Unreleased Replaces DEP 1 (flags aggregated from expanded rows), DEP 8 (a fold that expands a broadcast against the resolved axes), DEP 10 (a NULL struct expanded in the fold), DEP 11 (a re-added label starts fresh), DEP 16 (a NULL row expanded over every label in the owner map), DEP 20 (a keyed label's broadcasts staying gone after it is added again)

The design landed in the fold, the data model and the record. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: The owner map contains each layer's attribute keys as the layer wrote them. Where a deeper layer's row crosses a parent row, the fold adds an overlap row that the owner map assigns to the deeper layer. The fold reads no axis, and a read returns the rows the owner map assigns as written, NULL included. A reader settles each coordinate by the broadcast rule alone.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
fold_attributes expands each row that leaves a partial coordinate NULL against the resolved axis, one owner-map row per label. One broadcast over 60,000 entities and two scenarios takes 120,000 rows. A materialised revision persists that expansion, and a fold seeded from it misses every label added later.

A child that adds the entity n under a broadcast q = 0.9 reads n as 0.9, and as nothing once its parent is materialised. A label staged in a WorkingRecord over the parent reads as nothing in both cases. Over 210 random six-layer records, materialising or staging changes an answer in 95 to 128 records.

The expansion only settles which layer the owner map assigns a key to. Within a layer, datarecord keeps the more specific row, and across layers a read returns the deeper layer's row. The rules disagree only where rows of two layers cross, and one row at their overlap makes them agree.

docs.title: The owner map
docs.text:
The owner map has one row per layer and distinct key, NULL kept, and no depth:

<partial dims>   -- the key: exactly the partial dims and groups, NULL included
attribute
layer_uuid
varies      STRUCT(<coordinate>: BOOLEAN, ...)
broadcast   STRUCT(<coordinate>: BOOLEAN, ...)
breakpoints BOOLEAN

An overlap row sets labels where its layer's key is NULL, and has that layer's varies and broadcast. A read joins it to the layer's value row by one NULL-safe join on the key.

docs.title: Crossing
docs.text: A row sets a partial dim where its key has a label, and any other dim it varies along, so a series over snapshot sets snapshot. Only the dims the attribute uses count: its dims and the dims of its groups. Two rows cover a common key where, on each partial coordinate, they have the same label or one has NULL. They cross where they cover a common key and each row leaves NULL a dim that the other row sets.

docs.title: The fold
docs.text:
The fold folds a layer onto its parent's map in four steps:

  1. It drops the parent rows that contain a label the layer removes by DEP 20's diff, and never a row that is NULL there.
  2. It drops a parent row that a layer row covers, where the layer row sets no partial dim that the parent row leaves NULL.
  3. For each parent row and layer row that cross, it adds an overlap row that sets every label either row sets. A crossed parent row, or one that sets fewer dims, stays.
  4. It adds the layer's rows.

No step reads an axis. An overlap row is an ordinary row to every later fold, which drops, crosses or removes it like any other.

With partial = {entity, scenario}, a root writing (gas, NULL) = 50 and (wind, NULL) = 100, and a child writing (NULL, high) = 999:

(gas,  NULL) root    # as written
(wind, NULL) root
(NULL, high) child   # as written
(gas,  high) child   # overlap rows
(wind, high) child

A child writing (gas, high) = 70 instead leaves the root's rows, and the broadcast rule gives it (gas, high).

docs.title: A dim outside partial
docs.text: The key has no column for a dim outside partial, so a WorkingRecord settles a crossing there as it stages. A staged row that leaves such a dim NULL is also written out along a base row's labels there. A child writing (wind, NULL) = 0.9 over a root series at snapshots 0 and 1 also writes (wind, 0) and (wind, 1). The fold refuses a layer written otherwise that leaves such a crossing, naming the attribute, the dim and the key.

docs.title: The read
docs.text: A read returns the rows the owner map assigns as written: a NULL stays NULL, and an overlap row comes back with its labels. It expands no NULL and drops no row by depth. The read still drops each row with a dead label, and the row order stays unspecified. A reader applies the broadcast rule over the full coordinates, partial or not. Every crossing has a row that sets both, so a reader needs neither depth nor the list of partial dims.

docs.title: Where a NULL and a row apply
docs.text:
A NULL on a partial coordinate applies to every label of that axis, or every tuple of its group, at the revision read. That includes a label added below a materialised revision, a staged label and the first label of an axis that was empty when the broadcast was written. Adding the scenario mid below the first example's child reads (gas, mid) as 50.

A row applies at every coordinate that no more specific row covers, from any layer. The owner map assigns a deeper layer only the coordinates its rows apply at, not a key's whole extent along a dim outside partial. With x also over snapshot, a root writing (gas, NULL, 1) = 1.0 and a child writing (NULL, high, 0) = 2.0, (gas, high, 1) reads 1.0 from the root, where it read nothing before.

A label removed and added again takes every broadcast that covers it, written before or after the removal, and never a row that set it below the removal. DEP 20 changes to match: a keyed label's values from rows that set it below its removal stay gone.

Materialising changes no answer. A map persisted for another set of partial dims is ignored, and the read folds again.

docs.title: flags
docs.text: flags() aggregates bool_or over the owner map's varies, broadcast and breakpoints, per attribute. Both structs report only the dims the attribute uses, so ctype no longer reads true in broadcast for an attribute not over it. A broadcast that deeper layers shadow on every label still counts. flags(**categories) aggregates the same way over the rows that apply to the category.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: The workspace keeps the frozen prefix's map as the shared table owner_map_<key>_<rev>, <key> a hash of the key columns. A materialised revision writes resolved/owner_map.parquet last. A map an earlier release wrote is unsupported, and datarecord does not detect it.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
The fold settles ownership once, so the map needs no depth and the read drops no row by depth. Settling it by depth at each read costs more per read, in every way measured, and needs a reader that handles layers.

An overlap row takes its labels from the two rows, so the crossed parent row still applies, unchanged, to a later label. It takes its value from the deeper layer, whose value rows have the dims the overlap row's key leaves NULL. Any parent row more specific than the overlap, where the deeper row applies, is one that the deeper row covers, and step 2 has dropped it. A parent row that a deeper, more specific row covers stays as written, because there the two rules agree.

Crossing is judged over every dim the attribute uses, because a reader applies the broadcast rule over the full coordinates. Left as written, the root's (NULL, 0) beside the child's (wind, NULL) gives two rows at (wind, 0), and datarecord keeps neither.

The figures come from a prototype against DEP 20, each the median of three interleaved rounds run alone. Case 1 has 60,000 entities, 100 attributes and two scenarios over ten layers, with a materialised leaf and a child that adds one entity. Case 2 is a materialised child that broadcasts 20 of 40 attributes. The scaling cases vary the number k of partial dims: entity with 20,000 labels and k - 1 dims of three labels, every attribute over all of them. The realistic case (R) has nine layers and ten attributes, where the rows of each attribute set at most four different sets of dims. The worst case (W) has 2^k layers, each setting its own set of dims, so most layers cross the ones below. The series case (S) has 20,000 entities, two scenarios and 8,760 snapshots.

Case Map rows, before Map rows First read, before First read Repeated read, before Repeated read 1 12.0 M 7.50 M 2.60 s 2.98 s 0.036 s 0.025 s 2 4.80 M 1.20 M 0.77 s 0.24 s 0.018 s 0.007 s R k3 1.80 M 223 k 0.70 s 0.69 s 0.019 s 0.013 s R k4 5.40 M 223 k 1.85 s 0.75 s 0.049 s 0.015 s R k5 16.2 M 223 k 6.25 s 0.81 s 0.147 s 0.017 s W k3 720 k 8.8 k 0.70 s 0.56 s 0.028 s 0.020 s W k4 2.16 M 35 k 2.30 s 3.02 s 0.107 s 0.049 s W k5 6.48 M 163 k 13.7 s 20.1 s 0.315 s 0.160 s S k2 120 k 124 materialise 25.7 s 0.22 s

The first read folds, and materialising follows it. The read times leave out the reader's expansion. A read with two entities set in a staged layer over the materialised revision takes 1.0 to 2.8 times as long as before in the scaling cases, and 0.11 times in the series case.

The worst case's first read is 1.3 to 1.5 times as long for k of 4 and 5. Pairs of sets where neither contains the other grow from 1 at k = 2 to 55 at k = 4 and 285 at k = 5, and the fold joins along each pair. This DEP accepts that cost, because no workflow overrides one attribute along ever different sets of dims in a dozen layers.

Over 210 fuzzed records of six edit layers, with entity, scenario and connection in partial, reads and flags agree plain, materialised at depth 1 and 3, staged, and staged over a materialised parent. The plain read equals an oracle of the broadcast rule on 197. The other 13 hit the oracle's limits, such as a group emptied of tuples, a connection removed and added again within one layer, or a label new in the layer that writes a row over snapshot at it. No fuzzed record triggers the refusal of a layer written without WorkingRecord.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. The fold without axes, the read of rows as written, and staging along base labels outside partial.
  2. The tools and write_layer apply the broadcast rule over rows as written.
  3. Tests, CHANGELOG.md and the pages. The open question on broadcasts surviving materialisation closes.

Checks: every probe reads the same materialised or not, staged or committed, and the 210 fuzzed records read the same in all five ways.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• Keys with their depth, settled at every read: 1.55 to 2.1 times as long in the realistic case from k = 2, 31 times in the worst case at k = 5, and out of memory at 24.6 GiB for k = 6. A session cache of settled rows brings repeated reads to 0.15 to 0.90 times, but a first sweep takes 2.5 to 3.6 times, and 31 times at worst. An arg_max(depth) window brings the worst repeated read from 31 to 5.5 times, but the realistic case to 3.3 times. Building the cache root to leaf halves the worst first read but slows the realistic one by half. Disabling DuckDB's build_side_probe_side optimizer takes a build to 3.9 s against 9.3 s, but holds for every concurrent cursor. A cache shared across sessions needs a key over the partial dims and a size cap, and has a per-label file per attribute.
  • Splitting a crossed parent row along the axis: none of the pieces applies to a label added later, so (gas, mid) reads as nothing. On the first 70 fuzzed records, 8 differ from the oracle. The worst first read takes 65 s against 20 s, with 2.01 million map rows against 163,000.
  • Splitting every parent row along a dim that a deeper row sets: it splits where the two rules agree, and dropping shadowed rows at the read by an arg_max window reads at 2 to 8 times the split above.
  • Crossing judged over partial alone: a crossing on snapshot stays, which the rule cannot order.
  • The per-label map kept beside this one: a delta over every seed, three kinds of shared table, and materialising in 8.5 s against 3.4 s.
  • flags decided per label keeps the earlier flags exactly, at 3 to 24 times the time: 1.016 s against 0.043 s for a repeated flags() at the materialised leaf.
  • datarecord keeping the more specific row across layers: the fold cannot drop an earlier value set at a label under a later broadcast, so every read expands it, 0.045 s against 0.023 s on case 2.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• The tools settle rows by settle(rel, labels, flags), which expands a NULL only on a coordinate in broadcast and picks a row only where a coordinate is also in varies. Attr.resolve and Schema.resolve take labels and flags.
  • write_layer accepts two crossing rows where a row that sets both exists, so several layers flatten into one. The read of a staged layer refuses two crossing rows without one.
  • No fuzzed record has a series over more than one partial dim.
  • The worst case's slower first read, which Rationale accepts.

docs.title: DEP 22: a layer restates membership whole
DEP 22: a layer restates membership whole
docs.text: DEP 22 Title a layer restates membership whole Author Jonas Hoersch Status On hold (2026-10-22) Requires DEP 19 Created 2026-10-22 Version Unreleased Replaces DEP 1 (entity tombstones, and an order the fold generates), DEP 4 (the per-label axis fold, and partial as how many labels an axis layer carries), DEP 10 (group tombstones, by which the fold drops owner-map rows), DEP 11 (removal by tombstone, and dead labels as winning tombstones), DEP 12 (every property of a dim as a column of dims/<dim>.parquet), DEP 17 (a SubNetwork as an entity, and its tombstones), DEP 19 (a re-added key introduced where it is re-added)

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: DEP 22 is an alternative to DEP 20, and only one of the two is implemented. A layer that changes membership writes the key column of dims/<dim>.parquet or groups/<group>.parquet whole and in order. Each property moves to its own file, properties/<subject>.<name>.parquet, which the fold resolves per label, keeping the deepest layer's row. A property edit then writes only the rows it changes.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
DEP 20's motivation holds here unchanged. DEP 20's cost is storage that grows with the axis on every edit, properties included. A one-entity property edit writes 0.30 MB, and a connection.role edit restates 150,000 tuples.

A property can be bulky. A bus geometry of 64 vertices makes dims/bus.parquet 2.49 MB at 4,000 buses, against 17.5 kB for the labels alone. DEP 20 writes all of it on every bus edit, including a fix to one bus's geometry.

Only membership and order need a whole file. A property is one value per label, and no read relates one label's value to another's.

docs.title: Membership is its deepest file
docs.text:
DEP 20's rule that an axis is its deepest file holds with narrower files. dims/<dim>.parquet has the label column alone, and groups/<group>.parquet the group's struct column alone. A layer that changes only properties writes neither file.

DEP 20's removal, order and SubNetwork sections apply unchanged, except for the staging table. A removal is still the diff of a restatement against the previous one, so DEP 20's owner-map pruning and dead labels carry over. DEP 21 uses that diff and works over DEP 22 as over DEP 20.

docs.title: A property is a file of overrides
docs.text:
properties/<subject>.<name>.parquet has the subject's key column and the column <name>, one row per label the layer sets. bus.x lives in properties/bus.x.parquet, and connection.role in properties/connection.role.parquet, keyed by the connection struct. attributes/ is unchanged. A row sets the property for its label, NULL included. A label without a row keeps a shallower layer's value. One property per file keeps an unset cell apart from a NULL one with no mask, because a file has no cell its layer does not set.

A resolved property is, per label, the row of the deepest layer that has one. A resolved axis or group is the membership in order, with every property's fold joined on as a column. The API and Coords keep their shape. Properties of every subject fold per label, whether or not the subject is in partial.

docs.title: A removal cuts a label's properties
docs.text:
A property row counts only where it is deeper than every layer that removed its label. The fold takes each label's deepest removal from DEP 20's diffs, and drops its property rows at that depth and above. A label added again therefore starts with no property.

datarecord does not count a label removed and added again in one staging area as a removal. add stages a row of every declared property of each label it adds, NULL where no keyword sets it, so the label reads only the properties add gave it.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
DEP 20's refusals apply. datarecord also refuses a dims/ or groups/ file with any column beside its key, at read and in write_layer:

dims/bus.parquet carries columns ['x', 'y']; a property of bus is the file
properties/bus.<name>.parquet of the labels a layer sets it for
(.../design/format/#where-a-value-lives). Re-export the record.

An old layer with properties in an axis file then fails at read. DEP 20's silent case narrows to an old axis file with labels alone.

write_layer refuses a property file that is undeclared, has an extra column, has a key twice, or contains a label outside the membership. A read refuses the first three, and a row that contains a non-member falls out of the join onto the membership.

docs.title: The reference check
docs.text: DEP 20's check holds for group tuples. Where a layer writes rows of a property one_of a dim, or removes a label of that dim, the property is checked whole, in its final state, against the final dead labels. One row repairs a dangling value an ancestor left, and an edit of another property does not check that value.

docs.title: Caches and staging
docs.text:
A materialised revision writes resolved/dims/ and resolved/groups/ with every property's fold as a column, and a fold above it seeds from them. A NULL cell there reads as a row with NULL, which resolves the same as no row.

WorkingRecord stages membership as DEP 20 does, narrowed to the key and position. A property edit stages one row per label in a table per property, and reads no base row. remove also deletes the label's staged property rows. A read folds the staged property rows onto the frozen prefix's resolved properties as the deepest layer.

LayerSource and LayerData gain properties(), the (subject, name) pairs a layer has a file for, and property(subject, name). A write takes each column of RecordLike.properties as one property file, so a full export writes every property of every label.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Membership and order are facts about a whole axis, so DEP 20's case for a whole file holds for them. A property is a fact about one label, so a per-label override loses nothing, and set already treats it that way. partial keeps the one meaning DEP 20 gives it: which layer the owner map assigns an attribute's values to. A property varies along no dim except its subject. So a per-label override cannot make a read take part of one label's value from the layer and the rest from its parent, which is the case partial prevents.

Each figure is the median of five DuckDB runs over synthetic data at DEP 20's scale, 60,000 entities with four properties and 150,000 connections with role. The sizes before and under DEP 20 are DEP 20's.

Edit Before DEP 20 DEP 22 one entity's carrier 0.8 kB 0.30 MB 0.4 kB one connection's role one row 0.43 MB 0.4 kB add an entity one row 0.30 MB 0.30 MB, plus 4 rows remove an entity and its connections one row each 0.73 MB 0.72 MB edit one bus geometry (4,000 × 64) one row 2.49 MB one row add or remove a bus one row 2.49 MB 17.5 kB, plus 1 row per property chain of 20 edit layers 10 kB 5.57 MB 3.78 MB, estimated

The chain has 40,000 entities and 80,000 connections, and alternates removals and property edits. Its DEP 22 figure sums file sizes, a method that gives 5.56 MB for DEP 20's measured 5.57 MB. Labels dominate the synthetic axes: the entity labels take 297 kB of the file's 303 kB, and the connection keys 424 kB of 426 kB. So DEP 22 saves nothing over DEP 20 on an add or a removal. It saves where a layer edits properties, or where a subject has bulky ones.

What it costs: a read is slower, because it joins the split files. Assembling the entity axis from five files, one folded over 20 layers, took 37 ms into a table against 10.5 ms for one whole file. Folding the same 20 layers onto a materialised revision's wide file took 19 ms. The connections with role took 42 ms against 8 ms. The cut added 7 ms to a 25 ms fold of carrier. By DEP 20's measure, which fetched rows into Python, the fold before took 80 to 95 ms, the DEP 22 assembly 89 ms and one whole file 64 ms.

Staging copies less. The first membership edit copies labels and positions in 4.9 ms for the entities and 8.6 ms for the connections, against DEP 20's estimated 15 ms and 41 ms, and a property edit copies nothing. A read of the membership table takes 5.6 ms and 9.8 ms.

The fold applies six rules, where DEP 20's applies four and the earlier design's six. DEP 22 adds the deepest row per label and property, and the cut at a label's latest removal.

Module in src/datarecord/ Lines beyond DEP 20 For resolve/sources.py +30 to 40 properties(), property() and the key-only refusal resolve/coords.py +50 to 80 the property fold from a base column, the cut, the join store/write.py +40 to 60, −25 to 35 the property file checks, the reference check, one file per column mutable.py +20 to 40, −20 to 30 staging per property, add's NULL rows, _patch_axis without siblings store/cache.py 0, −5 to 15 the resolved files stay, where DEP 20 copies the deepest file

Beyond DEP 20, src grows by an estimated 140 to 220 lines and shrinks by 50 to 80. Against the earlier design that is 275 to 455 added and 150 to 210 deleted, where DEP 20 adds 135 to 235 and deletes 100 to 130.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. DEP 20's implementation, with the axis fold keeping each removed label's deepest removal.
  2. Sources, the fold, the writer and staging gain property files, as above.
  3. Fixtures write each property as its own file, and about eight new tests pin the rules above.
  4. Whichever of DEP 20 and DEP 22 is implemented, the other takes Superseded, with Superseded-By naming it.

Checks: DEP 20's checks. A property set by two layers on two labels reads per label. A label added again reads no property from below its removal, materialised or not, staged or committed.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• Properties kept in the axis file, NULL on labels a layer leaves alone: an untouched cell and a cell set to NULL read alike. A mask column per property would tell them apart, at a column per property in every restatement.
  • One properties/<subject>.parquet per subject: a layer that sets x on one bus and country on another carries each bus's other value from the parent. A hand-written file of that shape blanks the cell it leaves NULL.
  • Properties declared as attributes: the owner map keys them per label only for a subject in partial, so carrier.color would be restated whole. DEP 12 separates the two for reasons this DEP leaves standing.
  • A re-added label keeping its property rows from below its removal: a new bus would read an old bus's carrier and geometry.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• DEP 20's open issues apply unchanged.
  • A layer has up to one file per declared property, about 14 for a full PyPSA export. Each file adds requests on a remote store, and a read of properties["bus"] opens up to six files per layer.
  • An old axis file with labels alone, without a deleted column, still reads silently as a restatement.

docs.title: DEP 23: multi-dims replace groups
docs.text:
DEP 23 Title multi-dims replace groups Author Bryn Pickering Status Implemented (2026-10-26) Requires DEP 10, DEP 12, DEP 13, DEP 18, DEP 20 Created 2026-10-21 Version Unreleased Replaces the groups of DEP 2 and DEP 10

The design landed in the data model, the schema, editing and the record format. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: A group becomes a multi-dim: a dim declared under dimensions with over, whose labels are tuples of other dims' labels. It has its own table in dims/, and its coordinates are addressed as connection.bus, as properties are. A functional group's property {one_of: <dim>} becomes a property of the multi-dim, unchanged. The groups section and every public name with group in it go.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
A group already behaves as a dim does. The amendment to DEP 10 found that the fold treats it as a dim in every way. It is one struct column, broadcasts, is in partial or outside it, and has properties. DEP 20 made a layer restate its file whole, as for an axis file. Only its spelling still differs from a dim's, in each of these places:

A dim A group declared under dimensions declared under groups dims/bus.parquet groups/connection.parquet add, remove add_group, remove_group Schema.dimensions Schema.groups, group_columns, group_key, groups_of dims: [X] resolves a dim first dims: [X] resolves a group if no dim has the name a property {one_of: <dim>} may categorise it never categorised

So every reader looks up a name as a dim and then as a group, and every rule for both is stated twice.

docs.title: A multi-dim
docs.text:
A multi-dim is a dim whose labels are tuples of other dims' labels. It is declared under dimensions with over, as a group was, and has no dtype:

dimensions:
  entity: { dtype: str }
  bus: { dtype: str }
  snapshot: { dtype: datetime }
  role: { one_of: [input, output, attached] }
  connection: { over: { entity: entity, bus: bus } }
  corridor: { over: { from: bus, to: bus } }

properties:
  connection:
    role: { one_of: role }

attributes:
  efficiency: { dtype: float, dims: [connection, snapshot], default: 1 }

partial: [entity, bus, connection]
  • over is a list or a map from coordinate to dim, as a group's was. over: [entity, bus] is over: {entity: entity, bus: bus}, and corridor has two coordinates on bus. Each coordinate maps to a declared dim that is not a multi-dim.
  • datarecord refuses at load a dim that declares over beside dtype or one_of. A dim without over keeps its default dtype: str.
  • Its table is dims/connection.parquet, keyed by its struct column, with its properties as columns: connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role. A layer that changes its tuples or their properties writes it whole and in order.
  • Dimension.over has the map, and Schema.dimensions has every dim, multi or not.

docs.title: What DEP 10 settled
docs.text:
• A row addresses a multi-dim by one struct column named for it, with a field per coordinate in over order.
  • It may be listed in partial, and is then in the fold key. Otherwise it is outside partial and in no key.
  • A value is a whole tuple or NULL. datarecord refuses a struct with some fields NULL in set, in add and in the writer.
  • A NULL broadcasts over its live tuples, expanded against dims/connection.parquet as a NULL bus is against dims/bus.parquet.
  • datarecord refuses an attribute over a multi-dim and a dim named like one of its coordinates, such as dims: [connection, bus], because bus= would address both. A coordinate on bus under another name, such as port, may sit beside bus.
  • Removing a coordinate's label cascades: remove("bus", ["south"]) removes every tuple that contains south.

docs.title: Coordinates are addressed as properties are
docs.text:
connection.bus is the bus of each tuple, wherever DEP 13 lets a dotted name stand, Schema.resolve included. A coordinate is part of the key and not a property column, so datarecord refuses set("connection.bus", …) and names remove and add. datarecord resolves a default_by keyed on entity.ctype through the coordinate entity.

  • A selector keyword stays bare. bus="north" on an attribute over connection selects the tuples whose bus is north, coordinate first.
  • datarecord still refuses a property of a multi-dim named like one of its coordinates.
  • A multi-dim is never categorised. A property of it may refer to a dim with one_of, as role does, and still categorises nothing, whether partial lists the multi-dim or not. datarecord refuses a default_by keyed on one.

docs.title: A functional group is a property of a multi-dim
docs.text:
A group property {one_of: <dim>}, which DEP 18 put in place of a group's into, becomes a property of the multi-dim, declared the same way:

dimensions:
  plant_period: { over: [plant, period] } # was under `groups`
properties:
  plant_period:
    zone: { one_of: zone }

A property has one value per label of its subject, so one zone per tuple is a property. The live-label check, the remove refusal and NULL meaning none are those of any property that refers to a dim.

docs.title: Groups go
docs.text:
The groups section then has nothing left and goes. Group, Schema.groups, Schema.group_columns, Schema.groups_of, Schema.group_key, add_group, remove_group and the groups/ directory go, and dims: [X] resolves a dim and nothing else. A manifest with groups is refused as any unknown key is.

add and remove take a multi-dim's tuples as any frame DuckDB scans, with the struct column named for the multi-dim. That column is what record.dims["connection"] returns, so a read goes back in as it stands. A frame may instead have a column per coordinate, and a list of mappings from coordinate to label becomes that frame first. Every form then takes the same path and type checks. datarecord refuses a frame with both the struct column and a coordinate column as ambiguous:

w.add("connection", other.dims["connection"])  # another record's tuples, as read
w.add("connection", [{"entity": "g1", "bus": "north"}], role="output")
w.add("connection", pd.DataFrame({"entity": ["g2"], "bus": ["south"]}))
w.remove("connection", [{"entity": "g1", "bus": "north"}])

A property is a keyword, as for any dim, or a further column of the frame. datarecord refuses a tuple that contains a label missing from its coordinate's dim.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
A tuple set that is a dim in dims and a relation elsewhere has two kinds, and the caller picks one at each use. Declared under dimensions, it has one kind, with a table for its properties, and add and remove treat it as any dim.

dims/ already has one table per dim, keyed by that dim's column and restated whole. A multi-dim's table is keyed by its struct column, so a reader of the format looks in one place.

What it costs: every manifest with groups is rewritten, and every record re-exported, as groups/ moves to dims/. Every public name with group in it goes, and callers of add_group and remove_group call add and remove.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
w.set("efficiency", 0.9, entity="g1", bus="north")  # selector: the coordinates
w.set("connection.role", "input", entity="g1", bus="north")
w.set("connection.bus", "south", entity="g1")  # refused: a coordinate is the key

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Dimension.over, and the group struct-column machinery keyed on the dim.
  2. dims/<multi-dim>.parquet, with groups/ and resolved/groups/ dropped.
  3. add and remove take tuples, Schema.resolve resolves a coordinate, and the group names go.
  4. The PyPSA tool declares connection under dimensions, and fixtures are re-exported.
  5. Pages, usage pages and changelog.

Checks: the connection, broadcast, partial and cascade tests pass with connection under dimensions. The word group appears in no public name, and on no live page outside the DEPs. A PyPSA network round-trips with connection a multi-dim and role its property. datarecord refuses a zone that is not a live label on set, and refuses removing a zone that a value still refers to.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• A relation usable as a dim in dims: [connection]: a tuple set becomes a relation or a dim by where it is used.
  • No multi-dims at all, with dims: [entity, bus] and validity by a condition: this loses the struct column, the whole-or-NULL broadcast and the table for role.
  • A surrogate port dim with properties {one_of: entity} and {one_of: bus}: a value is written against a port label, and the tuple stops being the address.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Whether a multi-dim may be over another multi-dim. Nothing needs it yet, so datarecord refuses it until something does. It is on the open questions page.
  • Whether a functional mapping over two coordinates justifies a dim. plant_period exists only to have zone, and its labels must be written before the property can be. It is on the open questions page.
  • Whether a multi-dim in partial may be categorised, now that the open question on a group's categories becomes one on multi-dims. This DEP keeps a multi-dim uncategorised, and a later DEP may lift that.

docs.title: DEP 24: categories are enum dimensions
docs.text:
DEP 24 Title categories are enum dimensions Author Bryn Pickering Status Implemented (2026-10-26) Requires DEP 12, DEP 13, DEP 18, DEP 23 Created 2026-10-21 Version Unreleased

The design landed in the schema, the data model, the record format and the tools reference. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: A str dim may list its labels with one_of, as mathspec#915 does for a mathspec dimension. A category is then a label of such a dim, and a categorising property is a property {one_of: <dim>} that refers to it. DEP 18 landed that, and dropped the Enum dtype. This DEP adds two things. A dim with one_of has its axis derived from the list, so the schema lists its labels and no layer writes them. A multi-dim may be categorised, so that connection.role categorises connection.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
A closed set of values was two constructs, an Enum dtype on a property and a reference to a dim, and only one categorised. DEP 18 made them one: ctype and role are dims that list their labels, and entity.ctype: {one_of: ctype} categorises entity.

A one_of dim's labels are still data. The list only bounds the axis. A layer writes dims/ctype.parquet whole, as DEP 20 requires, and may drop a label of the list from it. PyPSA writes the whole list on every export, so the file restates the schema. datarecord checks a category that a default_by names against the list, yet that category may not be a live label in a given record.

A multi-dim is still never categorised. connection.role is {one_of: role}, role lists input, output and attached, and PyPSA lists connection in partial. Yet datarecord refuses a default_by keyed on connection.role, because only a dim in partial that is not a multi-dim has categories. DEP 23 made the group a multi-dim and left open whether the rule extends to one.

docs.title: What DEP 18 settled
docs.text: #81 proposed DEP 18 landed enum: [...] beside a String dim's dtype one_of: [...] on a str dim, mathspec#915's final key a property into an enum dimension a property {one_of: <dim>} a categorising property is one into an enum dimension, of a dim in partial the same rule, spelt one_of {Enum: [...]} refused at load refused, naming one_of PyPSA's component and role as enum dimensions PyPSA's ctype and role dims categories checked at load in a default_by and a selector checked against the dim's one_of

docs.title: A categorising property of a multi-dim
docs.text:
A property {one_of: <d>} of a multi-dim in partial, where d lists its labels, categorises the multi-dim by the rule for a dim:

dimensions:
  role: { one_of: [input, output, attached] }
  connection: { over: { entity: entity, bus: bus } }
properties:
  connection:
    role: { one_of: role }
partial: [entity, bus, connection]
  • connection.role categorises connection, because a multi-dim is a dim since DEP 23.
  • Schema.categorizing("connection") lists role, and default_for and flags key on it by plain name, as on entity.ctype.
  • A default_by keyed on connection.role applies to a value of connection: an attribute over it, or a property of it. datarecord checks its keys at load against role's one_of.
  • A selector keyword role= on an attribute over connection, or on a property of it, selects the tuples with that role. set("connection.note", v, role="output") works as set("entity.note", v, ctype="Generator") does.

docs.title: A one_of dim's axis is the schema's
docs.text:
A dim with one_of: [...] has its axis derived from the list, in list order:

  • No dims/<dim>.parquet is written or read for it, and record.dims["ctype"] is the list. The writer refuses a layer with such a file.
  • A record written whole hands over the axis among its dims. The writer drops the axis where it is the list, in the same order, and refuses any other, naming the dim and the difference.
  • datarecord refuses at load a property declared on it, because without a file no column can have one.
  • datarecord refuses add and remove on it, naming the schema.
  • Otherwise it is a dim. An attribute may range over it and a property may refer to it. A value outside the list is refused as dangling.
Before Under this DEP the list bounds the axis, and a layer writes dims/ctype.parquet whole the axis is the list, with no layer file add refuses a label outside the list, and remove works both refused PyPSA writes the whole list as the ctype and role axes on export the tool writes nothing for them a property that refers to ctype is checked against the resolved axis checked against the list, with no dead labels and no cascade a one_of dim may have properties refused

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Categories need a subject whose keys the owner map assigns per label, and partial makes a multi-dim such a subject, as it does a dim. Refusing them for a multi-dim alone would keep the one rule that set a group apart.

datarecord checks a category at load where it is named. That needs the vocabulary in the schema, and an axis that a layer may shrink lets a checked category be no live label. Deriving the axis from the list makes the axis and the list the same.

What it costs:

  • A record with a dims/ file for a one_of dim is re-exported without it. datarecord refuses a layer that writes one, and a RecordLike whose axis of it is not the list.
  • datarecord refuses at load a property declared on a one_of dim.
  • datarecord refuses add and remove on a one_of dim, so adding a PyPSA component type stays a schema change.
  • A schema that keyed a default_by on a multi-dim's property was refused, and now loads.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
schema.categorizing("connection")  # ("role",)
schema.default_for("efficiency", role="input")
w.set("efficiency", 0.95, role="output")  # selector: the category
record.flags(role="attached")
record.dims["ctype"]  # its `one_of` labels, in order
w.add("ctype", ["Hydrogen"])  # refused: a `one_of` dim's labels are the schema's

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. A one_of dim's axis is derived from the schema on read. The writer refuses its dims/ file, add, remove and properties on it are refused, and the PyPSA tool stops writing ctype and role.
  2. Schema.categorizing and Schema._categorized_by accept a multi-dim in partial, and the refusal of categories on a multi-dim goes.
  3. Category selection in set, flags and default_for joins on the multi-dim's struct column, as on a dim's column.
  4. The dims, properties, format and PyPSA pages. The open question on a multi-dim's categories moves to settled.

Checks: a one_of dim has no layer file, and record.dims of it is its list. A default_by keyed on connection.role loads, and a misspelt role in it fails at load. default_for and flags agree per role on a PyPSA network.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• Enum kept beside one_of dims: two ways to state "one of these labels", one categorising and one not, by dtype. DEP 18 settled it.
  • A one_of dim that a layer may grow beyond its list: a category in a default_by could then be checked only against the folded record, not at load.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• An axis that a layer writes, bounded by the list, the design before this DEP. A layer writes the axis, add refuses a label outside the list and remove works. A tool or layer then chooses which labels exist, and a one_of dim may have properties. The cost is a file that restates the schema, and a category that may not be a live label.
  • Whether a one_of dim may grow in a layer. Its labels are the schema's, so a custom PyPSA component is a schema change, not a data edit. That is the cost of checking categories at load.

docs.title: DEP 25: each layer has its own manifest
DEP 25: each layer has its own manifest
docs.text:
DEP 25 Title each layer has its own manifest Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented (2026-11-03) Requires DEP 9 Created 2026-10-29

The design landed in store, format, schema, layers and resolution. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: Each layer has its own manifest.json, which lists the layer's id, parent, full schema, files and a flat meta map. The layer manifests replace the store's one manifest.json and its revisions/ tree. A create-only claim.json reserves a layer's id and writing the manifest commits it, so a job may keep a revision open for days. Every file in a store is then written once.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Before this DEP, every write that widens the schema races on the store's one manifest.json through a bounded compare-and-swap. A writer can lose that race after writing its layer, and a credential that cannot read the manifest fails every write. With one schema per store, one branch's new attribute also widens the schema of its siblings.

A workflow has no place in the store for a run's id. A run that takes days writes layer files that no revision file lists yet, and a cleanup cannot tell them from a failed write. A standalone directory and a layer differ only by where the manifest sits, yet ws.at and store.layer read them under two rules.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
<location>/layers/<id>/
├── claim.json          # written when the id is reserved, kept
├── manifest.json       # written last: the revision exists from then
├── dims/<dim>.parquet
├── attributes/<attr>.parquet
└── resolved/           # materialised owner map, unchanged

<location>/manifest.json and <location>/revisions/ go. A standalone directory is one layer at its own URI, with parent: null in its manifest.json.

docs.title: The layer manifest
docs.text:
schema is the full schema the layer was written under, not a delta. files lists the dims and attributes the layer wrote, by declared name. meta is a flat map of str, int, float or bool values, set at the write, immutable and not inherited.

A child's schema must pass compatible_with against its parent's, and a root's may be any schema. A read opens exactly the files that files lists, globs nothing and ignores any other file in the layer. schema.meta stays, and a child inherits it with the rest of the schema. Schema.id goes.

docs.title: Claim and commit
docs.text:
Step File Write Contains claim claim.json create-only id, parent, meta, created data dims/, attributes/ unconditional the layer's parquet commit manifest.json create-only the layer manifest

A claim stays after the commit, so a second claim of one id fails at any time. A revision exists from the moment its manifest does. A layer with a claim and no manifest is pending, and no read opens it. The commit checks that the manifest's parent equals the claim's, and that its meta keeps every key of the claim's unchanged. It may add keys, such as an outcome the job learns at its end.

Data goes straight into layers/<id>/, so the local staging directory and its rename go. A local resolved/ file keeps its temporary name and rename, because no manifest write commits it. A remote write needs no rename, since an object appears whole or not at all.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
store.claim(*, parent: Revision | None, meta: Meta | None = None) -> Claim
claim.commit(source, *, meta: Meta | None = None) -> Revision
store.commit(source, *, parent: Revision | None, meta: Meta | None = None) -> Revision
store.commit(w, *, meta: Meta | None = None) -> Revision  # w a WorkingRecord
ws.write(source, uri, *, meta: Meta | None = None) -> Record

store.commit is store.claim(...).commit(source) in one call, and store.root and rev.child go. parent is a required keyword, so a new root is written with parent=None. store.commit refuses a parent from another store, naming both locations.

store.commit(w) writes w's edits as a child of w's base revision, and refuses a parent beside it. It refuses a base outside the store, and points to ws.write(w, uri), which writes w whole. claim.commit(w) refuses a w whose base is not the claim's parent.

A Claim passes between processes as a Revision does: it serialises as its location and id, and validates by reading its claim file.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: store.cleanup(ids=[...]) and store.cleanup(older_than=timedelta(days=14)) delete pending layers, and no other call deletes. cleanup never deletes a layer with a manifest, and refuses an id that is not pending, naming it.

docs.title: Listing and the cache
docs.text:
The workspace caches each committed manifest whole, since none ever changes, in a table revisions keyed by location and id. Its meta column is JSON, so each value has its type. Its schema column is a hash into schemas, which stores each distinct schema once. With a warm cache, building a Record reads no file.

  • revisions() lists layers/ once, and it and revision(id) read only the manifests the table lacks.
  • revisions(meta={...}) returns the revisions whose meta contains every pair given, as one query over the table.
  • claims() caches nothing, since a pending layer can still commit.

Rows are only ever added, and cleanup deletes only pending layers, so it never invalidates a row. Files gains delete(prefix) for the cleanup, and its Version precondition goes.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Each writer checks compatibility against its parent's manifest, which never changes, so no race remains. With a full schema, a read gets a revision's schema from one file, and the schema is small beside a layer.

With the files list, a remote read skips the listing per layer, so only revisions() lists layers/. A retried job's partial files do no harm, since no manifest lists them.

The claim makes a pending revision visible to a listing by meta, and to the cleanup, which must not delete a running job. Because the claim stays, one create-only write is enough to claim an id once, and no failed delete can leave the store between two states. A job may run for days, so no timeout is safe.

Below the API, a root and a child already took one code path, so the keyword parent turns the difference into an argument. A WorkingRecord has exactly one valid parent, so it supplies it.

schema.meta describes the record for a framework, such as PyPSA's network attributes, and a child inherits it. A revision's meta describes how one layer was made, such as a run id, and a child must not inherit it.

It costs:

  • datarecord cannot read an existing store, which has no layer manifests, so it is re-exported.
  • store.commit(w) writes w's edits, where rev.child(w) wrote its whole record. A whole record goes to ws.write.
  • A call that names the store and a parent names the store twice, so store.commit must refuse a mismatch, which rev.child could not make.
  • A new attribute exists only in a revision whose ancestry declares it.
  • Sibling branches may declare one name differently, which matters where their records are combined.
  • A cold listing reads one manifest per revision, each larger by its schema.
  • A failed local write leaves pending files for the cleanup, as a remote one does.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
rev = store.commit(source, parent=None, meta={"run_id": "base"})
rev.meta  # {"run_id": "base"}
rev.manifest.schema  # the schema rev was written under
claim = store.claim(parent=rev, meta={"run_id": "2026-10-29-c"})
submit(job, claim)  # the claim pickles; days later, in the job:
claim.commit(result, meta={"status": "optimal"})

store.revisions(meta={"run_id": "2026-10-29-c"})
store.claims()  # pending layers, with their meta

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Manifest and claim.json, and the write path through them, replacing store.root, rev.child, the staging rename and reconcile_schema.
  2. One read path from the manifest for ws.at and store.layer, and the cache.
  3. Claim, claims(), revisions(meta=...), cleanup and Files.delete.

Once built, no file in a store is written twice, resolved/ aside, and a commit that narrows its parent's schema leaves its layer pending.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• A schema delta per layer: reading a schema would fold the ancestry, and need a compatibility rule per delta.
  • Claiming an id by creating its directory: atomic only on a local filesystem, and S3 has no directories.
  • Dropping the claim after the commit: a reused id would fail days later at its manifest write. A failed delete would leave a committed layer that looks pending.
  • A heartbeat in the claim: a file a job rewrites for days, for a timeout that would fail every long job.
  • rev.child, with the parent as receiver: it splits one write into two calls, and a pending claim has no receiver.
  • A commit that keeps the claim's meta exactly: a job learns its outcome at its end, and would have to keep it outside the store.
  • Removals in the files list: a second way to remove, which the fold would also have to obey.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Combining records across branches that declare one name differently needs a schema merge or a refusal (DEP 14).
  • Materialising every K layers waits until owner-map size and fold time are measured on a large record.
  • Writing in steps, claim.write(...) before claim.commit(), for a job that stores results as they come. The writer's checks against the final axes would move to the commit.
  • A moving pointer, such as a named head or one child per parent, needs a mutable file with a compare-and-swap, and is left out.

docs.title: DEP 26: the fold reads each layer under its own schema
DEP 26: the fold reads each layer under its own schema
docs.text:
DEP 26 Title the fold reads each layer under its own schema Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented (2026-11-03) Requires DEP 25 Created 2026-10-30

The design landed in resolution, schema, store, editing and open questions. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: The fold reads each layer under the schema in that layer's manifest: its partial and its attributes' dims. A revision's owner map then depends on its ancestry alone, so its fold table and its materialised map stay valid whatever a descendant declares. Where a deeper layer's schema is wider, the fold first extends the map folded so far to it.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Before this DEP, every layer of an ancestry folds under one schema, the record's current one. Adding a dim to partial changes the owner map's key, so no materialised map or fold table keyed before the change stays usable. Every revision below the change then refolds its ancestry from the root, which materialisation exists to avoid. The workspace keeps one fold table per key for the same revision.

Widening an attribute's dims by a dim already in partial keeps the key, so a map folded before the change stays in use. Its rows for that attribute have varies and broadcast both false along the dim. The read's join then finds no stored key, and the attribute reads empty (#117).

With DEP 25, each layer has the full schema it was written under, and compatible_with holds along every ancestry. So partial and each attribute's dims only grow from a layer to its child, and the fold can read each layer as it was written.

docs.title: Each layer under its own schema
docs.text:
• A layer's owner-map rows are keyed by its own schema's partial dims, and its flags follow its own attributes' dims. Every source in a fold has its own layer's schema.
  • A revision's owner map is keyed by that revision's schema, and its read resolves under it.
  • The fold table is owner_map_<id>, with no key in its name. A materialised owner_map.parquet always stays usable.
  • read_owner_map, materialised and sources_to_read lose their schema parameter, and LayerSource.materialised its schema argument.

docs.title: Extending the map to a wider schema
docs.text:
Where a layer's schema is wider than the schema of its parent's map M, the fold extends M before folding the layer onto it. A map folded live and a materialised seed extend the same way. Two changes need an extension, whether or not d is new to the schema:

Change in the layer's schema Extension of M d added to an attribute's dims the field d in both flag structs, with broadcast.d set on the attribute's rows, which are NULL along d d joins partial a NULL key column for rows not varying along d, and a split of the others

The first extension marks in the flags that the rows broadcast along d, so the read joins them as broadcast and flags() reports them. No map then lacks a flag field that its revision's schema declares. Two consecutive layers with one schema extend nothing.
