The split divides a row with varies.d, an overlap row included, by the labels that its assigned layer wrote along d at that key:

  • One join of M's varying rows against the files of the layers they are assigned to gives one row per label, keyed as stored and NULL-safe on the old key. Where the layer also wrote the key NULL along d, it gives one more row, NULL there. A multi-dim's labels are its tuples.
  • The fold recomputes each split row's flags per new key, with the aggregate a layer's own rows use.
  • The fold drops each split row with a label of d removed at M's revision. The read hid those rows there, and once d is a key column, no read will.
  • While d is outside partial, the fold keeps the labels each restatement removed along d, seeded from a materialised base, minus the parent's axis. Usually there are none, and the fold skips this drop.
  • From the layer on, the fold prunes d by the layer's removals as it does any partial dim.
  • Where bool_or(varies.d) over M is false, as for a dim new to the schema, the projection alone is the extension.

No other compatible change affects the fold. To refuse a crossing along a dim outside partial, the fold judges the layer's rows against the extended map, under the layer's schema.

docs.title: Deleting a value along a dim outside partial
docs.text: A layer that restates a key along a dim outside partial and omits a label its parent had there deletes that value. A later widening of partial no longer brings it back. A WorkingRecord edit fills the untouched coordinates of the key. datarecord makes each WorkingRecord edit carry a label's whole extent, but a layer written another way need not.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
A layer's rows have the meaning that its own schema gives them. Only folding a layer under another schema forces datarecord to key a cache by schema. Read per layer, a revision's map is a function of write-once layers, so a cache is valid forever, with no key to check.

The split is needed because a NULL key column does not mean the same for every row. Take a root under partial = {entity} writing (gas, low) 1 and (gas, high) 2, and a child under {entity, scenario} writing (gas, high) 3. Extended with NULL, the root's map row becomes (gas, NULL), and its varies.scenario is still true. The read joins it only to the root's rows stored NULL along scenario, of which there are none, so (gas, low) is lost. Split, the owner map assigns (gas, low) and (gas, high) to the root, and the child's row covers the second. The read gives (gas, low) 1 and (gas, high) 3.

Recomputed flags keep each split row joined to the file rows its own key matches. A split row that inherited both varies.d and broadcast.d would also join the layer's row NULL along d, and return its label twice.

It costs:

  • A fold reads one schema per layer. DEP 25's cache contains it, so a warm read opens no file for it.
  • A read under a wider partial adds a projection, and a split join that reads the attribute files' key columns. It runs once per revision, cached with its fold, instead of a refold of the ancestry.
  • Adding a long axis such as snapshot to partial grows the map to a row per label where rows vary along it, as a refold does.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Nothing a user writes changes. After a descendant widens the schema, datarecord reads a materialised revision as it is, so rev.materialise() before a widening is no longer wasted.

rev.materialise()
child = store.commit(source, parent=rev)  # source declares scenario in partial
child.record.attributes["p_max_pu"]  # child folded onto rev's map, extended

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Each source has its layer's schema from its manifest, and _own and _over key and flag by it.
  2. _fold_onto extends the map wherever the schema widens, with the split and the drop of rows with removed labels. _as_stored and _owners lose their defaults for a missing flag field.
  3. The fold table becomes owner_map_<id>, and the schema parameter and the key check leave read_owner_map, materialised and sources_to_read.

Once built, each revision reads the same before and after a descendant widens the schema, with and without materialised maps. The example in the rationale reads (gas, low) 1 and (gas, high) 3. No workspace holds two fold tables for one revision.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• A NULL key column for every widening: it loses the rows varying along a dim that joins partial, as in the rationale's example.
  • Refolding the ancestry under the widest schema: it invalidates every cache below the widening, and reads a layer under a foreign partial.
  • Split rows inheriting their parent row's flags: a row that had a key both ways would return its label twice.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Whether WorkingRecord gets an explicit way to delete one value along a dim outside partial. Only a hand-written layer can.
  • Whether a layer may remove a dim d from partial. It would restate, as resolved, every key of its own partial at which a parent map row has a label of d. The fold would project d out of the parent's map, dropping every row with a label of d. It would refuse a layer leaving one uncovered. compatible_with would accept the smaller partial, and a helper would build such a layer from a revision.

docs.title: DEP 31: `select` returns a view of a record's labels
DEP 31: select returns a view of a record's labels
docs.text:
DEP 31 Title select returns a view of a record's labels Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented (2026-11-04) Requires DEP 12, DEP 20, DEP 23, DEP 24 Created 2026-11-02 Version Unreleased

The design landed in selecting, select a view and open questions. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: record.select(**labels) returns a Selection: a RecordLike at the labels named, which it takes as xarray's sel does. One label squeezes its dim out of the schema, and a list, a slice or a partial date string keeps it. A label that refers to a dropped label goes too, as in a removal. lift puts the squeezed labels back on rows computed over the selection.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text: PR 112 gives the PyPSA tool a select= argument on build and verify. Most of what it does follows from the schema alone: matching labels, squeezing a dim and dropping what refers to a dropped label. A frontend, a plot and a second tool would each write it again.

docs.title: The call
docs.text:
def select(record: RecordLike, /, **labels: Any) -> Selection: ...


class Selection:  # a RecordLike: schema, dims, properties, attributes, flags
    base: RecordLike  # the record selected from, never a Selection
    labels: Mapping[str, Any | list[Any]]  # as asked, normalised

    def select(self, **labels: Any) -> Selection: ...
    def lift(self, attribute: str, rel: DuckDBPyRelation) -> DuckDBPyRelation: ...

select takes any RecordLike, and Record.select calls it. The protocol does not grow.

labels contains the request, normalised. One label stays a label of the dim's dtype. A list stays a list, and a slice or a partial date string becomes the list of labels it matched. A dim's label is never a list, so isinstance(value, list) tells a squeeze from a kept dim. What propagation narrows shows only in the selection's axes.

view.base.select(**view.labels) is the same selection. Selection.select merges its keywords into labels, a later keyword replacing an earlier one of its dim, and selects base once.

docs.title: Keywords and values
docs.text:
A keyword is a dim's name, as in set. A keyword for a multi-dim's coordinate that is no dim, such as from=, narrows the tuples. Any other keyword is a property's name, which narrows its subject to the labels whose value, default applied, is selected. A NULL value is never selected. Coordinate and property keywords never squeeze, so their values are stored as lists. select refuses a property or coordinate name that two subjects declare, and a multi-dim's own name.

Value Selects The dim one label the label, as pandas' .loc matches it squeezed a partial date string, on a datetime axis every label in its span kept, even at one a list each label exactly, read as the dim's dtype kept, even at one slice(start, stop) the labels between, both ends inclusive, None open kept, even at one

A date string is partial where it is coarser than the axis, so "2013-02" on a daily axis selects February. In a list, a date string is one instant. A slice is pandas' label slice on the sorted labels of a number or datetime dim, and a partial date string at an end covers its span. Kept labels are in axis order, and every relation keeps the base's row order.

select refuses, naming the keyword:

  • a name that is no dim, coordinate or property, a label the axis lacks, and an empty list
  • a slice with a step, over a text axis, with an end the axis cannot compare, or covering no label
  • a squeezed label that another keyword's selection drops
  • squeezing every dim of a record that declares attributes

docs.title: Squeezing a dim
docs.text:
To squeeze d at the label l, select keeps l alone, so everything that refers to another label of d goes. Then:

  • d leaves the schema, with its axis and its properties.
  • A property that refers to d goes. A default_by keyed on it applies its entry for l as the default, and the keys before it still override.
  • Where a default_by lists l and a kept label is NULL on the property, select refuses the squeeze, because the label's value would change. The caller writes [l].
  • A multi-dim with a coordinate on d loses that coordinate, and one left with no coordinate is squeezed with it.
  • An attribute over d keeps its rows at l and those NULL on d, settled along d alone, without the column. One over squeezed dims alone is one value over no dim.
  • partial and every Flags lose d.

Any dim squeezes, and a reader that needs one refuses a selection without it.

docs.title: What goes with a dropped label
docs.text:
A selection keeps every axis closed under reference, as the writer keeps a layer's:

  • A label whose property, default applied, is a dropped label goes. A NULL stays.
  • A tuple that contains a dropped label goes, and its other labels stay.
  • This repeats until nothing goes, so dropping a country drops a bus through bus.state and state.country.
  • An attribute row that contains a dropped label, in a column or a struct field, goes. A row NULL there stays.

Propagation never runs the other way: a dim keeps a label even where no kept label refers to it. A removal follows the same rule, except that a removal refuses where a selection drops the referring label.

docs.title: Laziness and layers
docs.text:
select reads only the axes and properties it needs, and raises its refusals at the call. Every attribute stays a plan: a semi-join against the kept labels and a settle along each squeezed dim. A selection needs neither the layers nor partial.

A selection writes nothing, and WorkingRecord refuses it. Over a WorkingRecord, select resolves the narrowed axes at the call, so a label added later is outside them. An axis nothing narrows reads as the base's, and an attribute reads the base's later edits at the kept labels.

docs.title: Lifting rows back to the base
docs.text:
view.lift(attribute, rel) adds the squeezed labels back to rows computed over a selection, from labels and base.schema alone. It adds a column per squeezed dim of the attribute, and puts a squeezed coordinate back into its struct. An attribute the base declares over no squeezed dim comes back unchanged. With record.select(scenario="high"), price rows over bus, snapshot come back with scenario = high.

lift inverts a squeeze one way only. A base row NULL on the squeezed dim comes back at the label, where a write-back wants it.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Selection belongs to the record because the schema sets its rules: what refers to what, which tuples contain a label and how a NULL broadcasts. A tool that restated them would duplicate rules that the format already sets.

One label squeezes its dim for every reader, as in xarray. If it squeezed for one reader and not another, one call would give two selections.

labels records the request, and the request alone rebuilds the selection, so datarecord derives propagation and never stores it.

Propagation never runs back from a dropped label. Dropping a carrier nobody has would drop labels nobody selected.

lift uses only the labels asked for and the base's schema, not what a value means. The reader decides which results a subset may write.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
record.select(snapshot=slice("2013-02", "2013-03"))  # February and March
record.select(period=2030).select(carrier=["AC"]).labels
# {"period": 2030, "carrier": ["AC"]}

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. datarecord.select and Selection, exported beside settle, taken mostly from PR 112, with Record.select calling it. A tool adopts Selection in its own change.
  2. Once built, view.base.select(**view.labels) equals view relation by relation. view.lift of every attribute is a subset of the base's rows at the selected labels.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• select= on each tool's build and verify: each tool repeats the schema's rules.
  • A narrowing hook passed to select: it couples the selection to a tool, where a further select does the same.
  • A dim that one label does not squeeze, declared in the schema or by a reader: one call would give two selections.
  • Recording propagated labels: two records of one selection could disagree.
  • Dropping a label nobody refers to any more: it drops labels nobody selected.
  • A selection as a child layer: it writes, and a squeeze restates nothing.
  • Dropping a kept label NULL on a property instead of refusing the squeeze: one label and a list of it would keep different labels.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Naming a label by a property's value, such as a timestamp for snapshot=.
  • Whether a multi-dim left with one coordinate reads as that dim.
  • Editing through a selection, staging at the base's coordinates through lift.
  • A selection whose narrowed axes follow a WorkingRecord's edits, and registering a selection as DuckDB views.
  • Whether propagation applies a default that is not a live label (open questions).

docs.title: DEP 33: the fold is a fixed plan
DEP 33: the fold is a fixed plan
docs.text:
DEP 33 Title the fold is a fixed plan Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented (2026-11-03) Requires DEP 26 Created 2026-11-03

The design landed in resolution, editing and layers. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: The fold becomes one query with fixed joins, because each row's set of dims is a column value. A WorkingRecord then plans its relations without reading a staged row, so a relation built before an edit returns that edit. Where two staged edits cross, datarecord keeps the later edit.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
A row's set of dims is the partial dims on which its key has a label. Before this DEP, the fold runs joins for each pair of sets of dims in a layer's rows. Its plan then depends on the data, and on a 16-layer PyPSA ancestry the frozen fold runs 388 joins.

A WorkingRecord plans its relations from its staged rows, so a relation built before an edit misses it. When two staged edits cross, set refuses the second, so whether an edit succeeds depends on the order of a user's clicks.

docs.title: Sets of dims as data
docs.text:
A row's set of dims is a bitmask column. The fold of a layer's owner-map rows onto the map below runs three steps:

  • Prune: an anti-join is a query that keeps the rows with no match in another table. One anti-join per partial dim drops the parent rows that contain a removed label.
  • Cover: each parent row is copied once per subset of its set of dims, tagged with the subset and its labels. A semi-join (a query that keeps the rows that do have a match) matches the copies to the layer's rows. An anti-join then drops each parent row a layer row covers.
  • Cross: both sides expand to the sets of dims the other side's row may have, where neither set contains the other. One equi-join keeps the pairs whose labels agree on the dims both rows set, and each pair gives an overlap row.

An attribute over at most one partial dim cannot cross, which the schema shows, so its fold runs no crossing join. The query computes each row's candidate masks from its own mask and its attribute's partial dims, so the plan stays one size. The fold expands owner-map rows only, never value rows.

One fold serves the frozen layers and their materialised map, the staged layer, flags() and the write of a whole record. Under DEP 26, it first widens the map to each layer's schema, and builds the masks once per distinct layer schema.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
The refusals leave the fold:

  • A workspace refuses a frozen layer's unfilled rows when it first folds that layer.
  • The writer refuses a layer in which two rows cross and no row sets both. A read of a layer from another writer fails at the crossing.
  • set refuses an edit whose own rows cross, and rolls it back. It fills every row it stages, so it runs no check for unfilled rows.

docs.title: Contested layers
docs.text:
A layer is contested for an attribute where its rows have different sets of dims. Rows of such a layer cover some points twice, and the read keeps the more specific row there. A flag on each map row is true where its layer is contested. The read ranks the value rows of contested layers in one arm, and passes every other layer's rows through a second arm unranked. A frozen Record keeps its Python check, and takes the ranking arm only where a layer is contested.

No read is slower than before, at any depth or series length. A read may use more memory by a small constant, which does not grow with either.

docs.title: The staged layer
docs.text:
The plan of a WorkingRecord's relation never depends on the staged rows, only on the committed layers below them.

  • Every Record lists every dim and attribute its schema declares, and one with no rows gives an empty relation, not KeyError.
  • A WorkingRecord creates every staging table at once: each axis table as a copy of the base's axis, each attribute table empty. A one_of dim has none.
  • The staged layer has every axis, so dim_owners lists it for every dim, and the owner map may assign it keys of any attribute.
  • The fold always runs the anti-join for the labels a staged restatement removes, and folds the staged layer one attribute at a time.
  • The staged owner-map rows are in one table per attribute, which an edit refreshes inside its transaction. The fold, flags() and the write read them.
  • rollback() empties the attribute tables, refills each axis table from the base and drops no table.

Where a staged row crosses a new one and no staged row sets both, set stages one that does, with the new value. datarecord keeps the later edit.

The write skips a staged axis equal to the base's, in position order, and an empty attribute table. A remove that undoes an add writes nothing.

docs.title: The nearest fold at hand
docs.text: A fold seeds from the deepest proper ancestor whose fold is materialised or held by the workspace, and takes its owner map, axes and dead labels as the seed. The workspace keeps the seed while its connection lives, so a child opened after a commit folds one layer.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
With sets of dims as data, the work grows only with the rows that exist. Enumerating every set of dims the schema allows would fix the plan with joins on mostly empty inputs. The price is a copy of each owner-map row per set of dims it may be joined against, at most 2^k for k partial dims. One fold also replaces two that only the tests showed to agree.

The 16-layer PyPSA ancestry has 1,000 generators over 8,760 snapshots. Its frozen fold runs 171 joins instead of 388, in 0.68× the time and 0.45× the peak buffer memory. At every series length, the fold expands to at most 5,637 rows.

Folding all attributes at once binds every staging table into every relation, which costs seconds per relation for 150 attributes. Eager staging tables make a WorkingRecord take 0.4–0.5 s to create for 153 attributes, and keep a copy of every axis. In return, nothing tracks which axes an edit touched.

A user of an editor expects datarecord to keep the last edit, as set already does where two rows have one key.

Before this DEP, the read skips the ranking where a Python check finds no contested layer, which a fixed plan cannot run. Ranking every value row made one base layer with a long series read 5× slower, with 1 GB more memory. With the contested flag and the staged owner rows in tables, every read of the 16-layer ancestry is as fast or faster, most 3–10× faster. flags() takes 0.1 s instead of up to 2.7 s.

It costs:

  • Each edit recomputes the owner rows it touched, a few percent of a large set. On small data, a read uses a few tens of MB more.
  • DuckDB 2.0 re-binds every Python relation after any committed write, so a reader should hold few relations across an edit.
  • A cold fold, with no ancestor's fold at hand, stays linear in depth, at about 0.11 s per layer over 64 layers.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.5, entity="wind1")
rel = w.attributes["p_max_pu"]
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.7, scenario="high")

The second set crosses the first and also stages wind1 under high with 0.7, which rel returns.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Every declared dim and attribute listed, and eager staging tables.
  2. The fold with sets of dims as data, the contested flag and the staged owner tables.
  3. set keeps the last edit, and a held fold reused as a seed and by materialise.
  4. Each layer's owner rows aggregated once into its checkpoint.

Once built, the suite passes with crossing staged edits changed so that set keeps the last edit. Owner maps equal the per-pattern fold's on every equivalence run and on a map it materialised, and a relation built before an edit equals one built after.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• Masks from the powerset of partial coordinates, folding all attributes at once: the prototype's plan became intractable.
  • Sets of dims enumerated per attribute from the schema: joins on sets no row has.
  • Candidate masks as a constant list: at nine partial dims, the plan takes 4.4 s to build, against 0.04 s for masks computed per row.
  • Candidate masks joined from a table per schema: it ties on PyPSA, and adds joins and memory.
  • Ranking every value row on read, for the reason in Rationale.
  • Refusing a set that crosses a staged row: whether an edit succeeds would depend on click order.
  • A checkpoint every few layers: the checks and the crossing join each read the map below, so the plan doubles per layer without one. A depth-16 fold with a checkpoint every fourth layer takes 25 s, against 3 s.
  • Separate schemas or attached databases, to avoid the re-bind: DuckDB re-binds every relation regardless.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• The checks in set and in the write still enumerate sets of dims per pattern, with fetches that depend on the data.
  • set spreads a broadcast that is scenario-scoped or crossing into one staged row per entity and snapshot.
  • When a deep ancestry should materialise its map, to bound a cold fold's depth.
  • Each edit runs in its own transaction, so it fails inside a caller's open transaction on the same cursor.

docs.title: DEP 34: `register` creates one view per relation
DEP 34: register creates one view per relation
docs.text:
DEP 34 Title register creates one view per relation Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented (2026-11-03) Requires DEP 25, DEP 26, DEP 33 Created 2026-11-02 Version Unreleased

The design landed in record, store and format. Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: record.register(name) creates a DuckDB schema name in the workspace's database. It contains one view per dim, per property subject and per declared attribute, in the nested schemas name.dims, name.properties and name.attributes. Any client of that database, a SQL client over a DuckDB server included, then reads the record without Python. Over a WorkingRecord, datarecord creates the views once and they stay live. Every edit shows in them as soon as it commits, because DEP 33 makes each relation a fixed plan.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
A frontend reads a revision and edits it through a server. The server opens a revision in a Workspace, wraps it in a WorkingRecord, and gives the frontend a name to query over a DuckDB server. The frontend then sends edits, reads them back, and finally asks for a commit.

Before this DEP, each server builds these views itself. A prototype wraps the SQL of each relation (the DuckDB query object that a read returns), from sql_query(), in CREATE VIEW, with one catalog per revision and three schemas inside. It works for a frozen record and fails for an edited one:

  • DuckDB stores a view's query when the view is created. The query of a relation over a WorkingRecord depends on the staged rows. So after an edit that changes the query, the view still runs the old one. DEP 33 makes the query fixed, which removes this fault.
  • The SQL of a staged relation refers to Python objects by name, which are gone when the view is next read.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
View One per Columns name.dims.<dim> dim, a dim with one_of included the axis, as record.dims[dim] name.properties.<d> dim that declares properties as record.properties[d] name.attributes.<a> attribute the schema declares as record.attributes[a], empty where it has no rows

Two records under one schema register the same views, since every record lists every declared dim and attribute (DEP 33).

name is a top-level schema in the workspace's database, so every cursor and every connection to it sees the views. The views are raw: a NULL coordinate means every label, two rows can cover one point, and no property default is applied. Settling rows by the broadcast rule is the client's task.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
• Record.register(name: str) -> None creates name and its views, and adds a row for name to the workspace's registered table, in one transaction. It raises if name exists.
  • Workspace.unregister(name: str) -> None drops name with its views and its row, in one transaction.
  • Workspace.registered() -> DuckDBPyRelation reads the registered table, with the columns name, revision, working and created. For a WorkingRecord, revision is the revision it was opened on. A SQL client reads the table itself.
  • WorkingRecord.rollback() leaves the views valid, since it refills the staging tables rather than dropping them (DEP 33).
  • store.commit(w) leaves the views on w as they are. A server drops them and registers a WorkingRecord on the new revision.

docs.title: Consistent states
docs.text: Every state a reader on another cursor can observe is a state that some sequence of whole edits could leave. An edit that writes several statements orders them so that each committed step is such a state, or commits them as one. A removal drops a multi-dim's tuples before the label they contain.

docs.title: Schema changes
docs.text: A WorkingRecord has no method that changes its schema, which changes only at commit. A method that changes it must refuse a change to a column or the fold of an existing view. Widening an attribute's dims, adding a property and adding a dim to partial are such changes. Adding an attribute or a dim must add its view.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
Views created once and never replaced keep a client's queries valid through any edit, with no notification between server and client. Replacing a view whenever an edit creates something new would couple the record to its registrations, and a client's query could fail between two edits.

Raw views keep the record's lazy model, in which a NULL coordinate means every label. Settled views would have to materialise every broadcast.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
w = WorkingRecord(store.revision(layer_uuid).record)
w.register("edit_3f2a")

SELECT entity, value FROM edit_3f2a.attributes.p_nom;
SELECT * FROM edit_3f2a.properties.bus WHERE carrier = 'AC';

w.set("p_nom", 150.0, entity="wind1")  # the next SELECT reads 150.0
child = store.commit(w)
ws.unregister("edit_3f2a")
WorkingRecord(child.record).register("edit_8c01")

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Edits leave only consistent states: one transaction per edit, with the frozen fold tables built before the first edit.
  2. register and unregister. The connection's _create_view creates a view with the path (name, kind, view) and the SQL of _render(rel, literals=True, wrap_text=True). DuckDBPyRelation.create_view makes the same call with a plain name. The call keeps alive the Python objects a relation reads. The public method takes one identifier only, so DuckDB is capped at the newest release the suite passed on. A test reads a view from another cursor after the relation is collected.
  3. register builds every relation before it creates any view. Each view changes the catalog, and DuckDB re-binds a relation built before that change, step by step, the next time it derives from it. What every relation of a record shares is built once: its coords, the fold of its frozen layers and the staged layer's base. A union of relations is rel.union_by_name, not con.sql over the captured relations, which binds the whole captured text again. On a PyPSA record with 168 views, this took registering from 20–25 s to about 9.5 s in a prototype. A single transaction around all creates showed no clear gain.

The check: views registered on a fresh WorkingRecord, then set, add and remove on attributes, properties, plain dims and multi-dims. After each step, every view equals the relation built afresh. On the 168-view PyPSA record of note 3, register takes at most 10 s. A second thread reading after every committed statement observes no inconsistent state.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• One catalog per revision, attached as :memory:, with three schemas inside. DuckDB 2.0 nests schemas, so the workspace's database suffices, and the views read its tables without naming the catalog.
  • One flat schema with prefixed names, dim_bus and attr_p_nom. Nested schemas keep each kind's names apart without a naming convention.
  • CREATE VIEW … AS rel.sql_query(). The text refers to Python objects that are released with the relation, and breaks on a relation with parameters.
  • A two-step registration through a helper view in main. It works with public API only, and clutters main with one view per relation.
  • Replacing views on structural edits, for the reason in Rationale.
  • Marking a registered schema instead of listing it in a table. DuckDB 2.0 does not implement comments on schemas. A comment on every view adds a catalog change per view. A marker view inside each schema is found only by a reserved view name, and a table needs no reserved name.
  • Leaving discovery to the server. A crashed server leaves schemas that no one can tell from the workspace's own.
  • MERGE INTO in place of a transaction per edit. Every edit also writes the staged owner tables, so no edit fits in one statement: set takes two or three, and rollback nine. Without a transaction, a reader saw a half-written edit in about half its reads. Inside one, MERGE was 5–30% slower than DELETE and INSERT, and no more consistent.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Schema changes that alter an existing view: refused for now, or replacing the views they affect.
  • Settling in the client: settle ported to the frontend, and a page on the raw format for SQL clients.
  • Cleanup: who unregisters an abandoned schema, and by what rule. The registered table lists them, and DuckDB 2.0 has no comments on schemas to mark them by.
  • A public create_view that takes a qualified name, to request upstream.
  • DuckDB 2.0 lets a reader on another cursor see part of a committed transaction that writes about 300,000 rows or more, in 0.1–1% of reads. No edit can rule it out until DuckDB does, and it is to be reported upstream.
  • register or the first read of a view runs the cold fold of a deep revision, once per lineage in a workspace. It stays linear in depth until a revision's map is materialised.
  • The workspace holds the fold of every revision a server opens for the life of its connection: who drops it, and when.

docs.title: DEP 35: the workspace keeps the tables a record reads
DEP 35: the workspace keeps the tables a record reads
docs.text: DEP 35 Title the workspace keeps the tables a record reads Author Jonas Hörsch Status Draft (2026-11-04) Requires DEP 33, DEP 34 Created 2026-11-04

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: The tables a workspace creates move out of main into three schemas. _fold contains each revision's fold, _staged each WorkingRecord's staging tables, and _scratch a call's intermediates. A record or a registration that reads a nested schema takes a hold on it. The workspace drops the schema when its last hold is released, at the record's close() or the registration's unregister. A WorkingRecord collected unclosed releases its holds, and a Record collected unclosed passes them to the workspace.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Before this DEP, a long-lived workspace, such as a server that opens a revision per request, grows without bound. Two kinds of table are never dropped:

  • The fold tables of each revision, owner_map_<rid>, dims_<dim>_<rid>, dead_<name>_<rid> and dim_owners_<rid>. The first cursor to read an unmaterialised revision creates them. Every record and WorkingRecord of the revision, a descendant's cold fold and their registered views read them.
  • The staging tables staged_*_<layer> of each WorkingRecord, about 310 for a PyPSA record, which it and the views registered on it read.

Every other table lives within one call, which drops it. DuckDB drops a table that a view reads without complaint, and the view fails only when next queried. A relation has no reference to the record it came from.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Schema Contains Created by main schemas, revisions, registered the workspace _fold.<rid> owner_map, dims_<dim>, dead_<name> and dim_owners of revision rid the first cursor to fold rid _staged.<layer> a WorkingRecord's staging tables WorkingRecord(...) _scratch a fold's checkpoints, an edit's snapshot, the PyPSA exporter's joins the call using them, which drops them <name> the views of a registration (DEP 34) register(name)

The workspace creates _fold, _staged and _scratch with itself, so register refuses them as taken names. The id in a nested schema's name keys its tables, which no longer carry it.

docs.title: Holders
docs.text:
Holder Takes a hold on Releases on a Record _fold.<id> of each layer it folds close() a WorkingRecord as a Record over its base, and its _staged.<layer> close(), or garbage collection a registration every schema the registering record has a hold on Workspace.unregister(name) the workspace every schema of a Record collected unclosed never

A record takes its holds at construction, whether the schemas exist yet or not. A Record over rid folds the layers down to the deepest materialised ancestor, and reads _fold.<rid> and any ancestor's _fold.<id> it has a hold on. When the last hold on a schema is released, the workspace drops the schema with every table in it. A registration takes its hold inside the transaction that creates its views, so no unregister finds the schema without a hold.

A registration's row in registered lists its schemas in a held column. A workspace opened on a file takes those holds again for it, so its views still read, and unregistering one drops them.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
• Record.close() -> None releases the record's holds. A second call does nothing.
  • Record is a context manager, which closes it on exit.
  • Garbage collection closes a WorkingRecord that is still open. A Record collected unclosed passes its holds to the workspace.
  • A closed record refuses every read and edit with an error that states it is closed.
  • Revision.record builds a new record once the one it caches is closed.
  • WorkingRecord(...) is refused while its cursor has an open transaction, because the workspace's own cursor could not see the staging tables to drop them.

docs.title: Lifetime of a relation
docs.text: A relation taken from a record, such as record.attributes["p_nom"], is valid while the record is open. Once the record is closed and no other hold covers its tables, reading the relation fails with DuckDB's missing-table error. A WorkingRecord's relation fails the same way once it is collected. A relation of a Record collected unclosed stays valid. A registered view stays valid until it is unregistered, whatever happens to the record.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
close() frees a workspace when the caller chooses, as a server answering a request needs. The finaliser covers a forgotten WorkingRecord. One weakref.finalize serves both: close() detaches it and releases, so the release runs at most once.

A Record's finaliser passes its holds on rather than releasing them. In store.revision(rid).record.attributes["p_nom"].df(), nothing keeps a name for the record, so the collector may take it before .df() runs. A release there would drop the fold that .df() reads, and the read would fail at random. The workspace keeps a forgotten Record's tables as it did before this DEP. A closed Record has no holds left. Nobody reads a WorkingRecord that way, and its staging tables are worth dropping.

A Record takes a hold on every layer's fold it reads, because the workspace would otherwise drop an ancestor's fold with the ancestor's last record.

A schema per revision and per record is the unit of a hold. One DROP SCHEMA … CASCADE drops a WorkingRecord's staging tables, and the holds list a handful of schemas, not hundreds of tables. Nesting keeps the top level that a SQL client sees to main, the three schemas and the registrations.

A registration takes holds on the schemas of its record rather than on the tables its SQL reads. The two sets cover the same tables, and by taking the record's set, datarecord need not parse the views.

The holds are in a Python mapping on the Workspace, behind one lock. A record cannot outlive the process, and a registration, the one holder that can, is a row of registered, which a reopened workspace lists.

A finaliser can run in any thread at any allocation, even inside a transaction on that thread's cursor. The workspace therefore drops schemas on a cursor of its own, under the lock. The lock also stops a lookup on another thread finding a schema between its last release and its drop.

It costs a contract: a relation is valid only while its record is open, or while its WorkingRecord is uncollected.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
with Record.at(uri) as r:
    df = r.attributes["p_nom"].df()

w = WorkingRecord(store.revision(layer_uuid).record)
w.register("edit_3f2a")
w.close()  # the views still read: the workspace keeps their tables for the registration
ws.unregister("edit_3f2a")  # the staging tables are dropped

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. The holder registry on Workspace, under one lock.
  2. WorkingRecord: close(), the finaliser, the refusal after close, and the registration's holds.
  3. The layout, with every table moved into _fold, _staged and _scratch.
  4. Record: its holds, close(), the finaliser that passes holds on, and the refusal after close. A WorkingRecord reads a Record base through its own open copy, so closing the caller's base leaves its edits working.

Once built, a workspace that opens and closes records, edits and registrations in a loop ends with only main's tables and three empty schemas. A view registered on a closed record reads until it is unregistered. A read after close() raises the closed error, and a relation of a Record collected unclosed still reads.

docs.title: Rejected ideas
docs.text:
• Only a finaliser: the caller cannot choose when to free a workspace, and a record in a reference cycle waits for the cycle collector.
  • A Record's finaliser releasing, as a WorkingRecord's does: a chained read would fail whenever the collector runs between taking the relation and fetching it.
  • Only close(): every forgotten record leaks.
  • Holds kept in a DuckDB table: the Python holders do not survive a reopen, and a registration, which does, is a row of registered.
  • A top-level schema per revision and per record: the top level fills with ids.
  • A table prefix per kind in main: the workspace drops a record's tables one by one, and a SQL client sees them all.
  • Evicting shared tables by age or size: it breaks a live record's relations silently.
  • Dropping a revision's shared tables once it is materialised: a live record's relations still read them.
  • Relying on DuckDB to refuse a drop: it tracks no view's dependencies.

docs.title: Open issues
docs.text:
• Who unregisters an abandoned registration, and by what rule. Unregistering frees its tables, so the rule sets how long they stay.
  • Whether a record's planned relations form a reference cycle with it, which would delay its finaliser to the cycle collector.
  • A workspace reopened on a file keeps an earlier run's _staged and _fold schemas, which its registrations may read and no record has a hold on. Nothing sweeps those that no held column lists.

docs.title: DEP N: Title
docs.text:
DEP N Title the decision, as a short statement in sentence case Author Name Status Draft | Accepted | On hold | Implemented | Superseded | Rejected, with its date Requires the DEPs this one builds on, linked (omit if none) Created YYYY-MM-DD Version the datarecord release it ships in, Unreleased until then (omit while a draft) Replaces the DEP this one makes obsolete, linked (omit if none) Superseded-By the DEP that makes this one obsolete, linked, with the part it replaces (omit if none)

Once implemented, this paragraph reads: The design landed in [x](…) and [y](…). Where they and this DEP differ, follow those pages. It links the reference and about pages the design landed in.

A DEP is under 1,500 words. Each rule is stated once, in the section it belongs to. Cut what restates a rule, narrates how the design was found, or describes internals you can look up in the code.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: What changes, in two or three sentences.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text: The problem, in the terms of someone who uses datarecord today.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text: The design: what the schema, the format on disk and the API become, as short statements or a table.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Why this design, only where the rule does not already state it, in a short paragraph each. Then what it costs: what breaks, what gets slower and what becomes harder to state in a schema or a call.

docs.text: What a user writes with it, as short examples of what changes. On implementation these move to the how-to guides.

docs.text: The steps it is built in, in order, one line each, and the checks that pass once it is built. On implementation, where the build departs from the text above.

docs.title: How-to guides
docs.text:
Each guide finishes one task, and assumes you have taken the first tutorial.

  • Declare a schema with dims, properties, categories, attributes and partial.
  • Read a record as wide and long relations, from a directory or from SQL.
  • Select part of a record with select, and lift rows back.
  • Edit a record with set, add and remove, then commit.
  • Branch and materialise revisions in a tree.
  • Store a record locally, on S3 or across processes.
  • Use the PyPSA tool to build, solve and write results back.
  • Present a framework object as a record, for a tool author.

docs.title: Branch and materialise
docs.text: This guide shows how to branch scenarios as sibling revisions, find and materialise a revision, and write a whole record as a layer. The examples use root, rev and store from Your first record. Layers defines a revision and a layer, and the fold defines how a read combines them.

docs.title: Branch a scenario
docs.text:
Commit two WorkingRecords over the same revision, and give each revision a meta entry to find it by:

def scenario(parent, name, p_nom):
    with WorkingRecord(parent.record) as w:
        w.set("p_nom", p_nom, entity="wind1")
        return store.commit(w, meta={"scenario": name})


high = scenario(rev, "high", 150.0)
low = scenario(rev, "low", 60.0)
print(high.parent == low.parent == rev.id)

True

high and low are siblings, each a layer with one row over rev. A meta value is a string, a finite number or a boolean.

docs.title: Find a revision
docs.text:
store.revisions(meta=...) returns the revisions whose meta contains every pair you pass. ancestry() returns the ids from the root down:

for revision in store.revisions(meta={"scenario": "high"}):
    print(revision.meta, revision.ancestry() == [root.id, rev.id, high.id])
print(len(store.revisions()))
print(store.revision(low.id).record.attributes["p_nom"].df())

{'scenario': 'high'} True
4
  entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0  wind1     p_nom         NaN   60.0
1   gas1     p_nom         NaN   50.0

One revision matches, the store contains four, and low has its own p_nom for wind1. store.revision(id) loads one revision by its id.

docs.title: Read one layer alone
docs.text:
store.layer(id) reads a revision's layer without its ancestors:

print(store.layer(low.id).attributes["p_nom"].df())

  entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0  wind1     p_nom         NaN   60.0

The layer contains only the row that the commit of low wrote.

docs.title: Materialise a revision
docs.text:
materialise() writes a revision's fold under its layer's resolved/ directory. A read of it or of a descendant then stops there and opens no layer above it:

high.materialise()
higher = scenario(high, "higher", 200.0)
print(higher.record.attributes["p_nom"].df())

  entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0   gas1     p_nom         NaN   50.0
1  wind1     p_nom         NaN  200.0

The values are the same with or without materialise. Materialise a revision that many reads or children start from, such as the base of a set of scenarios.

docs.title: Write a whole record as a layer
docs.text:
store.commit writes any record whole as a child of parent, and with parent=None as a new root:

copy = store.commit(higher.record, parent=None, meta={"from": "higher"})
print(copy.parent, copy.ancestry() == [copy.id])

None True

The new root contains the folded values of higher, with no history.

docs.title: Claim a revision before its data exists
docs.text:
store.claim reserves a revision id under a parent, and claim.commit writes the layer later, from the same or another process:

claim = store.claim(parent=rev, meta={"run": "b"})
print([c.id for c in store.claims()] == [claim.id])
done = claim.commit(higher.record, meta={"status": "done"})
print(done.meta)

True
{'run': 'b', 'status': 'done'}

done has the claim's meta and the commit's. The commit may add meta keys but not change those of the claim. A claim that is never committed stays pending, and no read opens it, until you clean it up:

from datetime import timedelta

stale = store.claim(parent=rev)
print(store.cleanup(ids=[stale.id]) == [stale.id])
print(store.cleanup(older_than=timedelta(days=14)))

True
[]

cleanup returns the ids it deleted: the stale claim, then none older than 14 days. Store a record shows how to hand a claim to another process.

docs.title: Declare a schema
docs.text:
This guide shows how to declare each part of a schema, and how to check a changed schema against the old one. The data model defines each term.

This schema has every part the sections below use:

from datarecord import AttributeSpec, Dimension, PropertySpec, Schema

schema = Schema(
    dimensions={
        "entity": Dimension(dtype="str"),
        "ctype": Dimension(one_of=["Generator", "Load", "StorageUnit"]),
        "bus": Dimension(dtype="str"),
        "carrier": Dimension(dtype="str"),
        "snapshot": Dimension(dtype="datetime"),
        "connection": Dimension(over=["entity", "bus"]),
    },
    properties={
        "entity": {
            "ctype": PropertySpec(one_of="ctype"),
            "carrier": PropertySpec(one_of="carrier"),
            "sign": PropertySpec(
                dtype="float", default=1.0, default_by={"entity.ctype": {"Load": -1.0}}
            ),
        },
        "bus": {
            "carrier": PropertySpec(one_of="carrier", default="AC"),
            "x": PropertySpec(dtype="float"),
        },
    },
    attributes={
        "p_nom": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"entity"}, default=0.0, unit="MW"),
        "p_max_pu": AttributeSpec(
            dtype="float", dims={"entity", "snapshot"}, default=1.0, unit="per unit"
        ),
        "p_min_pu": AttributeSpec(
            dtype="float",
            dims={"entity", "snapshot"},
            default=0.0,
            default_by={"entity.ctype": {"StorageUnit": -1.0}},
        ),
        "efficiency": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"connection"}, default=1.0),
    },
    partial={"entity", "bus", "connection"},
)

docs.title: Declare the dims
docs.text: Give each dim a Dimension with a dtype of "str", "int", "float" or "datetime". Where the schema fixes the labels, as for ctype, pass one_of with the list instead. Such a dim has no axis file and no properties, and add refuses its labels.

docs.title: Declare a multi-dim
docs.text:
Pass over with the dims whose labels form its tuples. A list is short for a mapping in which each coordinate is named after its dim:

print(schema.multi_dims, schema.over("connection"))

('connection',) {'entity': 'entity', 'bus': 'bus'}

over("connection") returns the mapping that the list stands for. To name a coordinate differently from its dim, pass the mapping, as in Dimension(over={"from": "bus", "to": "bus"}) for a line between two buses.

docs.title: Declare properties
docs.text:
Under properties, key each property by its subject dim and give it exactly one of dtype and one_of. With one_of, the property's values are labels of the dim you give, as the values of entity.carrier are labels of carrier. A property name belongs to its subject, so bus.x and an attribute x are two names.

datarecord refuses a spec with both:

PropertySpec(one_of="carrier", dtype="str")

pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for PropertySpec
  Value error, a property declares exactly one of `dtype` and `one_of`, not both [type=value_error, input_value={'one_of': 'carrier', 'dtype': 'str'}, input_type=dict]
    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.13/v/value_error

docs.title: Set a default per category
docs.text:
A default_by overrides default for some categories, on a property or an attribute alike. Key it on the dotted name of a categorising property, such as entity.ctype:

print(schema.categorizing("entity"))
print(schema.default_for("p_min_pu", ctype="StorageUnit"))
print(schema.default_for("entity.sign", ctype="Load"))

('ctype',)
-1.0
-1.0

ctype is the one categorising property of entity, and a storage unit's p_min_pu and a load's sign both default to -1.0. If the subject dim is outside partial, datarecord refuses the default_by:

Schema(**schema.model_dump() | {"partial": {"bus", "connection"}})

pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for Schema
  Value error, property entity.sign's `default_by` is keyed by 'entity.ctype', which is a property of 'entity', which `partial` does not list [type=value_error, input_value={'version': 1, 'dimension...onnection'}, 'meta': {}}, input_type=dict]
    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.13/v/value_error

docs.title: Declare attributes
docs.text:
Give each attribute a dtype and the dims it varies over, multi-dims included, and a default for a point that no row covers. unit and description are stored as written and never interpreted:

print(schema.coordinates_of("efficiency"))

('connection',)

efficiency is keyed by the one connection coordinate, a struct of entity and bus. datarecord refuses a dim in dims that the schema does not declare:

Schema(
    dimensions={"entity": Dimension(dtype="str")},
    attributes={"p_nom": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"entity", "bus"})},
)

pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for Schema
  Value error, attribute 'p_nom' is addressed by undeclared dims ['bus'] [type=value_error, input_value={'dimensions': {'entity':...}), breakpoints=False)}}, input_type=dict]
    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.13/v/value_error

docs.title: Choose partial
docs.text:
List in partial the dims along which a child layer overrides one label's value. Leave out a dim whose values change together, such as snapshot for a time series. Layers states the rule.

PyPSA.verify reports snapshot in partial, and PyPSA.build raises for it (tools).

docs.title: Check a changed schema against the old one
docs.text:
compatible_with returns one reason per change that stops datarecord reading layers written under the old schema with the new one. An empty list means datarecord can still read them:

cost = AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"entity", "snapshot"})
wider = Schema(
    **schema.model_dump() | {"attributes": schema.attributes | {"marginal_cost": cost}}
)
retyped = Schema(
    **schema.model_dump()
    | {
        "attributes": schema.attributes
        | {"p_nom": AttributeSpec(dtype="int", dims={"entity"})}
    }
)
print(wider.compatible_with(schema))
print(retyped.compatible_with(schema))

[]
["attribute 'p_nom' dtype float -> int"]

Adding an attribute is compatible, and retyping one is not. store.commit runs the same check against the parent's schema, and raises a ValueError that lists the reasons.

docs.title: Edit a record
docs.text:
This guide shows how to stage edits on a WorkingRecord, check them, and commit them as a child revision. The examples use record, rev, store and ws from Your first record.

You make a WorkingRecord over a committed Record, and a read of it returns that record with the edits applied. Each edit runs in its own transaction, so a refused edit stages nothing.

docs.title: Set attribute values
docs.text:
Name the attribute, then the value, then a keyword per coordinate. Pass a scalar for one value at each label named, a list for one value per label in order, or a mapping keyed by label:

import pandas as pd

from datarecord import WorkingRecord

w = WorkingRecord(record)
w.set("p_nom", 120.0, entity=["wind1", "gas1"])
w.set("p_nom", [120.0, 60.0], entity=["wind1", "gas1"])
w.set("p_nom", {"wind1": 120.0, "gas1": 60.0})
print(w.attributes["p_nom"].df())

  entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0  wind1     p_nom         NaN  120.0
1   gas1     p_nom         NaN   60.0

Each set replaces the rows it names, so the last one stands. Pass a series to set values along the coordinate its index is named after. Pass a property as a keyword to set values at the labels that match it when you call set:

series = pd.Series([0.2, 0.6, 0.4], index=pd.Index([0, 1, 2], name="snapshot"))
w.set("p_max_pu", series, entity="wind1")
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.95, ctype="Generator", carrier="gas")
print(w.attributes["p_max_pu"].df())

  entity  snapshot attribute  breakpoint  value
0  wind1         2  p_max_pu         NaN   0.40
1   gas1      <NA>  p_max_pu         NaN   0.95
2  wind1         1  p_max_pu         NaN   0.60
3  wind1         0  p_max_pu         NaN   0.20

wind1 has its series, and gas1, the one gas generator, has one row with snapshot NULL. A coordinate you pass no keyword for is NULL, which means every label, those added later included. To set only the labels there are now, name them or their category. set also takes a long frame from pandas, polars, Arrow or DuckDB with a column per coordinate and a value column.

docs.title: Set a property
docs.text:
Name a property by its subject, subject.name:

w.set("entity.carrier", "gas", entity="wind1")
print(w.properties["entity"].df())

  entity      ctype carrier
0  wind1  Generator     gas
1   gas1  Generator     gas

wind1 now has the carrier gas. A plain name is an attribute, so w.set("carrier", ...) raises a KeyError that suggests entity.carrier.

docs.title: Roll back the staged edits
docs.text:
rollback discards every staged edit:

w.rollback()
print(w.properties["entity"].df())

  entity      ctype carrier
0  wind1  Generator    wind
1   gas1  Generator     gas

The properties are as committed again.

docs.title: Add and remove labels
docs.text:
add takes a dim, its labels, and a keyword per property. A multi-dim takes tuples as mappings from coordinate to label. Add a label before you set a value at it or use it in a property or a tuple:

w.add("carrier", ["solar"])
w.add("entity", ["pv1"], ctype="Generator", carrier="solar")
w.add("connection", [{"entity": "pv1", "bus": "south"}])
w.set("p_nom", 40.0, entity="pv1")
w.remove("bus", ["north"])
print(w.dims["connection"].df())

                           connection
0  {'entity': 'gas1', 'bus': 'south'}
1   {'entity': 'pv1', 'bus': 'south'}

remove takes out every tuple with north in its bus field, with its values. It refuses a label that is still a property's value:

w.remove("carrier", ["gas"])

ValueError: `remove('carrier', ...)` is refused: `entity.carrier` names them at [('gas1', 'gas')]; `set` those to another label or None first

The message lists where entity.carrier still has the value gas. Layers describes what else a removal removes.

docs.title: Check the staged edits
docs.text:
A read of the WorkingRecord returns its edits applied, and edits contains only what you staged:

print(sorted(w.edits.axes()), sorted(w.edits.attributes()))
print(w.edits.attribute("p_nom").df())

['bus', 'carrier', 'connection', 'entity'] ['p_nom']
  entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0    pv1     p_nom         NaN   40.0

edits has the four axes you changed, each restated whole, and the one p_nom row of pv1. A relation you took before an edit returns the edit too:

rel = w.attributes["p_nom"]
w.set("p_nom", 45.0, entity="pv1")
print(rel.filter("entity = 'pv1'").df())

  entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0    pv1     p_nom         NaN   45.0

rel returns the 45.0 that you staged after taking it.

docs.title: Commit the edits
docs.text:
store.commit(w) writes the edits as a child of the revision w was made over. Close the WorkingRecord once you no longer read it:

child = store.commit(w)
w.close()
print(child.parent == rev.id)
print(child.record.dims["bus"].df())

True
     bus
0  south

The child's bus axis has south alone.

To write a WorkingRecord whole, as a standalone directory with no parent, pass it to ws.write. A with block closes it on exit:

import os

with WorkingRecord(child.record) as w:
    w.set("p_nom", 30.0, entity="pv1")
    flat = ws.write(w, os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "flat"))
print(flat.attributes["p_nom"].df())

  entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0  wind1     p_nom         NaN  100.0
1   gas1     p_nom         NaN   50.0
2    pv1     p_nom         NaN   30.0

The directory contains the values of every layer, with the edit applied.

docs.title: Present a framework object as a record
docs.text: This guide shows how to wrap a framework's own object so that any reader of a record reads it, and how to commit it. It is for a tool author, who knows the framework. RecordLike is the protocol the wrapper satisfies, and the data model defines the shapes below.

docs.title: Implement the six members
docs.text:
RecordLike is a structural protocol, so a class with its six members satisfies it without importing anything from datarecord. The members are schema, con, dims, properties, attributes and flags, and the record states what each returns.

A mapping may be a plain dict. A dim with one_of needs no entry in dims, because its axis is the schema's list.

docs.title: Write the wrapper
docs.text:
This framework's object has a table of units and a table of hourly availability. The wrapper declares a schema for them and renames their columns to the record's:

from collections.abc import Sequence
from dataclasses import dataclass

import pandas as pd
from duckdb import DuckDBPyConnection

from datarecord import AttributeSpec, Dimension, Flags, PropertySpec, Relations, Schema
from datarecord.resolve.fold import Fold

SCHEMA = Schema(
    dimensions={
        "entity": Dimension(dtype="str"),
        "ctype": Dimension(one_of=["Generator", "Load"]),
        "snapshot": Dimension(dtype="int"),
    },
    properties={"entity": {"ctype": PropertySpec(one_of="ctype")}},
    attributes={
        "p_nom": AttributeSpec(dtype="float", dims={"entity"}, default=0.0),
        "p_max_pu": AttributeSpec(
            dtype="float", dims={"entity", "snapshot"}, default=1.0
        ),
    },
    partial={"entity"},
)


class Fleet:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.units = pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "name": ["wind1", "gas1"],
                "kind": ["Generator", "Generator"],
                "capacity": [100.0, 50.0],
            }
        )
        self.availability = pd.DataFrame(
            {"name": ["wind1"] * 3, "hour": [0, 1, 2], "pu": [0.3, 0.8, 0.5]}
        )


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FleetRecord:
    fleet: Fleet
    con: DuckDBPyConnection
    schema: Schema = SCHEMA

    @property
    def dims(self) -> Relations:
        units = self.con.from_df(self.fleet.units)
        hours = self.con.from_df(self.fleet.availability)
        return {
            "entity": units.project("name AS entity"),
            "snapshot": hours.project("hour::BIGINT AS snapshot")
            .distinct()
            .order("snapshot"),
        }

    @property
    def properties(self) -> Relations:
        units = self.con.from_df(self.fleet.units)
        return {"entity": units.project("name AS entity, kind AS ctype")}

    @property
    def attributes(self) -> Relations:
        units = self.con.from_df(self.fleet.units)
        hours = self.con.from_df(self.fleet.availability)
        return {
            "p_nom": units.project(
                "name AS entity, 'p_nom' AS attribute, NULL::DOUBLE AS breakpoint, capacity AS value"
            ),
            "p_max_pu": hours.project(
                "name AS entity, hour::BIGINT AS snapshot, 'p_max_pu' AS attribute,"
                " NULL::DOUBLE AS breakpoint, pu AS value"
            ),
        }

    def flags(self, **categories: str | Sequence[str]) -> dict[str, Flags]:
        return Fold.as_one_layer(self).flags(**categories)

Fold.as_one_layer reads the wrapper's rows as one layer and answers flags as a record written from them would. The PyPSA tool answers flags the same way.

docs.title: Check the wrapper reads as a record
docs.text:
from datarecord import RecordLike, Workspace, select

ws = Workspace()
record = FleetRecord(Fleet(), ws.con)
print(isinstance(record, RecordLike))
print(record.flags(ctype="Generator")["p_max_pu"])
print(select(record, snapshot=1).attributes["p_max_pu"].df())

True
Flags(varies=frozenset({'entity', 'snapshot'}), broadcast=frozenset(), breakpoints=False)
  entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0  wind1  p_max_pu         NaN    0.8

p_max_pu varies along both dims, and the selection at snapshot 1 returns wind1's 0.8. isinstance checks only that the members exist. The select call is the test that the relations have the shapes the reference states.

docs.title: Commit the wrapper
docs.text:
store.commit and ws.write take the wrapper as they take any record, and validate every row as they write it:

import tempfile

store = ws.store(tempfile.mkdtemp())
root = store.commit(record, parent=None)
print(root.record.properties["entity"].df())

  entity      ctype
0  wind1  Generator
1   gas1  Generator

The committed root has both units as generators. A WorkingRecord stages edits over a committed Record alone, so commit the wrapper before you edit it:

from datarecord import WorkingRecord

WorkingRecord(record)

TypeError: a `WorkingRecord` folds its staged rows over a `Record`'s layers, and a FleetRecord has none: write it first, `WorkingRecord(ws.write(source, uri))`

WorkingRecord(root.record) stages edits over the committed wrapper.

docs.title: Build relations on demand
docs.text:
Where building a relation costs a read, as for a file on a remote store, return a LazyRelations instead of a dict. It lists its keys at once and builds a relation when a reader looks one up:

from datarecord import LazyRelations

lazy = LazyRelations(("p_nom", "p_max_pu"), lambda name: record.attributes[name])
print(list(lazy), "p_nom" in lazy)

['p_nom', 'p_max_pu'] True

Listing the keys and testing for one builds no relation.

docs.title: Read a record
docs.text:
This guide shows how to read a record's labels, properties and attributes, settle its rows, and read it from a directory or from SQL. You need a record: the examples use record, store, rev and ws from Your first record. Every read goes through RecordLike, so the same calls work on a revision, a directory, a WorkingRecord, a selection or a framework's own object.

Every value is a DuckDB relation, a query plan that DuckDB runs only when you call .df(), .pl() or .to_arrow_table().

docs.title: Read labels and properties
docs.text:
dims[dim] returns a dim's axis in axis order, and properties[dim] returns its labels with every property, one row per label. To read one category, filter on the property:

print(record.dims["snapshot"].df())
print(record.properties["entity"].filter("ctype = 'Generator'").df())

   snapshot
0         0
1         1
2         2
  entity      ctype carrier
0  wind1  Generator    wind
1   gas1  Generator     gas

The axis lists the three snapshots in order, and the filter keeps both generators. A multi-dim's axis is one struct column, such as connection, with a field per coordinate.

docs.title: Read attributes long
docs.text:
attributes[name] returns the stored rows, one per value, in no promised order. A row has the attribute's own coordinates, then attribute, breakpoint and value:

print(record.attributes["p_max_pu"].filter("entity = 'wind1'").df())

  entity  snapshot attribute  breakpoint  value
0  wind1         2  p_max_pu         NaN    0.5
1  wind1         1  p_max_pu         NaN    0.8
2  wind1         0  p_max_pu         NaN    0.3

Each row is one value of wind1's series. A NULL coordinate means every label of its dim (the broadcast rule). An attribute row has no property column, so join properties on the key to filter by category.

docs.title: Plan a read with flags
docs.text:
flags(**categories) returns, per attribute, the dims some row sets (varies) and the dims some row leaves NULL (broadcast), counting only rows for the category:

flags = record.flags(ctype="Generator")
print(flags["p_max_pu"])

Flags(varies=frozenset({'entity', 'snapshot'}), broadcast=frozenset({'snapshot'}), breakpoints=False)

snapshot is in both sets, so some generators have a series and others a constant. A dim in varies alone has a label in every row.

docs.title: Apply the broadcast rule
docs.text:
To get one row per label at each point, pass settle the rows, the labels of each coordinate to expand, and the attribute's flags:

from datarecord import settle

gens = record.properties["entity"].filter("ctype = 'Generator'").select("entity")
labels = {"entity": gens, "snapshot": record.dims["snapshot"]}
print(settle(record.attributes["p_max_pu"], labels, flags["p_max_pu"]).df())

  entity  snapshot attribute  breakpoint  value
0   gas1         2  p_max_pu         NaN    0.9
1   gas1         1  p_max_pu         NaN    0.9
2   gas1         0  p_max_pu         NaN    0.9
3  wind1         1  p_max_pu         NaN    0.8
4  wind1         0  p_max_pu         NaN    0.3
5  wind1         2  p_max_pu         NaN    0.5

settle expands gas1's NULL snapshot over the three snapshots and drops rows of labels you did not pass. A coordinate you leave out of labels stays as written. The record reference lists what each flag costs.

A point that no row covers takes the attribute's default. Schema.default_for gives it per category:

print(record.schema.default_for("p_max_pu", ctype="Generator"))

1.0

A generator with no p_max_pu row has a value of 1.0.

docs.title: Read a directory
docs.text:
ws.write writes any record as a standalone directory, and ws.at reads one:

import os

uri = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "copy")
ws.write(record, uri)
print(sorted(os.listdir(uri)))
print(ws.at(uri).attributes["p_nom"].df())

['attributes', 'dims', 'manifest.json']
  entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0  wind1     p_nom         NaN  100.0
1   gas1     p_nom         NaN   50.0

The directory contains a manifest and a folder per kind of file, and ws.at returns the same values. It takes an s3:// URI too (Store a record). The format page lists each file.

docs.title: Read from SQL
docs.text:
register creates a DuckDB schema with a view per dim, property subject and attribute, so a client that speaks only SQL reads the record:

record.register("base")
print(ws.con.sql("SELECT entity, value FROM base.attributes.p_nom").df())
print(ws.registered().project("name, working").df())
ws.unregister("base")

  entity  value
0   gas1   50.0
1  wind1  100.0
   name  working
0  base    False

The query returns the stored p_nom rows, and registered() lists the registration. The views contain the rows as stored, so a SQL client applies the broadcast rule itself. A view over a WorkingRecord returns every edit as you stage it.

docs.title: Close a record
docs.text:
datarecord keeps a record's fold in workspace tables until you close the record. Use a with block, and fetch what you need inside it:

with store.revision(rev.id).record as record:
    p_nom = record.attributes["p_nom"].df()
record.attributes["p_nom"]

ValueError: this `Record` is closed and its folds released; read the revision's `record` again (https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/reference/store/#the-database)

p_nom contains the values, and any later read of the closed record raises ValueError.

docs.title: Select part of a record
docs.text:
This guide shows how to read a record at some of its labels with select, and put squeezed labels back on rows you compute. The examples use record from Your first record.

select(record, **labels) takes any RecordLike and returns a selection, which is a record too. record.select(**labels) is the same call. select writes nothing, and the selection's attributes stay plans on record.con.

docs.title: Keep some labels of a dim
docs.text:
Pass a list to keep those labels and the dim:

from datarecord import select

view = select(record, bus=["north"])
print(view.dims["connection"].df())
print(view.dims["entity"].df())

                            connection
0  {'entity': 'wind1', 'bus': 'north'}
  entity
0  wind1
1   gas1

select drops the connection at south with its bus. gas1 stays, because select drops the tuples over a dropped label and keeps the other labels of those tuples. A slice(start, stop) on a number or datetime axis, or a partial date string such as "2013-02", keeps the dim too.

docs.title: Squeeze a dim
docs.text:
Pass one label to squeeze its dim out of the selection's schema:

view = select(record, carrier="wind")
print(view.schema.dims)
print(view.properties["entity"].df())

('entity', 'ctype', 'bus', 'snapshot')
  entity      ctype
0  wind1  Generator

carrier and the property entity.carrier are gone, and so is gas1, whose carrier was dropped. On an attribute, select settles rows along the squeezed dim and drops its column:

view = record.select(snapshot=1)
print(view.attributes["p_max_pu"].df())

  entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0   gas1  p_max_pu         NaN    0.9
1  wind1  p_max_pu         NaN    0.8

gas1's value, stored with snapshot NULL, applies at snapshot 1. To keep the dim at one label, pass a list of one:

print(record.select(snapshot=[1]).attributes["p_max_pu"].df())

  entity  snapshot attribute  breakpoint  value
0   gas1      <NA>  p_max_pu         NaN    0.9
1  wind1         1  p_max_pu         NaN    0.8

The dim stays, and gas1's row keeps its NULL snapshot.

docs.title: Narrow a selection
docs.text:
Call select on a selection to add keywords. labels returns what you asked for, and base returns the record selected from:

narrow = view.select(carrier=["gas"])
print(narrow.labels, narrow.base is record)
print(narrow.dims["entity"].df())

{'snapshot': 1, 'carrier': ['gas']} True
  entity
0   gas1

The keywords merge, and base is the record you started from, never a selection. narrow.base.select(**narrow.labels) rebuilds the same selection, so pass labels on to rebuild it elsewhere.

docs.title: Lift rows back to the base
docs.text:
Rows computed over a selection lack the squeezed dims. lift adds each squeezed label back on the columns that the base declares the attribute over:

doubled = view.attributes["p_max_pu"].project("entity, value * 2 AS value")
lifted = view.lift("p_max_pu", doubled)
print(lifted.df())

  entity  snapshot  value
0  wind1         1    1.6
1   gas1         1    1.8

The lifted rows have snapshot 1 again, so w.set("p_max_pu", lifted) stages them on a WorkingRecord over the base. An attribute that the base declares over no squeezed dim comes back unchanged.

docs.title: Check what select refuses
docs.text:
select raises at the call, naming the keyword:

record.select(snapshot=7)

ValueError: `select(snapshot=7)` names a label the axis lacks (https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/reference/selecting/)

The message contains the call and a link to the rule. Selecting lists every keyword form and refusal.

docs.title: Store a record
docs.text: This guide shows how to set up a workspace and its stores, write a standalone directory, connect to S3, and read from several threads or processes. The examples use record, rev and ws from Your first record.

docs.title: Set up a workspace and a store
docs.text:
A Workspace is a DuckDB database, in memory unless you pass a file. ws.store(uri) returns the one store at that location:

import os

from datarecord import Workspace

work = Workspace(os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "work.duckdb"))
data = tempfile.mkdtemp()
print(work.store(data) is work.store(data))

True

A second call returns the same store, and the database contains no record's data. Records of stores on one workspace join, because their relations share its database. work.write refuses a relation from another workspace:

work.write(record, os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "elsewhere"))

ValueError: this relation was built on another connection or thread; build it on `record.con` in this thread, or hand over a pandas, polars or arrow frame to land

The relations of record are planned on ws, so work cannot read them. To combine records, open their stores on one workspace.

docs.title: Write a standalone directory
docs.text:
ws.write(source, uri) writes any record as one directory with no parent, and ws.at(uri) reads it back. The URI must not exist yet, not even as an empty directory:

uri = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "plants")
written = ws.write(record, uri)
print(sorted(os.listdir(uri)))
ws.write(record, uri)

['attributes', 'dims', 'manifest.json']
FileExistsError: /private/var/folders/.../plants/ already exists; a standalone record is written to a URI that does not exist yet

The second write raises, because uri exists. The manifest is written last, so a write that fails leaves no record. Delete the failed write's data files before you write there again. The format page lists each file.

docs.title: Open a record on S3
docs.text:
Install the remote extra, which adds boto3:

pip install datarecord[remote]

Then pass an s3:// URI wherever a path goes:

store = ws.store("s3://bucket/my-record")
record = ws.at("s3://bucket/out/")

The credentials and the endpoint come from the AWS environment variables and config files. Set AWS_ENDPOINT_URL to connect to a self-hosted server, which must honour conditional writes.

docs.title: Read from several threads
docs.text:
ws.con is the calling thread's DuckDB cursor, so every thread can read one record. Build each relation in the thread that fetches it:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor


def p_nom(entity):
    return (
        record.attributes["p_nom"].filter(f"entity = '{entity}'").df()["value"].item()
    )


with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool:
    print(list(pool.map(p_nom, ["wind1", "gas1"])))

[100.0, 50.0]

Each thread built its own relation and fetched one generator's p_nom. A relation or a WorkingRecord belongs to the thread that built it, and another thread's write path refuses it.

docs.title: Hand a revision to another process
docs.text:
A Revision or a Claim serialises as its id and its store's location, as JSON or as a pickle:

import pickle

from datarecord import Revision

payload = rev.model_dump_json()
print(payload)
again = Revision.model_validate_json(payload)
print(again.ancestry() == rev.ancestry())
print(pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(rev)).id == rev.id)

{"id":"702b30e4-66fd-43b3-96ea-4fdddbca7232","store":"/private/var/folders/.../tmpl4cn2v4a"}
True
True

The JSON has the id and the store's location, and the loaded revision has the same ancestry. The loaded revision attaches to Workspace.process(), the one workspace a process creates on first use, and datarecord reads its manifests from the store. Build a source for claim.commit on that workspace, since a relation from another workspace is refused. Writers never share a file, so several processes can commit to one store at once (the store).

docs.title: Use the PyPSA tool
docs.text: This guide shows how to export a PyPSA network as a record, check and edit it, solve it, and commit the results. It also shows how to build from a selection, write an edited network over its parent and solve a collection. You need datarecord[pypsa]. The tools page lists what the PyPSA tool reads from a record and writes back.

docs.title: Export a network
docs.text:
PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, con) presents a pypsa.Network as a record on the workspace's connection. Commit it as a root:

import tempfile

import pandas as pd
import pypsa

from datarecord import WorkingRecord, Workspace
from datarecord.tools.pypsa import PyPSA

n = pypsa.Network(snapshots=pd.date_range("2030-01-01", periods=3, freq="h"))
n.add("Carrier", ["wind", "gas"])
n.add("Bus", ["north", "south"])
n.add(
    "Generator",
    "wind1",
    bus="north",
    carrier="wind",
    p_nom=100,
    p_max_pu=[0.9, 0.4, 0.1],
)
n.add("Generator", "gas1", bus="south", carrier="gas", p_nom=80, marginal_cost=50)
n.add("Load", "load1", bus="south", p_set=60)
n.add("Line", "line", bus0="north", bus1="south", x=0.1, s_nom=100)

ws = Workspace()
store = ws.store(tempfile.mkdtemp())
root = store.commit(PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, ws.con), parent=None)
print(root.record.properties["connection"].df())

                            connection      role
0  {'entity': 'wind1', 'bus': 'north'}  attached
1   {'entity': 'gas1', 'bus': 'south'}  attached
2  {'entity': 'load1', 'bus': 'south'}  attached
3   {'entity': 'line', 'bus': 'north'}     input
4   {'entity': 'line', 'bus': 'south'}    output

Each component is a label of entity with its type in entity.ctype, and each of its ports is a connection tuple with a role. Buses and carriers are labels of the dims bus and carrier. to_datarecord raises UnsupportedRecordError for a network in which two components of different types share a name.

docs.title: Check a record before a build
docs.text:
