PyPSA.verify(record) returns a Requirements that is falsy when PyPSA can build the record. A value that a component type does not take is left out of the build and listed in ignored:

w = WorkingRecord(root.record)
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.95)
report = PyPSA.verify(w)
print(bool(report), sorted(report.ignored))

False [('Line', 'p_max_pu'), ('Load', 'p_max_pu')]

The value with no entity applies to every entity, and PyPSA.build passes it only to the types that take it, here the generators. A missing input makes the report truthy, and report.describe() lists it:

w.rollback()
w.remove("bus", ["north"])
print(PyPSA.verify(w).describe())

attributes [('Generator', 'bus'), ('Line', 'bus1')]

wind1 and line lost their connections at north, so each lacks a port's bus. PyPSA.build raises UnsupportedRecordError with the same list for such a record.

docs.title: Edit the inputs
docs.text:
Stage edits with PyPSA's names. A property is named by its subject, so bus.x is a bus's x position and x is a line's reactance:

w.rollback()
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.95, ctype="Generator", carrier="gas")
w.set("bus.x", 10.2, bus="north")
inputs = store.commit(w)

Commit edited inputs before a solve, so that the results layer has a parent.

docs.title: Build and solve the network
docs.text:
PyPSA.build(record) returns a pypsa.Network:

net = PyPSA.build(inputs.record)
print(net.generators.p_max_pu)
print(net.optimize(solver_name="highs", log_to_console=False))

name
wind1    1.00
gas1     0.95
Name: p_max_pu, dtype: float64
('ok', 'optimal')

wind1's series is in net.generators_t.p_max_pu, and its static value is PyPSA's default.

docs.title: Write the results back
docs.text:
With results_only=True and the record the network was built from as base, to_datarecord presents only what the solve produced. Commit it as a child of inputs:

results = PyPSA.to_datarecord(net, ws.con, results_only=True, base=inputs.record)
solved = store.commit(results, parent=inputs)
price = solved.record.attributes["marginal_price"].df()
print(price.pivot(index="snapshot", columns="bus", values="value"))

bus                  north  south
snapshot
2030-01-01 00:00:00   -0.0   -0.0
2030-01-01 01:00:00   50.0   50.0
2030-01-01 02:00:00   50.0   50.0

A result is an attribute like any input, and a read of solved returns both. PyPSA.build(solved.record) puts the results back into net.buses_t.marginal_price. A later solve over solved writes another child, and where both set the same row, a read returns the later solve's value.

docs.title: Build from a selection
docs.text:
PyPSA.build takes a selection of a record and builds the network of its labels. Along a dim the network keeps, such as snapshot or bus, pass a list, because one label of it is refused:

try:
    PyPSA.build(inputs.record.select(bus="south"))
except ValueError as err:
    print(err)
south = PyPSA.build(inputs.record.select(bus=["south"]))
print(list(south.generators.index), list(south.lines.index))

A network is built from a selection squeezing `period`, `scenario` or a dim of the record's own, not ['bus']: select one label as a list of one to keep the dim
['gas1'] []

wind1 and line attach to the dropped bus north, so build leaves them out of the network.

One label of period or scenario squeezes the dim, and a list of one keeps it. A network with two investment periods shows the difference:

mp = pypsa.Network(snapshots=pd.date_range("2030-01-01", periods=2, freq="h"))
mp.set_investment_periods([2030, 2040])
mp.add("Bus", "hub")
mp.add("Generator", "gas", bus="hub", p_nom=100, marginal_cost=50)
mp.add("Load", "demand", bus="hub", p_set=40)
periods = store.commit(PyPSA.to_datarecord(mp, ws.con), parent=None)
view = periods.record.select(period=2030)
one = PyPSA.build(view)
kept = PyPSA.build(periods.record.select(period=[2030]))
print(list(one.investment_periods), one.snapshots.nlevels)
print(list(kept.investment_periods), kept.snapshots.nlevels)

[] 1
[2030] 2

one is a single-period network over the timesteps of 2030, and kept is a multi-period network with 2030 as its only period.

Write the results of a network built from a selection with base=view. to_datarecord puts each row back at the labels the selection squeezed:

one.optimize(solver_name="highs", log_to_console=False)
results = PyPSA.to_datarecord(one, ws.con, results_only=True, base=view)
solved_2030 = store.commit(results, parent=periods)
print(solved_2030.record.attributes["marginal_price"].df()[["snapshot", "value"]])

                                            snapshot  value
0  {'period': 2030, 'timestep': 2030-01-01 00:00:00}   50.0
1  {'period': 2030, 'timestep': 2030-01-01 01:00:00}   50.0

The prices are at the snapshots of period 2030, and 2040 has none. Selecting before a build lists what build drops on top of the selection.

docs.title: Write an edited network over its parent
docs.text:
To write back a network you edited in PyPSA, pass the record it was built from as base. to_datarecord then writes only the values that changed:

edit = PyPSA.build(inputs.record)
edit.generators.loc["gas1", "p_max_pu"] = 1.0
edit.generators.loc["gas1", "marginal_cost"] = 60.0
layer = PyPSA.to_datarecord(edit, ws.con, base=inputs.record)
print({name: len(rows) for name, rows in layer.attributes.items() if len(rows)})
edited = store.commit(layer, parent=inputs)
print(edited.record.attributes["p_max_pu"].filter("entity = 'gas1'").df())

{'p_max_pu': 1, 'marginal_cost': 1}
  snapshot scenario entity attribute  breakpoint  value
0      NaT     None   gas1  p_max_pu         NaN    1.0

The layer has one row for each edit. gas1's p_max_pu is back at PyPSA's default of 1.0, and the layer writes it, so the 0.95 of inputs no longer shows through.

docs.title: Solve a collection
docs.text:
A set of networks solved apart, such as one per weather year, is a pypsa.NetworkCollection whose index names a dim of its own. PyPSACollection.to_datarecord writes it as one record:

from datarecord.tools.base import UnsupportedRecordError
from datarecord.tools.pypsa import PyPSACollection

calm = PyPSA.build(inputs.record)
calm.generators_t.p_max_pu["wind1"] = [0.3, 0.2, 0.1]
members = pd.Series({2012: PyPSA.build(inputs.record), 2013: calm})
collection = pypsa.NetworkCollection(members.rename_axis("weather_year"))
years = store.commit(PyPSACollection.to_datarecord(collection, ws.con), parent=None)
attributes = years.record.schema.attributes
print(sorted(attributes["p_max_pu"].dims), sorted(attributes["p_nom"].dims))

['entity', 'scenario', 'snapshot', 'weather_year'] ['entity', 'scenario']

p_max_pu differs between the members, so it varies over weather_year. p_nom is the same in both and keeps the dims PyPSA declares.

PyPSA.build refuses a record with a dim of its own. Build it with PyPSACollection.build, solve each member, and write the results over the record:

try:
    PyPSA.build(years.record)
except UnsupportedRecordError as err:
    print(err)
built = PyPSACollection.build(years.record)
for member in built.networks:
    member.optimize(solver_name="highs", log_to_console=False)
results = PyPSACollection.to_datarecord(
    built, ws.con, results_only=True, base=years.record
)
solved_years = store.commit(results, parent=years)
price = solved_years.record.attributes["marginal_price"].df()
south_price = price[price["bus"] == "south"]
print(south_price.pivot(index="snapshot", columns="weather_year", values="value"))

record cannot build a pypsa model; missing: unsupported dims ['weather_year']
weather_year         2012  2013
snapshot
2030-01-01 00:00:00  -0.0  50.0
2030-01-01 01:00:00  50.0  50.0
2030-01-01 02:00:00  50.0  50.0

In the calm year 2013, gas runs at every snapshot, so the price at south is gas's marginal cost of 50 throughout. A collection over period is a myopic solve, one network per investment period, and a collection lists the rules of both kinds.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: These pages describe what datarecord does: what a record contains, what each call accepts, returns and refuses, and what is on disk.

docs.title: A record and its data
docs.text:
What a record contains, and the calls that read, select and edit it.

  • The data model: dims, multi-dims, properties, categories, attributes and the broadcast rule.
  • The schema: every key a schema accepts, its dtypes, names and compatible changes.
  • The record: the RecordLike protocol, relations, flags and settle.
  • Selecting: select, squeezing, dropped labels and lift.
  • Editing: WorkingRecord, set, add, remove and edits.

docs.title: Layers and storage
docs.text:
How revisions stack, how a read combines them, and what is on disk.

  • Layers: revisions, the tree, partial and removing labels.
  • Resolution: the fold, the owner map and crossing rows.
  • The record format: the files of a record on disk.
  • Workspace and store: Workspace, Store and their files.

docs.title: Tools and lookup
docs.text:
The tools that hand a record to a framework, and where to look up a word or a signature.

  • Tools: the tool's schema and the PyPSA tool.
  • Glossary: each project word and the page that defines it.
  • Python API: every public name, rendered from its docstring.

docs.title: The data model
docs.text:
This page describes what a record contains: dims and their labels, multi-dims, properties and categories, attributes, and the broadcast rule for an attribute's rows. A record is the object you hold: dims, properties and attributes under one schema, exposed as DuckDB relations through RecordLike. Record, WorkingRecord and Selection are records. The reasons for each choice below are on the about page.

The examples read one record of the running example, whose schema the schema reference declares. It has the entities wind, gas and dc, the buses north and south, and the snapshots 0, 1 and 2.

docs.title: Dims and labels
docs.text:
A dim is a set of unique labels that values vary along, declared by a Dimension under dimensions. A label is one value of a dim, unique within it, typed by the dim's dtype. An axis is the labels one dim has in one record, in order, which record.dims[dim] returns:

record.dims["entity"].fetchall()

[('wind',), ('gas',), ('dc',)]

The axis lists the three entities in axis order.

A label exists because its axis has a row for it, whether or not any attribute row contains it. The schema declares no order. A record's data is the data each of its revisions adds (a layer), and resolution states which layer's file sets the axis order.

docs.title: A dim with one_of
docs.text: A dim with one_of has exactly the labels its list declares, in list order. Its axis comes from the schema and from no file, so record.dims["ctype"] returns Generator, Link and Load in every record of the schema. Its column is an ENUM of the labels. A dim with one_of has no properties, and add and remove refuse it: a new label is a schema change. Otherwise it is a dim like any other, which an attribute may range over and a property may refer to.

docs.title: Multi-dims
docs.text:
A multi-dim is a dim declared with over, whose labels are tuples of other dims' labels and list the combinations that exist. connection over (entity, bus) lists which entity attaches to which bus:

record.dims["connection"].fetchall()

[({'entity': 'wind', 'bus': 'north'},), ({'entity': 'gas', 'bus': 'south'},),
 ({'entity': 'dc', 'bus': 'north'},), ({'entity': 'dc', 'bus': 'south'},)]

The link dc attaches to both buses, and each generator to one.

A multi-dim is one struct column named for it, in its axis and in every attribute row over it. A coordinate is one named position in a key: a column of an attribute's rows, or a field of a multi-dim's tuple. The struct has one field per coordinate, in over order, each typed as the dim it draws on. Two coordinates may draw on one dim, such as from and to of a corridor between two buses. Each coordinate draws on a dim that is no multi-dim.

The struct's value is a whole tuple or NULL. A struct with some fields NULL, such as {entity: dc, bus: NULL}, matches no tuple, and set, add and store.commit refuse it.

connection.bus is the bus coordinate wherever a dotted subject.name stands. Schema.resolve("connection.bus") returns connection and the dim bus that the coordinate draws on. A coordinate is part of the key and has no value of its own, so datarecord refuses set("connection.bus", ...). A tuple changes only through a remove of the old tuple and an add of the new one.

Removing a label that a tuple contains removes the tuple and its values (layers). For a multi-dim with no tuples, record.dims returns an empty relation.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
A property is a value per label of its subject dim, declared by a PropertySpec under properties. It is stored as a column of that dim's axis file, so it has no dims of its own. You name it subject.name, such as entity.carrier or connection.role, and a plain name always means an attribute. record.properties[subject] returns the subject's key and every property declared for it:

record.properties["entity"].fetchall()

[('wind', 'Generator', 'wind'), ('gas', 'Generator', 'gas'), ('dc', 'Link', None)]

The columns are entity, ctype and carrier, and dc has no carrier because no layer wrote one.

A property's name belongs to its subject. bus.x and an attribute x are two names, and carrier may be a property of entity, a property of bus and a dim at once. A multi-dim's tuples are its labels, so a multi-dim may have properties too.

A property may refer to a dim with one_of in place of dtype, and its values are then that dim's labels. A value that is not NULL must be a label the record has. set and add refuse a label the axis lacks, and remove refuses a label that is still a property's value. A NULL value refers to no label. A chain such as bus to state to country is two properties, bus.state and state.country, which a reader joins.

A property has one value per label and does not vary along another dim. A mapping that varies, such as a bus's country per scenario, is a multi-dim over (bus, scenario) with a property country.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
A category is a label's value of a categorising property. A property categorises its subject when two conditions hold:

  • The subject is in partial, the dims along which a layer overrides one value per label, a multi-dim among them.
  • The property refers to a dim with one_of.

entity.ctype refers to ctype, which has one_of, and entity is in partial, so ctype categorises entity. entity.carrier refers to carrier, which has no one_of, so it categorises nothing. Schema.categorizing("entity") lists ("ctype",), the categorising properties in declaration order.

A category selects labels and keys a default:

  • flags(ctype="Generator"), a set keyword and a select keyword each apply to the labels with that category.
  • default_by keyed entity.ctype gives a default per category, which Schema.default_for(name, ctype="Load") returns.

The keyword is the property's plain name, ctype. A category that no label has selects no label. When set changes a label's category, the label keeps its attribute values, and a read per category uses the current category.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
An attribute is the values at points over the dims its AttributeSpec lists, stored as long rows, one file per attribute. A point is one label or NULL on each coordinate of an attribute, which is where a row's value applies. Each row has the attribute's coordinates, then attribute, breakpoint and value:

record.attributes["p_max_pu"].order("snapshot").fetchall()

[('wind', 0, 'p_max_pu', None, 0.3), ('wind', 1, 'p_max_pu', None, 0.8),
 ('wind', 2, 'p_max_pu', None, 0.5), (None, None, 'p_max_pu', None, 1.0)]

wind has a value per snapshot, and the last row, NULL on both coordinates, gives 1.0 at every other point.

An attribute's coordinates are the entries of its dims, with a multi-dim as its one struct column, so p_nom has entity alone. An attribute is indexed over each dim its dims lists and each dim that a coordinate of one of its multi-dims draws on. dims sets which coordinates address a value and nothing about what the value means. A solve's results are attributes too, which a child layer inherits like any other row.

breakpoint is NULL in an ordinary row. On an attribute with breakpoints, a curve is one row per breakpoint, with breakpoint the abscissa and value the ordinate there. datarecord checks no property of the curve, such as convexity.

docs.title: The broadcast rule
docs.text:
The broadcast rule is the rule that a NULL coordinate means every label of its dim. Where rows cover one point, datarecord keeps the row that leaves no dim NULL that another row there sets. The settled rows below take the rows of p_max_pu above and give one row per point:

Settling p_max_pu over its axes by the broadcast rule The attribute p_max_pu has four rows: wind at snapshots 0, 1 and 2 with 0.3, 0.8 and 0.5, and one row with entity and snapshot NULL and value 1.0. Settled over the entity axis wind, gas, dc and the snapshot axis 0, 1, 2, the result has one row per point: wind keeps its own three values, because a row that sets entity and snapshot is more specific than the NULL row, and gas and dc take 1.0 at every snapshot from the NULL row. attribute rows p_max_pu entity snapshot value wind 0 0.3 wind 1 0.8 wind 2 0.5 NULL NULL 1.0 axis entity entity wind gas dc axis snapshot snapshot 0 1 2 settled rows one per point entity snapshot value wind 0 0.3 wind 1 0.8 wind 2 0.5 gas 0 1.0 gas 1 1.0 gas 2 1.0 dc 0 1.0 dc 1 1.0 dc 2 1.0 settle NULL takes every label, the most specific row is kept from the NULL row rows and axes given settled rows

wind keeps its three values, because a row that sets both coordinates is more specific than the NULL row. gas and dc take 1.0 at every snapshot.

A NULL coordinate means every label of its dim, labels that a later layer adds included. set("p_max_pu", 0.9) writes one row with entity NULL, which applies to every entity, loads included. A value for some categories is one row per label: set("p_max_pu", 0.9, ctype="Generator") writes a row for wind and one for gas.

A row that sets a dim is more specific than one that leaves that dim NULL. Where two rows of one layer each leave NULL a dim that the other row sets, neither is more specific. store.commit refuses such a layer, naming the attribute and the point. Rows of two layers meet the same way, and the fold adds a row that sets both where they cross.

A point that no row covers takes the attribute's default, from default_by for the label's category, else default. A default is never stored. record.attributes returns the rows as written, NULL included, and a reader applies the rule with settle and the default with Schema.default_for.

docs.title: A multi-dim's column
docs.text:
A multi-dim's struct column broadcasts over its tuples. A NULL connection means every tuple, and a whole tuple means one:

A multi-dim's tuples, and a NULL struct that applies to each of them The axis of the multi-dim connection lists four tuples, each with a field per coordinate, entity and bus: wind north, gas south, dc north and dc south. The attribute efficiency has a row with connection NULL and value 1.0, and a row at the tuple dc south with value 0.9. A row with entity dc and bus NULL matches no tuple, so no such row exists. Settled over the axis, the result has one row per tuple: dc south keeps 0.9 and the three other tuples take 1.0 from the NULL row. axis connection, a field per coordinate entity bus wind north gas south dc north dc south attribute rows efficiency connection value NULL 1.0 {dc, south} 0.9 settled rows one per tuple connection value {wind, north} 1.0 {gas, south} 1.0 {dc, north} 1.0 {dc, south} 0.9 no row: {dc, NULL} is no tuple settle a NULL struct takes every tuple axis and rows given settled rows no row

The tuple {dc, south} keeps 0.9, and the three other tuples take 1.0 from the NULL row.

The dims a multi-dim draws on broadcast on their own. A coordinate stays inside its struct, so bus inside connection is a field, and an attribute over the dim bus has a separate bus column. An attribute's dims may not list a multi-dim beside a dim with the name of one of its coordinates. A keyword such as bus= would then address both.

docs.title: Wide and long rows
docs.text:
A record returns dims and properties wide, with one row per label or tuple, and attributes long, with one row per value:

Relation Columns dims["entity"] entity dims["connection"] connection STRUCT(entity, bus) properties["entity"] entity, then one column per property attributes["p_max_pu"] entity, snapshot, attribute, breakpoint, value an attribute over connection connection, attribute, breakpoint, value

An attribute row has no property columns. To read one category's rows, a reader joins properties["entity"], filtered on the category, on entity. To read a multi-dim's fields flat, a reader takes connection.bus in SQL or unnests the struct.

See also

  • The schema declares every name on this page.
  • The record lists what each accessor returns.
  • Layers describes how a layer writes and removes labels.
  • Why the data model is shaped this way.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
A WorkingRecord is a record that stages edits over a base Record and reads back with the edits applied. An edit is a set, add or remove on a WorkingRecord, staged until store.commit writes the edits as a child layer. Nothing is written until then. The examples edit rev, the revision of the running example's record that the data model reads.

from datarecord import WorkingRecord

w = WorkingRecord(rev.record)
rel = w.attributes["p_nom"]
w.set("p_nom", 150.0, entity="wind")
rel.order("entity").fetchall()

[('gas', 'p_nom', None, 50.0), ('wind', 'p_nom', None, 150.0)]

wind has 150.0 before any write, and the relation taken before the edit returns it too.

WorkingRecord is a subclass of Record, so every read member of the record applies, with the edits as one more layer on the base. The base is a Record, and WorkingRecord raises TypeError for any other RecordLike, a Selection included:

a `WorkingRecord` folds its staged rows over a `Record`'s layers, and a Selection has none: write it first, `WorkingRecord(ws.write(source, uri))`

docs.title: The shape of an edit
docs.text:
Each edit stages rows of one file of the format:

Edit Stages Keyed by set an attribute rows of attributes/<attr>.parquet the attribute's coordinates set a property the subject's axis, with one column of the labels set changed the subject's label add labels or tuples the dim's axis, with the rows added the dim's label remove labels or tuples the dim's axis without them, and each multi-dim without the tuples that contain them the dim's label

A layer restates each axis it changes whole, whatever partial sets: every label the axis has, with the edits applied, in axis order.

docs.title: set
docs.text:
set(name, value, **coords) stages values of one attribute, or of one property named subject.name.

import pandas as pd

series = pd.Series([0.1, 0.2], index=pd.Index([0, 1], name="snapshot"))
w.set("p_nom", 150.0, entity=["wind", "gas"])  # one value at each label
w.set("p_nom", [150.0, 80.0], entity=["wind", "gas"])  # a value per label, in order
w.set("p_nom", {"wind": 150.0, "gas": 80.0})  # a value per label, keyed
w.set("p_max_pu", series, entity="gas")  # a series indexed by snapshot
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9)  # every entity, now and later
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9, ctype="Generator")  # every generator there is now
w.set("efficiency", 0.9, entity="dc", bus="south")  # one connection
w.set("entity.carrier", "wind", entity="dc")  # a property, by its subject

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text:
Every coordinate is a keyword, a multi-dim's coordinates included, because the schema declares which coordinates exist. A keyword has one label or a list of labels, and set stages the value at each. A coordinate with no keyword is NULL, which by the broadcast rule means every label, labels added later included.

set packs a multi-dim's coordinates into its struct column, so entity="dc", bus="south" stages connection = {entity: dc, bus: south}. You give every coordinate of a multi-dim or none, and none stages a NULL struct, which means every tuple. A coordinate is named by its own name, such as from= and to= of a corridor.

docs.title: Property keywords
docs.text:
A keyword that is not a coordinate of the attribute is the plain name of a property of a dim the attribute is indexed over. It selects the labels whose value matches on the record as staged, and set stages one row per label. set stores nothing of the filter, so its rows do not apply to a label added later. Several keywords intersect: ctype="Generator", carrier="wind" selects the wind generators. A property of a multi-dim selects its tuples the same way, and a coordinate keyword such as bus="north" narrows them.

set refuses a dotted keyword, a property name that several of those dims declare, and a property keyword beside its own dim's coordinate keyword.

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
value Meaning Keywords scalar staged at every listed combination an omitted coordinate broadcasts sequence aligned by position exactly one list keyword, of the same length mapping keys are labels of one coordinate the one coordinate without a keyword series index is labels of one coordinate the index's name, else the one coordinate without a keyword frame supplies its own keys single labels that complete it

A frame is a DuckDB relation, or a pandas, polars or arrow frame that DuckDB scans. Over a multi-dim, a frame has the struct column, such as connection STRUCT(entity, bus), and set refuses one with the coordinates as flat columns. set never infers a mapping's coordinate from its labels, and refuses the call where neither the index name nor the keywords settle it.

set casts a frame column to its declared type where the cast widens it. It casts a smaller integer to BIGINT, a number to DOUBLE, a timestamp of any precision to TIMESTAMP, and text to and from an ENUM. set refuses any other type, and a timestamp with a time zone.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
set("entity.carrier", value, ...) changes one column of the subject's axis rows and keeps the other columns. Its value is a mapping or series from label to value, a scalar with keywords that select the labels, or a scalar for every label. A categorising property is set the same way, and the label keeps its attribute values under its new category. set refuses a coordinate, such as connection.bus, because a coordinate is part of the key:

`set('connection.bus', ...)` names a coordinate of the multi-dim 'connection', part of its key rather than a value; `remove` the tuples and `add` them with the new label instead

docs.title: A later set
docs.text:
A later set replaces each staged row of the attribute that one of its own rows covers. A row covers another when, at every coordinate, it has the same label or is NULL. set("p_nom", 0.9, entity=["wind"]) followed by set("p_nom", 0.95) stages one row, and wind is 0.95. In the other order both rows stay, and wind is 0.9, because datarecord keeps the more specific row.

Where a new row and a staged row each leave NULL a dim that the other row sets, set adds a row that sets both:

w.rollback()
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.5, entity="gas")
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.7, snapshot=1)
w.edits.attribute("p_max_pu").order("entity, snapshot").fetchall()

[('gas', 1, 'p_max_pu', None, 0.7), ('gas', None, 'p_max_pu', None, 0.5), (None, 1, 'p_max_pu', None, 0.7)]

gas at snapshot 1 is 0.7, the later value, so the order of two edits sets a value and never makes an edit fail.

A set of one value along a dim outside partial also stages the key's other values, as the record reads them. w.set("p_max_pu", series, entity="gas") with a series over snapshots 0 and 1 stages snapshot 2 as well, at the 1.0 that gas read before.

docs.title: add and remove
docs.text:
add(dim, labels, **columns) stages labels of dim, each as one whole row of its axis.

w.add("carrier", ["solar"])
w.add("entity", ["pv"], ctype="Generator", carrier="solar")
w.add("connection", [{"entity": "pv", "bus": "south"}])
w.remove("connection", [{"entity": "dc", "bus": "south"}])
w.remove("entity", ["gas"])

columns are the dim's properties by plain name, each a scalar for every label or a sequence aligned to labels. A property with no keyword is NULL on the row, because add restates the row whole. A new label goes after the axis's last, and a label of the base that this record removed goes back to its base position. A label exists because its axis row exists, so add with no columns is an edit of its own.

A multi-dim's labels are tuples, which add and remove take in one of three forms:

  • a frame with the struct column, as dims["connection"] returns it
  • a frame with one column per coordinate
  • a list of mappings from coordinate to label

A frame may have property columns beside the tuples, and then each property keyword is a scalar. add refuses a frame that has both the struct column and a coordinate column, and a tuple with a coordinate missing or NULL.

remove(dim, labels) stages the axis without labels. Every value keyed by a removed label goes, and so does every tuple, of any multi-dim, that contains one, with the tuple's values. remove("bus", ["south"]) removes every connection at south. remove refuses a label that is still the value of a property referring to dim, on the record as staged:

`remove('carrier', ...)` is refused: `entity.carrier` names them at [('wind', 'wind')]; `set` those to another label or None first

add and remove refuse a dim with one_of, whose labels are the schema's. add refuses an attribute as a keyword, and points at set.

A remove after a set on the same label takes effect, because a removed label has no values. An add after a remove brings the label back with its values, staged ones included. The tuples that contained it stay removed until you add them.

docs.title: edits
docs.text:
w.edits is the staged layer alone: each attribute that has staged rows, and each axis that differs from the one in the base. store.commit(w) writes it as a child of the revision w was built over, and the fold reads the rest from the parent. ws.write(w, uri) writes w itself, the base with the edits applied, as a standalone directory.

child = store.commit(w)
child.parent == rev.id

True

A write clears nothing, so w returns the same rows until rollback() clears every staged row. An add undone by a remove leaves no axis in edits. claim.commit(w) refuses a claim whose parent is not the revision w was built over, because the edits are a difference from that revision.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
set, add and remove check each edit when it is staged, so the error points at the line that made it. They raise on:

  • an undeclared attribute, property or keyword, or a keyword the attribute does not vary over
  • a plain name that only properties have, naming their dotted forms: set("carrier", ...) suggests entity.carrier
  • a label that its dim's axis, as staged, lacks, for every dim
  • a tuple that its multi-dim, as staged, lacks
  • a tuple with a label that its coordinate's axis lacks, naming the multi-dim, the coordinate and up to three labels
  • a label that a dim with one_of does not list
  • a value of a property that refers to a dim and is no label of it, NULL excepted
  • a label or frame column whose type does not fit its dtype
  • a sequence whose length differs from its keyword's
`set('p_nom', ...)` names 'entity' labels ['coal'], which the staged axis does not hold; `add` them first (https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/reference/editing/#validation)

docs.title: Transactions and staging
docs.text:
Each edit runs in one transaction on the record's cursor. A refused edit rolls back whole, so the staged rows are as they were before it. DuckDB nests no transaction, so WorkingRecord and each edit raise duckdb.TransactionException while you hold a transaction open on the same cursor.

The staged rows are in DuckDB tables in the workspace's database, never in your files. On a workspace at :memory: they go when the workspace closes. close() drops them, a with block calls it on exit, and so does garbage collection if you never call it. After close(), a read, an edit or edits raises ValueError. A WorkingRecord over a closed Record keeps working, and one over a closed WorkingRecord refuses its edits.

See also

  • The record lists the read members that a WorkingRecord shares.
  • Layers describes what a committed layer may contain and which values and tuples a removal deletes.
  • Edit a record shows the steps.
  • The WorkingRecord API lists every signature.

docs.title: The record format
docs.text: A record on disk is a directory of parquet files and JSON manifests. Any parquet library, such as pandas or polars, can open the parquet files. This page describes the files of a layer, top down, then the views that a registered record adds to the database.

docs.title: The layout
docs.text:
A layer of a store lies under layers/<id>/ of the store's location. A standalone directory has the same layout at its own URI, with no claim.json and no resolved/.

<location>/layers/<id>/
├── claim.json                  # written when the store hands out the id
├── manifest.json               # written last: the revision exists from here
├── dims/<dim>.parquet          # one axis per dim the layer restates
├── attributes/<attr>.parquet   # one attribute per file, results included
└── resolved/                   # written by materialise()
    ├── dim_owners.parquet
    ├── dead/<dim>.parquet
    └── owner_map.parquet

Each file takes the declared name unchanged, so the dim bus is dims/bus.parquet and the attribute p_nom is attributes/p_nom.parquet. A read opens the files that the manifest lists, and no other.

docs.title: claim.json
docs.text:
claim.json lists the id, the parent, the claimed meta and when the store handed out the id. The store writes it create-only and keeps it after the commit, so an id is claimed once.

{ "id": "4731e41b-…", "parent": "9716e2ef-…", "meta": { "run": "a" }, "created": "2026-11-05T17:37:14.912772Z" }

docs.title: manifest.json
docs.text:
A Manifest is a layer's manifest.json, which lists its id, parent, full schema, files and meta. The writer writes it last and create-only, and the revision exists from that moment.

Key Contains id the layer's UUID parent the parent's UUID, null for a root and for a standalone directory schema the full schema the layer was written under files {"dims": [...], "attributes": [...]}: the declared names of the files the layer wrote meta the revision's own meta: a flat object of strings, integers, finite floats and booleans 
{"id": "4731e41b-…", "parent": "9716e2ef-…", "schema": {…}, "files": {"dims": ["entity"], "attributes": ["p_nom"]}, "meta": {"run": "a"}}

A layer that restates only the entity axis and writes only p_nom lists those two files. meta describes one revision, such as a run's id, and a child does not inherit it. schema.meta describes the record, and a child inherits it with the rest of the schema.

docs.title: dims/<dim>.parquet
docs.text:
An axis file contains every label of one dim at the layer's revision, in axis order, one row per label. Its first column is the key, named for the dim, and each further column is one property of the dim.

dims/entity.parquet       entity | ctype | carrier | sign | type
dims/connection.parquet   connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role
  • A property is NULL in a row where no layer wrote a value for that label.
  • A multi-dim's file is keyed by one struct column named for it, with a field per coordinate. Its rows are every tuple of the multi-dim at the layer's revision.
  • A dim with one_of has no file. The writer refuses a layer that has one.
  • A layer removes a label or tuple by writing the file without it (removing labels).

docs.title: attributes/<attr>.parquet
docs.text:
An attribute file contains the long rows of one attribute: its own coordinates, then the columns every row has.

<coordinate> ... | attribute | breakpoint | value

The coordinates are the dims that the attribute's dims declare, multi-dims first, each multi-dim as one struct column.

Attribute Columns p_nom over entity entity, attribute, breakpoint, value p_max_pu over entity and snapshot entity, snapshot, attribute, breakpoint, value efficiency over connection connection STRUCT(entity, bus), attribute, breakpoint, value

A NULL coordinate means every label of its dim, by the broadcast rule. breakpoint is NULL except on the rows of a curve. value has the attribute's dtype, since each file contains one attribute.

Widening p_nom over scenario adds a scenario column to the files written from then on. A file written before has no scenario column, and a read takes its rows as NULL there.

docs.title: Where a value lives
docs.text:
The section of the schema that declares a name sets the file its values go in.

Declared as Is stored in property of a dim a column of dims/<dim>.parquet property of a multi-dim a column of dims/<multi-dim>.parquet attribute, any dims the long rows of attributes/<attr>.parquet

A property is named by its subject, so bus.x is a column of dims/bus.parquet, and an attribute x is attributes/x.parquet. An axis file has no attribute values.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
An axis file has one row per label, so two entities named north collide whatever their ctype. A bus named north is a label of another dim and collides with neither.

An attribute row has the label alone, so a p_nom row has an entity column and no ctype column. datarecord never renames a label: a tool reports a collision in a framework's names.

docs.title: resolved/
docs.text:
Revision.materialise() writes a revision's fold under resolved/. No manifest lists these files, a read opens each by name, and a layer's data stays as it was.

File Contains dim_owners.parquet a row (dim, layer_uuid, has_dead) per axis: the layer whose dims/<dim>.parquet is the revision's axis dead/<dim>.parquet the removed labels of a dim, written only where has_dead is true owner_map.parquet the owner map, written last

A revision is materialised once owner_map.parquet exists. dim_owners.parquet points into ancestor layers by UUID rather than copying their files.

docs.title: Registered views
docs.text:
record.register(name) creates the DuckDB schema name in the workspace's database, with a view per dim, property subject and attribute. A SQL client of that database reads the record through these views.

View One per Reads as name.dims.<dim> dim, a dim with one_of included record.dims[dim] name.properties.<dim> dim that declares properties record.properties[dim] name.attributes.<a> attribute the schema declares record.attributes[a], empty with no rows

The views are the record's relations unsettled: a NULL coordinate means every label, two rows may cover one point and no default applies. Over a WorkingRecord, a view returns each edit once set, add or remove returns.

register raises if name exists, and refuses the name of a database attached to the workspace. Workspace.unregister(name) drops the schema, its views and its row in the registered table.

docs.title: The registered table
docs.text:
Every registration is a row of the workspace's registered table, which Workspace.registered() returns.

Column Contains name the schema revision the revision the record reads, or the base revision of a WorkingRecord working whether the record is a WorkingRecord held the database schemas the workspace keeps for it created when the record was registered

See also

The storage page argues for parquet, the manifest written last and the views. Read a record shows a read from SQL.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
This page lists each word that datarecord's pages use in one meaning only, with a link to the page that defines it.

Word Meaning record the object you hold: dims, properties and attributes under one schema, exposed through RecordLike dim a set of unique labels that values vary along, declared by a Dimension under dimensions axis the labels one dim has in one record, in order, which record.dims[dim] returns label one value of a dim, unique within it, which is a tuple on a multi-dim multi-dim a dim declared with over, whose labels are tuples of other dims' labels coordinate one named position in a key: a column of an attribute's rows, or a field of a multi-dim's tuple point one label or NULL on each coordinate of an attribute, where a row's value applies property a value per label of its subject dim, named subject.name, stored as a column of that dim's axis file category a label's value of a property of a dim in partial that refers to a dim with one_of attribute the values at points over the dims its AttributeSpec lists, stored as long rows, one file per attribute indexed over of an attribute: each dim its dims lists, and each dim that a coordinate of one of its multi-dims draws on the broadcast rule a NULL coordinate means every label of its dim, and where rows cover one point, datarecord keeps the row that leaves no dim NULL that another row there sets schema the Schema of a record: the dims, properties, attributes and partial that may exist partial the dims along which a layer overrides one value per label layer the data one revision adds on top of its parent, written once revision the id of one layer in a store, whose manifest lists its parent to remove a label to restate its dim's axis without it, which removes its values and the tuples that contain it the fold the step that builds the owner map along a revision's ancestry, one layer at a time the owner map the fold's result: per attribute, each key a layer wrote and the layer the map assigns it to to cross of two rows of two layers, to cover a common point where each row leaves NULL a dim that the other row sets to materialise to write a revision's owner map and pointers to its axes under resolved/, so that a read stops there manifest a layer's manifest.json: its id, parent, full schema, files and meta registered view a DuckDB view that Record.register creates for a SQL client store one location, local or on S3, that contains the layers of a tree of revisions workspace the DuckDB database and file access that its stores share claim a revision id that a store reserves before the layer is written reader code that reads a record through RecordLike, such as a tool or your script flags per attribute, the dims some row sets (varies) and the dims some row leaves NULL (broadcast) to settle rows to apply the broadcast rule to long rows with settle, one row per label passed at each point selection the Selection that select(record, **labels) returns: a record at the labels named to squeeze to select one label of a dim, which drops the dim from the selection's schema to lift to put the squeezed labels back on rows written over a selection, with Selection.lift edit a set, add or remove on a WorkingRecord, staged until store.commit writes it as a child layer tool a module under datarecord.tools that translates between a record and one framework framework a modelling framework, such as PyPSA, that builds a model from a record

docs.title: Layers
docs.text: This page describes revisions, the tree they form, partial, what a layer may contain and how a layer removes a label. How datarecord reads the layers of a revision as one record is on the resolution page.

docs.title: Revisions
docs.text:
The data one revision adds on top of its parent (a layer) is a directory under layers/<id>/ of a store, written once. The id of one layer, whose manifest lists its parent, is a revision, which you hold as a Revision. A revision with no parent is a root, and a revision exists from the moment the store writes its manifest.

root = store.commit(source, parent=None)
w = WorkingRecord(root.record)
w.set("p_nom", 60.0, entity="gas")
child = store.commit(w)
child.parent == root.id  # True
child.ancestry()  # [root.id, child.id]

ancestry() lists the ids from the root to the revision, root first, which is the order in which the fold reads their layers.

Member Is id the layer's UUID store the Store that contains the layer manifest the layer's Manifest: id, parent, schema, files, meta parent the parent's id, None for a root meta the revision's own meta, which a child does not inherit record the revision as a Record: its layer folded over its ancestors' ancestry() the ids from the root to this revision materialise() writes the revision's fold under resolved/

See also

The store page describes claims, commits and serialising a revision. Branch and materialise shows the calls in use.

docs.title: The tree
docs.text:
Revisions form a tree. Revisions that share one parent are branches, each with its own layer over the same ancestry. A branch never reads a sibling's layer.

Each manifest lists its parent, so datarecord resolves a revision id to its ancestry from the store's location alone.

docs.title: Write-once
docs.text:
A layer's data is written once. Claim.commit, which Store.commit wraps, writes the layer's files and then its manifest, create-only. After that, datarecord writes into the layer directory only under resolved/, when you materialise the revision. A read gives the same answers with or without those files.

A read opens exactly the files the manifest lists, and ignores any other file in the directory.

See also

Layers and partial argues for write-once layers. The format page lists the files of a layer.

docs.title: partial
docs.text:
partial is the set of dims, declared as Schema.partial, along which a layer overrides one value per label. Along any other dim, a layer restates the whole extent of each key it touches. The owner map assigns an attribute's values to a layer per key. The key is the attribute's dims that are in partial, with the attribute's name:

key(attribute) = (attribute.dims ∩ partial, attribute)

With partial = {"entity"}, p_max_pu over entity and snapshot is keyed per entity. The owner map assigns the snapshot series of each entity whole to one layer:

A layer overrides one label along a dim in partial and restates the series along any other With partial dims entity, the root writes p_max_pu for gas and wind at snapshots 0 and 1. The child changes wind at snapshot 1 to 0.9. It writes rows for wind alone, since entity is in partial, and restates wind's whole series, 0.5 and 0.9, since snapshot is not. The read takes gas from the root and wind from the child. root layer p_max_pu entity snapshot value gas 0 0.2 gas 1 0.3 wind 0 0.5 wind 1 0.6 child layer partial {entity} entity snapshot value wind 0 0.5 wind 1 0.9 read p_max_pu entity snapshot value gas 0 0.2 gas 1 0.3 wind 0 0.5 wind 1 0.9 fold entity is in partial: the child writes wind alone. snapshot is not: the child restates wind's whole series.

The child changes wind at snapshot 1 and so writes wind's whole series. The read takes gas from the root, since the child writes no gas row, and wind from the child. A WorkingRecord stages the rest of the series for you: set("p_max_pu", 0.9, entity="wind", snapshot=1) also stages wind's row at snapshot 0.

  • A multi-dim in partial is in the key as its struct column, so a layer overrides one tuple's value. With connection outside partial, a layer that changes one connection's efficiency restates every connection's.
  • The owner map assigns a curve whole to one layer, because breakpoint is in no key.
  • partial applies to attribute values alone. A layer that changes an axis restates the whole axis, whatever partial contains (removing labels).
  • Only a property of a dim in partial can be categorising (the data model).
  • The fold reads each layer under the schema in its own manifest, so a child may add a dim to partial (a wider schema).

Under the PyPSA schema's partial, a layer overrides one bus's v_nom and restates every carrier's co2_emissions, because carrier is not in partial.

See also

The schema page lists the partial key and what it accepts. Layers and partial argues for putting partial on the dim.

docs.title: What a layer may contain
docs.text: The writer checks each file of a layer against the schema in the layer's manifest, as it writes the file. A refused layer stays pending, and no read opens it.

docs.title: Types
docs.text: The writer casts each column to its declared dtype, from a wider type of the same kind or from a column of NULLs alone. It refuses any other type, naming the attribute, property or dim and its dtype.

docs.title: Attribute files
docs.text:
• The writer refuses an attribute that the schema does not declare.
  • An attribute file has exactly its attribute's own coordinates, then attribute, breakpoint and value (the long schema). The writer refuses a file that lacks a coordinate, or that has a column the attribute is not over.
  • A multi-dim's column is a struct with exactly its coordinates as fields, and the writer refuses a tuple with some fields NULL and not all.
  • The writer refuses two rows of one attribute at one point that set the same dims. It also refuses two rows there where each row leaves NULL a dim that the other row sets, unless a third row sets both.

docs.title: Axis files
docs.text:
A dims/<dim>.parquet file contains the whole axis at the new revision, in order, with each label's properties. The writer refuses a file for an undeclared dim or a dim with one_of, and a file with a label twice. It refuses a column other than the key and the subject's declared properties. It also refuses a file with its parent's labels in a different order from the parent's, and a new label may sit anywhere:

ValueError: dims/entity.parquet puts entity 'wind' out of its parent's order; a restatement keeps the order of the labels its parent holds and places a new one anywhere (https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/reference/data-model/#dims-and-labels)

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
The labels and tuples in every row of a layer are on the layer's final axes. The final axis of a dim is the layer's own file, or else the parent's resolved axis. The writer refuses an attribute row with a label or tuple outside the final axes. It refuses a multi-dim's tuple that contains a label outside its coordinate's final axis the same way:

ValueError: attributes/p_max_pu.parquet names 'entity' labels ['coal'], which the layer's dims/entity.parquet does not hold; add them there or drop those rows (https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/reference/layers/)

docs.title: LayerData
docs.text:
LayerData is the protocol the writer reads: the rows of one layer, as pairs of an enumerator and a read.

class LayerData(Protocol):
    @property
    def schema(self) -> Schema: ...
    def axes(self) -> set[str]: ...
    def axis(self, dim: str) -> DuckDBPyRelation | None: ...
    def attributes(self) -> set[str]: ...
    def attribute(self, name: str) -> DuckDBPyRelation | None: ...

axis returns the rows of one axis file, and attribute the long rows of one attribute file. Store.commit, Claim.commit and Workspace.write also take a RecordLike, such as a framework object that a tool presents, and read its relations through these pairs.

See also

Store a record shows a write from start to end.

docs.title: Removing labels
docs.text:
To remove a label is to restate its dim's axis without it, which removes its values and the tuples that contain it. remove(dim, labels) on a WorkingRecord writes one layer that restates the axis without the labels, and every multi-dim over dim without the tuples that contain them:

Removing a label removes its values and the tuples that contain it The root contains the entity axis gas, wind, coal, the connection tuples gas north and coal north, and p_nom for all three entities. The child restates the entity axis as gas and wind, and the connection axis as gas north. It writes no p_nom file. The read has no coal label, no coal north tuple and no p_nom row for coal. root layer dims/entity entity gas wind coal dims/connection connection (gas, north) (coal, north) attributes/p_nom entity value gas 50 wind 100 coal 80 child layer remove coal entity gas wind connection (gas, north) entity value no file read entity gas wind no row: coal is removed connection (gas, north) no row: contains coal entity value gas 50 wind 100 no row: coal is removed fold root layer child layer removed no row or no file

The child writes no p_nom file, and the read still has no p_nom row for coal. A removal applies to every attribute. On a dim in partial the fold drops each parent row that has the label, and on any other dim the read drops it. A row that leaves the dim NULL stays, and applies to the labels that remain.

  • A removed tuple takes its values. The labels in it keep their other rows, so removing (gas, north) leaves gas.
  • remove refuses a dim with one_of, whose axis is the schema's list.
  • A sibling branch keeps a label that one branch removes.
  • A label added again after its removal has none of the values it had below the removal. Every row that leaves its dim NULL applies to it again, whichever layer wrote the row.

The writer refuses a layer that leaves a removed label in a reference. A reference is a multi-dim's tuple, or a property that refers to a dim. The writer checks each subject whose rows contain a label the layer removes. It also checks each property of a subject the layer restates against every label removed so far. So where an ancestor left such a reference, the writer refuses the next layer that restates its subject. remove refuses a label while a property has it as a value.

See also

Edit a record shows add and remove. Layers and partial argues for removal as restatement.

docs.title: The record
docs.text:
RecordLike is the read-only protocol that every record satisfies: a schema, a DuckDB connection, three mappings of relations and flags. A reader is code that reads a record through RecordLike, such as a module that translates a record for PyPSA (a tool), or your script. Record, WorkingRecord, Selection and a framework's own object all satisfy the protocol, and a reader codes against it alone. The reasons for one interface over a directory and a tree are on the about page.

Record is the class datarecord returns from Revision.record and Workspace.at(uri). The examples read the record of the running example that the data model describes.

docs.title: schema
docs.text: schema is the record's schema. A Record returns the schema of the deepest revision's data (its last layer), and a Selection returns its base's schema without the dims it squeezed.

docs.title: con
docs.text: con is the DuckDB connection that every relation of the record is planned on. A Record returns the calling thread's cursor of its workspace, so a relation belongs to the thread that built it (store). A reader plans its own frames and SQL on con beside the record's relations.

docs.title: dims
docs.text: dims maps every dim the schema declares to a relation of its axis: the label column alone, one row per label, in axis order. A multi-dim's relation is its one struct column, such as connection STRUCT(entity, bus). A dim with one_of returns its list, and a dim that no layer has labels for returns an empty relation with its declared column.

docs.title: properties
docs.text: properties maps every subject that declares properties to a relation of the subject's key and one column per property, named by the property's plain name. The values are as stored, with no default applied, so NULL means that no layer wrote a value. Schema.default_for("entity.carrier", **categories) returns a property's default.

docs.title: attributes
docs.text:
attributes maps every attribute the schema declares to a relation of its long rows: the attribute's coordinates, then attribute, breakpoint and value. The rows are as written, in no promised order:

  • A NULL coordinate stays NULL, and a reader applies the broadcast rule itself, with settle or its own SQL.
  • Two rows may cover one point, of one layer or of two. Where they do, the record has one row there that leaves no dim NULL that another row there sets.
  • A point that no row covers has no row, and Schema.default_for gives its default.

An attribute that no layer has rows for returns an empty relation with its declared columns.

docs.title: flags
docs.text:
Flags are what record.flags(**categories) returns: per attribute, which dims its rows set and which they leave NULL.

Field Value varies the dims that some row of the attribute sets broadcast the dims that some row leaves NULL breakpoints whether any row has a breakpoint

flags() answers for the whole record in one query. Only attributes with rows have an entry, so set(record.flags()) lists the attributes the record has rows for. Each set has only dims that the attribute is addressed by, multi-dims included, and a dim outside its dims is in neither set.

flags(**categories) answers for the labels of one category. Each keyword is a categorising property of one dim, by its plain name, with one category or a list. Only rows that apply to a matching label count: a row that has the label, and a row that leaves its dim NULL.

record.flags(ctype="Generator")["p_max_pu"]

Flags(varies=frozenset({'snapshot', 'entity'}), broadcast=frozenset({'snapshot', 'entity'}), breakpoints=False)

snapshot is in both sets, because wind has a row per snapshot and gas takes its value at every snapshot from the NULL row. The flags describe the rows as written, so a NULL row that more specific rows cover at every label still puts its dim in broadcast.

flags raises ValueError when the keywords categorise several dims, or none:

['carrier'] categorize no dim; a categorizing property is a property of a `partial` dim that refers to a dim with `one_of`

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
Relations is Mapping[str, DuckDBPyRelation], the type of dims, properties and attributes. A Record returns LazyRelations, which builds each relation when a reader first looks it up. Listing the keys reads no file, and building a relation reads the file's footer, which is one round trip on a remote store.

A relation is a query plan, and nothing is read until a reader fetches it with .fetchall(), .df(), .pl() or .to_arrow_table().

docs.title: Beyond the protocol
docs.text: Record has members that RecordLike does not require.

docs.title: select
docs.text: record.select(**labels) returns a selection of the record, as select(record, **labels) does for any RecordLike.

docs.title: close
docs.text:
close() releases the tables in which the record's fold is kept, and a with block calls it on exit. The workspace drops a table once no open record and no registration reads it. Calling close() again does nothing, and closed is True from the first call on.

After close(), a read raises ValueError, and a relation taken before fails on fetch with DuckDB's missing-table error. revision.record returns a new record once the one it cached is closed. A record you never close leaves its tables in place for the workspace's life, so a chained read such as store.revision(rid).record.attributes["p_nom"].df() succeeds.

docs.title: register
docs.text: record.register(name) creates a DuckDB view per dim, property subject and attribute, for a SQL client (format).

docs.title: settle
docs.text:
To settle rows is to apply the broadcast rule to long rows with settle(rel, labels, flags), giving one row per label passed at each point. settle expands each NULL on a coordinate in labels over the labels passed, and drops a row with a label outside them. At each point it keeps the row that leaves no coordinate in labels NULL that another row there sets.

Settling p_max_pu over the generators The attribute p_max_pu has rows for wind at snapshots 0, 1 and 2 with 0.3, 0.8 and 0.5, and one row with entity and snapshot NULL and value 1.0. settle takes labels for entity alone, the generators wind and gas. The NULL row expands over them, so gas and wind each get a row at snapshot NULL with 1.0. snapshot is not in labels, so it stays as written: wind keeps its series beside its row at snapshot NULL. dc is no generator, so it has no row. attribute rows p_max_pu entity snapshot value wind 0 0.3 wind 1 0.8 wind 2 0.5 NULL NULL 1.0 labels entity entity wind gas settled rows over entity entity snapshot value gas NULL 1.0 wind 0 0.3 wind 1 0.8 wind 2 0.5 wind NULL 1.0 settle NULL entity takes wind and gas, snapshot stays as written from NULL row from NULL row no row: dc is no generator rows and labels given settled rows

Over the generators wind and gas, the NULL row gives each a row at snapshot NULL, beside wind's series.

A coordinate left out of labels stays as written, and its NULL counts as one more label:

from datarecord import settle

flags = record.flags(ctype="Generator")
gens = record.properties["entity"].filter("ctype = 'Generator'").select("entity")
rows = settle(record.attributes["p_max_pu"], {"entity": gens}, flags["p_max_pu"])
rows.order("entity, snapshot").fetchall()

[('gas', None, 'p_max_pu', None, 1.0), ('wind', 0, 'p_max_pu', None, 0.3),
 ('wind', 1, 'p_max_pu', None, 0.8), ('wind', 2, 'p_max_pu', None, 0.5),
 ('wind', None, 'p_max_pu', None, 1.0)]

dc is no generator, so its rows are gone. snapshot is not in labels, so gas keeps one constant row, and wind keeps its series beside a row at snapshot NULL. Passing "snapshot": record.dims["snapshot"] as well gives one row per generator and snapshot.

labels maps each coordinate to a relation of its labels, or of a multi-dim's tuples, in a column of the coordinate's name. flags sets how much work the query does, and flags that overstate the rows give the same result more slowly:

The coordinate is in settle varies only keeps the rows with a label passed broadcast only expands each row over the labels passed varies and broadcast expands, then keeps the most specific row

filter=False keeps a row with a label outside labels as written, for a reader whose own join on the labels drops it. Where every row at a point leaves NULL a coordinate that another row there sets, the query raises duckdb.Error on fetch, naming the point.

See also

  • The data model defines dims, properties, attributes and the broadcast rule.
  • Selecting describes select and Selection.
  • Editing describes WorkingRecord.
  • Read a record shows the steps.
  • The record API lists every signature.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
This page describes how datarecord reads the layers of a revision as one record. It covers axes, the owner map, crossing rows, what a read returns, flags, materialised revisions and a directory.

A read returns one row at each point, by two rules. Within one layer, datarecord keeps the more specific row, by the broadcast rule. Across layers, a read returns the deeper layer's row where rows of two layers meet.

A read takes the layers through the fold to the owner map The root layer and the child layer feed the fold, which builds the owner map: the layer it assigns each key to. A fold at hand, materialised on disk or kept by the workspace, seeds the fold so that it starts partway. The read joins to the map the files of the layers it lists, and returns each attribute's rows as written. A reader settles each point by the broadcast rule. root layer layers/<root>/ child layer layers/<child>/ owner map a layer per key fold at hand rows as written per attribute reader settles fold seeds read

The step that folds a revision's layers one at a time, root first (the fold), builds the owner map. The map lists, for each attribute, each key a layer wrote and the layer it assigns the key to. A read of an attribute joins to the map the files of the layers it lists, and returns the rows as written. A reader settles each point by the broadcast rule.

docs.title: Axes
docs.text:
A layer that changes an axis restates it whole, so a revision's axis is the deepest dims/<dim>.parquet on its path from the root. A layer with no file for a dim leaves its parent's axis as it is.

Each axis resolves to the deepest file for it The root layer contains dims/entity.parquet with gas and wind, and dims/scenario.parquet with low and high. The child layer restates the entity axis as gas, wind and solar, and has no scenario file. The resolved entity axis is the child's file and the resolved scenario axis is the root's. root layer dims/entity.parquet entity ctype gas Generator wind Generator dims/scenario.parquet scenario low high child layer dims/entity.parquet entity ctype gas Generator wind Generator solar Generator scenario no file: axis unchanged resolved entity entity ctype gas Generator wind Generator solar Generator scenario scenario low high deepest

The child's entity file is the resolved entity axis, and the root's scenario file is the resolved scenario axis.

  • A multi-dim's axis resolves the same way, from its file keyed by its struct column.
  • The labels of an axis come in the deepest file's row order, the axis order. A label added again after its removal sits where the file that adds it puts it.
  • A property is a column of its subject's axis file, so its values change only when a layer restates the axis.
  • A dim with one_of has no file, and its axis is the schema's list at every revision.

docs.title: The owner map
docs.text:
The owner map is the fold's result: per attribute, each key a layer wrote and the layer the map assigns it to. A key is the attribute's dims in partial and the attribute's name. The map contains no values, so its size does not depend on the length of a series or a curve.

Column Contains one per dim in partial the key's label, or NULL where the row leaves the dim NULL. A multi-dim is one struct column attribute the attribute's name layer_uuid the layer the map assigns the key to varies a struct with a boolean per dim: whether the layer's rows of this key set the dim broadcast a struct with a boolean per dim: whether the layer's rows of this key leave the dim NULL breakpoints whether the layer's rows of this key form a curve

The map has each key as its layer wrote it, a NULL included. It has one row per layer and distinct key, and one overlap row for each pair of rows that cross.

docs.title: Folding a layer onto its parent
docs.text:
The fold takes the parent's map and the layer's own keys, and returns the layer's map. Three terms describe how the rows of two layers meet:

Term Of two rows, means sets a row sets a dim in partial where its key has a label, and any other dim of the attribute where its rows vary along it covers on each dim in partial, the two rows have the same label, or one of them has NULL crosses the two rows cover a common point, and each row leaves NULL a dim that the other row sets

The fold runs three steps, in this order:

  1. It drops each parent row that has a label or tuple that the layer removes, on a dim in partial. A row that leaves the dim NULL stays.
  2. It drops each parent row that a row of the layer covers, where the layer's row sets every dim that the parent row sets.
  3. It adds the layer's rows, and one overlap row for each parent row that a row of the layer crosses.

Take partial = {"entity", "scenario"} and a root that sets p_nom for gas, wind and coal. Its child removes coal, sets gas to 60 and then sets 999 for the scenario high:

One layer folds onto its parent's owner map With partial dims entity and scenario, the parent's owner map contains the root's rows gas NULL, wind NULL and coal NULL. The child removes coal and writes gas NULL 60, NULL high 999 and gas high 999. The fold drops the root's coal row, which has the removed label, and the root's gas row, which the child's gas NULL covers. It adds the child's three rows and one overlap row, wind high, which the owner map assigns to the child, where the root's wind NULL crosses the child's NULL high. parent map p_nom entity scenario layer gas NULL root covered wind NULL root coal NULL root removed child layer p_nom, removes coal entity scenario value gas NULL 60 NULL high 999 gas high 999 owner map after the fold entity scenario layer wind NULL root gas NULL child NULL high child gas high child wind high child overlap fold drop removed, drop covered, add rows and overlaps root layer child layer overlap row dropped by the fold

The fold drops the root's coal row, which has the removed label, and the root's gas row, which the child's gas row covers. It keeps the root's wind row and adds the overlap row (wind, high), which the owner map assigns to the child. The child's own (gas, high) is a row that its WorkingRecord staged, because the second set crosses the first.

A parent row that sets fewer dims than a covering row of the layer stays as written. A child that writes only (gas, high) = 70 leaves the root's (gas, NULL) in the map. By the broadcast rule, a read takes (gas, high) from the child.

docs.title: Crossing rows
docs.text:
Two rows of two layers cross where they cover a common point and each row leaves NULL a dim that the other row sets. At such a point neither row is more specific, so the broadcast rule alone does not settle it. The fold therefore adds an overlap row, which the owner map assigns to the deeper layer, with every label that either row sets.

The fold adds an overlap row where rows of two layers cross With partial dims entity and scenario, the root writes p_nom for gas and wind with scenario NULL, and the child writes p_nom 999 for scenario high with entity NULL. The owner map has these three rows and two overlap rows that it assigns to the child, gas high and wind high. The read returns five rows: gas NULL 50, wind NULL 100, NULL high 999, gas high 999 and wind high 999. root layer p_nom entity scenario value gas NULL 50 wind NULL 100 child layer p_nom entity scenario value NULL high 999 owner map entity scenario layer gas NULL root wind NULL root NULL high child gas high child overlap wind high child overlap read p_nom entity scenario value gas NULL 50 wind NULL 100 NULL high 999 gas high 999 wind high 999 fold read root layer child layer overlap row

The child's (NULL, high) crosses both root rows, so the map gains (gas, high) and (wind, high), which it assigns to the child. At (wind, high) the overlap row sets both dims, so by the broadcast rule the value there is 999. The crossed parent rows stay as written, and (wind, low) is 100.

A later fold treats an overlap row as any other row, which it may drop, cross or remove.

docs.title: Where a row applies
docs.text:
A NULL on a dim in partial means every label of that dim's axis as resolved at the revision read. A row therefore applies to a label added below the revision that wrote it, or one staged in a WorkingRecord. In the example above, a child that adds the scenario mid has (gas, mid) at 50.

A row applies at every point that no more specific row covers, whichever layer wrote it. So a read returns a deeper layer's value only at the points its rows apply to. With p_max_pu over entity, scenario and snapshot, a root row (gas, NULL, 1) = 1.0 and a child row (NULL, high, 0) = 2.0 leave (gas, high, 1) at 1.0, from the root.

docs.title: Reading an attribute
docs.text:
record.attributes[name] returns the attribute's rows from the layers that the map assigns a key to, as written. A key left NULL stays NULL. Where the map has an overlap row, the read also returns a value at the overlap row's labels. That value comes from the layer the map assigns the overlap row to. The read expands no NULL, settles no point, and returns rows in no fixed order. An attribute that no layer wrote is an empty relation, typed as declared, and the reader applies the schema's default.

A layer may contain rows of one attribute that set different dims in partial. The child above is one: its (gas, NULL), (NULL, high) and (gas, high) all apply at (gas, high). At such a point the read keeps the layer's row that leaves no dim NULL that another row there sets. Where no row does, the read fails, naming the attribute and the point. A curve is kept or dropped whole.

See also

The record page describes RecordLike and settling rows. Why the owner map contains keys as written gives the reasons for the map's shape.

docs.title: Labels outside the key
docs.text:
A dim outside partial is in no key, so the fold reads none of its labels. The read drops each row that has a removed label on such a dim, or a removed tuple of such a multi-dim. A removed label is one that a layer's restatement dropped and the revision's axis lacks.

Take partial = {"entity"}, a root with p_max_pu for wind at snapshots 0, 1 and 2, and a child that removes snapshot 2:

A read drops a row with a removed label on a dim outside partial With partial entity alone, the root writes p_max_pu for wind at snapshots 0, 1 and 2 with 0.3, 0.8 and 0.5, and the snapshot axis 0, 1, 2. The child restates the snapshot axis as 0 and 1, which removes snapshot 2, and writes no p_max_pu file. snapshot is in no key, so the owner map assigns wind to the root. The read returns the root's rows at snapshots 0 and 1 and drops the row at snapshot 2. root layer p_max_pu entity snapshot value wind 0 0.3 wind 1 0.8 wind 2 0.5 read p_max_pu entity snapshot value wind 0 0.3 wind 1 0.8 root layer snapshot axis snapshot 0 1 2 child layer snapshot axis snapshot 0 1 read keeps the root's rows, drops snapshot 2 restate without 2 no p_max_pu file root layer child layer read removed label, dropped row

The child writes no p_max_pu file, yet the read drops the root's row at snapshot 2 and returns its other two rows.

With connection outside partial, a connection attribute's key is the attribute's name alone. Removing a tuple then removes its values at read, as it does for a multi-dim in partial at the fold.

docs.title: A dim outside partial
docs.text:
A crossing along a dim outside partial has no key column for an overlap row to set. A WorkingRecord settles such a crossing as it stages. Where a staged row leaves the dim NULL over a parent row that sets it, the commit also writes the value along the parent's labels.

A child that leaves a dim outside partial NULL is written along the parent's labels With partial dims entity alone, the root writes p_max_pu over snapshot for every entity: NULL 0 0.2 and NULL 1 0.5. The edit sets wind to 0.9 with snapshot NULL. store.commit writes the child layer as wind NULL, wind 0 and wind 1, all 0.9, so the child's rows set every dim that the root's rows set. The fold refuses a layer with the first row alone. root layer p_max_pu entity snapshot value NULL 0 0.2 NULL 1 0.5 edit set(..., entity="wind") entity snapshot value wind NULL 0.9 child layer as written entity snapshot value wind NULL 0.9 wind 0 0.9 wind 1 0.9 read wind snapshot value 0 0.9 1 0.9 commit A layer with the first row alone: the fold refuses it.

With partial = {"entity"}, the child's rows at wind set every dim that the root's rows set. Nothing crosses, and wind is 0.9 at each snapshot. The fold refuses a layer written another way that leaves such a crossing. It checks the layer when a workspace first folds it:

ValueError: layer 0f74b479-422a-4364-b29f-36758ea3105c leaves 'snapshot' NULL for 'p_max_pu' at {'entity': 'wind'} where a parent row names it; write it along the parent's 'snapshot' labels there, as `WorkingRecord.set` does

docs.title: A wider schema
docs.text:
The fold reads each layer under the schema in its own manifest. A child's schema may be wider than its parent's where the change passes compatible_with. The fold then extends the parent's map to the child's schema before it folds the child.

  • Where a dim is added to an attribute's dims, the parent's rows of that attribute broadcast along it.
  • Where a dim is added to partial, the fold splits each parent row that varies along it by the labels that its layer wrote there.
The fold splits the parent's rows by their labels when a dim joins partial The root, under partial entity, writes gas low 1 and gas high 2. The child, under partial entity and scenario, writes gas high 3. The fold splits the root's map row by the scenarios the root wrote: gas low and gas high, both assigned to the root. The child's gas high covers the second, which the fold drops. The read gives gas low 1 and gas high 3. root layer partial {entity} entity scenario value gas low 1 gas high 2 child layer partial {entity, scenario} entity scenario value gas high 3 parent map, split entity scenario layer gas low root gas high root covered read p_nom entity scenario value gas low 1 gas high 3 split fold dropped by the fold

Under partial = {"entity"}, the owner map assigns gas's scenarios whole to the root. Under the child's partial = {"entity", "scenario"}, the fold splits the root's row into (gas, low) and (gas, high), and the child's (gas, high) covers the second. The read gives (gas, low) 1 and (gas, high) 3.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
The fold computes varies, broadcast and breakpoints for each row of the map from the layer's rows of that key. An overlap row takes the flags of the layer row it comes from. record.flags() unions them per attribute:

flags() unions the owner map's flag fields per attribute The owner map contains p_max_pu for wind, which sets snapshot, p_max_pu for gas, constant over snapshot, and p_nom with entity NULL. flags() takes the union per attribute: p_max_pu varies along entity and snapshot and broadcasts along snapshot, and p_nom broadcasts along entity and scenario. owner map flag fields set to true attribute entity varies broadcast p_max_pu wind entity snapshot - p_max_pu gas entity snapshot p_nom NULL - entity scenario flags() attribute varies broadcast p_max_pu entity snapshot snapshot p_nom - entity scenario

p_max_pu has snapshot in both sets, because wind's rows set it and gas's row leaves it NULL. p_nom broadcasts along entity and scenario, the two dims it is over.

  • flags(**categories) unions the flags of the rows that apply to the labels of those categories. A row NULL on the dim applies to every label.
  • Each struct has a field for every dim the schema declares. A dim that a multi-dim draws on has its own field, so flags() reports bus as broadcast for a marginal_price constant over buses.
  • The flags describe the rows in the map. So a NULL row that deeper rows cover at every label still puts its dim in broadcast.

See also

The record page describes what a reader does with flags.

docs.title: Materialised revisions
docs.text:
To materialise a revision is to write its owner map, pointers to the files of its axes and its removed labels under layers/<id>/resolved/, with Revision.materialise(). A read of a descendant then stops at that revision and reads no layer above it.

A fold starts from the deepest proper ancestor whose fold is at hand, either materialised on disk or kept as tables by the workspace.

A fold starts from the nearest fold at hand The ancestry runs root, a, b, c, d, child. Revision a is materialised on disk, and the workspace keeps the fold of c as tables. For a record opened on child, the fold starts from c, the deepest fold at hand, and folds d and then child onto it. Root, a and b are not read. root not read a materialised b not read c fold held d parent layer child child layer the fold: seeded from c, then folds d, then child parent to child

For a record opened on child, the fold starts from c, the deepest fold at hand, and folds d and then child onto it. It reads nothing of root, a or b.

  • A read gives the same answers after you materialise, and opens fewer layers.
  • datarecord never starts a revision's fold from that revision's own cache.
  • A materialised map has keys as written, so a NULL in it applies to a label that a descendant adds.
  • A read under a wider schema extends a materialised map as it extends one folded live.

See also

The format page lists the files under resolved/. Branch and materialise shows when to call materialise().

docs.title: A directory
docs.text:
